sources.title: Pharma giants pay millions to Russian distributor entangled in corruption allegations to win cancer drug business
sources.text: Skip to content I n selling its blockbuster anticancer drug Keytruda to the Russian government, the pharmaceutical giant Merck turned to a hospital supplier with friends in high places: Alexey Repik, a now-sanctioned oligarch close to Russian President Vladimir Putin and fluent in the ways of Russia and Western business. A native of Moscow, trained as an economist, Repik started R-Pharm in 2001 after selling his car and borrowing $15,000 from his mother. Serving as an intermediary for pharmaceutical firms bidding on massive government contracts for medicine, the firm took off. In 2009, the year New Jersey-based Merck forged a strategic alliance with R-Pharm, the Russian company was expanding and soon teamed up with other Western firms and formed new lines of business. Repik amassed billions of dollars, a mansion in San Francisco and a precious collection of modern art and Japanese prints. He enjoyed high-stakes poker events at luxury casino hotels in the West, joining high-roller pros and gaining a reputation as a somewhat aggressive and unorthodox player. And he attracted scrutiny. Some in the media questioned whether insider connections to government officials helped him win contracts. Repik brushed off the question. “In the classical sense, no,” he said in a 2015 interview. “Officials and shadow leaders have never stood behind us.” R-Pharm also faced scrutiny from Russia’s Federal Antimonopoly Service, which investigated whether the firm coordinated bidding with other medicine distributors and in separate cases engaged in anticompetitive conduct designed to maintain high drug prices and influence winners. Yet R-Pharm kept growing, deepening its relationship with Merck by sharing manufacturing know-how and producing medicines jointly. Along the way, Repik became a political heavyweight. He met one-on-one with Putin, was invited to mingle with the super elite at the World Economic Forum and attended Donald Trump’s first presidential inauguration festivities in 2017. The oligarch bragged on Facebook that he was able to “check the handshake strength” of the president-elect. And news investigations later found that an offshore company linked to Repik owned a Bombardier business jet apparently used by one of Putin’s daughters. Alexey Repik’s Facebook post from the U.S. election night in 2016 shows him in a red Make America Great Again hat, giving a thumbs up. Image: via Facebook Merck wasn’t the only major Western drugmaker to partner with a politically connected Russian distributor entangled in corruption allegations. Nor was it the only one to operate in a system in which improper payments, conflicts of interest, bid rigging and inflated medicine prices were recurring public concerns. Now confidential whistleblower reports obtained by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists say that four pharmaceutical giants paid tens of millions of dollars to proxies to supply lifesaving drugs to Russian government entities as part of a corrupt system that helped keep prices high and limit access for cancer patients and others with serious ailments. The probe into the role of intermediaries in Russia’s cancer medicine infrastructure, by ICIJ, Proekt and the Swiss media outlet Republik, is part of ICIJ’s Cancer Calculus project. The series explores strategies that pharmaceutical firms use to maintain multibillion-dollar monopolies and to keep cancer drug prices high — at the expense of patients and depleted healthcare resources around the world. The new whistleblower reports say that between 2020 and 2023, the drug companies provided “excessive” bonuses to R-Pharm and other intermediaries in Russia, even as those middlemen participated in dubious bidding practices or faced scrutiny for alleged bid rigging or anticompetitive conduct. sources.title: How Beijing's Africa ambitions, financed by China's mega banks, triggered a crisis in Zambia - ICIJ
sources.text: Skip to content CHINA CAPITAL How Beijing’s Africa ambitions, financed by China’s mega banks, triggered a crisis in Zambia Chinese banking giants piled loans onto the debt-ridden country, then adopted a hardball stance when it came time to repay, documents show. By Micah Reddy Image: Ben King / ICIJ / Getty Images October 26, 2026 A s Kanangwa Newlove walked through her 10-acre farm just outside Lusaka, Zambia, one day in October 2025, she felt as if her dreams were withering away in front of her. The spinach, lettuce and mustard wilted in the heat. Tomatoes shriveled on their vines. She uprooted entire rows of organic vegetables — once sought-after by discerning customers, now rotting in the sun — and fed them to her pigs. “The crops that suffered the most without water were our mainstay,” she told a reporter for the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists. “There was nothing we could do. There was no water for the crops because there was no electricity.” Every few days, she needed nearly 8,000 gallons of water from borehole pumps to keep her farm going. The pumps required a reliable supply of electricity, but since March 2024, Zambia’s rolling blackouts had left swathes of the country without power, turning everyday tasks into Herculean struggles. Sometimes she had only four hours of power a day. The blackouts had a “cascading effect,” Newlove said. Without electricity she couldn’t refrigerate the few meager vegetables she could harvest. She stopped breeding and slaughtering animals. She was unable to sell to many of her regular customers, like local “mom and pop shops.” She had to drastically reduce the area she farmed and cut back on planting, and she couldn’t hire seasonal workers. The rolling blackouts affecting Newlove’s farm were a result of “load shedding,” scheduled power cuts meant to reduce demand on the grid. ZESCO, the state-owned power company supplying almost all of Zambia’s energy needs, alerted its customers to the load shedding schedule, but these schedules weren’t consistent or reliable, Newlove told ICIJ, making it hard to plan how to maintain — or save — her crops. “One week you’d get a schedule from, say, morning to midday and you’d make a plan based on that,” she said. “Then, without prior notice, it would change.” She couldn’t run a farm on four hours of electricity. For the first time since she’d started the farm over a decade earlier — a labor of love she launched while working for a social enterprise — she began to wonder if she’d need to shut it down. “Farmers are optimistic people until that is obliterated entirely by reality. … It’s a mammoth thing to fathom, that you’re going to kill a business that you’ve worked so hard for for so many years,” she said. Kanangwa Newlove started farming just outside Lusaka in 2012, selling organic produce to local businesses. Image: Micah Reddy / ICIJ Newlove and other small-business owners across Zambia faced collapse amid a perfect storm in which environmental and economic shocks were exacerbated by the country’s deep-seated financial problems. Zambia — where roughly 60% of the population lives in poverty — is overwhelmingly dependent on hydropower, but a severe drought in 2024 left dams empty and forced ZESCO to ration electricity usage. While Zambia is drought-prone, ZESCO’s financial woes left it uniquely ill-prepared for the drought, the worst in decades. The company was sinking financially. Among its biggest expenses was a long-term loan of nearly $285 million from the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) with tough repayment terms. The loan was signed more than a decade before, in 2011, and in the following years, ZESCO had taken on more and more debt from ICBC and other Chinese lenders. Beholden to Chinese creditors, the power utility mirrored Zambia, one of the world’s most indebted countries and the first in Africa to default on its sovereign debt during the COVID-19 pandemic. sources.title: Tax Filing: IRS Should Enhance Ghost Preparer Identification and Compliance Efforts in a Comprehensive Preparer Strategy | U.S. GAO
sources.text:
Tax Filing: IRS Should Enhance Ghost Preparer Identification and Compliance Efforts in a Comprehensive Preparer Strategy | U.S. GAO Skip to main content GAO-27-108176 Published: Oct 15, 2026. Publicly Released: Oct 16, 2026.
Ghost preparers are paid tax preparers who hide their identities on returns and avoid accountability for making errors, committing fraud, or stealing refunds. But ghost preparers are hard for IRS to identify—leaving taxpayers responsible for errors or fraud.
The IRS has started addressing this problem, but its efforts are fragmented. For example, relevant data is scattered across several databases. This makes it hard for IRS to use this information to better understand ghost preparer behavior and protect taxpayers.
IRS also doesn't have a strategy, goals, or ways to measure the success of its efforts.
Our recommendations address these issues.
A pen points to the paid preparer section of a tax return.
Ghost preparers are paid tax preparers who do not comply with requirements to identify themselves on tax returns they prepare for others. Ghost preparers may intentionally leave identifying information off to get away with filing fraudulent income tax returns, stealing taxpayers’ refunds, and stealing taxpayers’ identities. Courts have ordered individual ghost preparers to pay millions in restitution to the government, but according to Internal Revenue Service (IRS) officials, the total effect of ghost preparers is likely greater, in part, because ghost preparers are difficult to detect.
IRS maintains some data on identified ghost preparers, but the systems IRS uses to track ghost preparer cases and outcomes are not connected and have limitations that impede their usefulness. As a result, IRS does not know how many ghost preparers it has identified, investigated, and addressed. Better understanding existing data, including its limitations, would help IRS direct enforcement resources and protect taxpayers from fraudulent returns or stolen refunds.
IRS identifies and addresses ghost preparers through data analysis, referrals, taxpayer education, and enforcement actions such as investigations. However, these efforts are fragmented across six offices and IRS is missing opportunities to share information and better address risks. A comprehensive, coordinated preparer strategy, including efforts addressing ghost preparers, could help IRS better align resources with risks and identify additional needs.
Notional Example of Fragmented Activities Compared to a Comprehensive, Coordinated Strategy
While IRS has some activities to address ghost preparers, including data analysis and taxpayer education, it has not developed measurable objectives or performance goals. Defining objectives, goals, and performance measures could help IRS reliably assess whether its efforts are reducing ghost preparer activity and adjust its strategy and allocate resources more effectively.
Paid tax preparers prepared more than half of all tax returns in fiscal year 2025 and have an enormous effect on IRS’s ability to administer tax laws effectively. However, ghost preparers may hide their identities to avoid accountability and leave taxpayers responsible for inaccurate or fraudulent returns they prepare.
GAO was asked to examine IRS’s efforts to address ghost preparers. This report (1) describes how ghost preparers have harmed taxpayers and IRS, (2) assesses the extent to which IRS maintains data on ghost preparers, and (3) evaluates IRS actions to identify and address ghost preparers.
GAO reviewed federal court cases, and IRS documentation and data. GAO compared IRS’s efforts to leading practices for evidence-based policymaking and consumer education planning. GAO also interviewed IRS and Department of Justice officials and stakeholder groups, such as IRS oversight and industry groups.
GAO is making three recommendations including that IRS identify opportunities to enhance data collecting, sharing, and analysis to

sources.title: Ciara Mageean: Funeral of Olympian takes place - BBC News
sources.text:
Image source, Press Association Image caption, Ciara Mageean's funeral took place in Portaferry, County Down By Cormac Campbell BBC News NI south east reporter Published 3 November 2026, 16:20 GMT
Olympian Ciara Mageean has been described as a "truly remarkable, immensely talented and inspirational human being" in a tribute read out at her funeral.
Hundreds of people have paid their respects to the runner at her funeral on Tuesday.
The former European champion and two-time Olympic runner died on Sunday after she was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer.
Among those in attendance at the funeral in Portaferry, County Down, were Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill, as well as fellow Olympian Rhys McClenaghan and 1972 gold medallist Lady Mary Peters.
Mageean's funeral cortege was given a guard of honour by Portaferry GAC and her former school, Assumption Grammar in Ballynahinch.
Image source, Pacemaker Her death comes less than three weeks after her marriage to her long-term partner Thomas Moran.
Mourners began arriving at around midday for the 2:00 GMT requiem Mass at St Patrick's Church.
Family, friends and those wishing to pay their respects followed the funeral cortege the short distance along the Ballyphilip Road from Mageean's family home to the church.
Others in attendance included representatives for Irish President Catherine Connolly and the Irish Government, Social Democratic and Labour Party leader Claire Hanna, GAA President Jarlath Burns and former boxer Paddy Barnes.
Image source, PA Image caption, European champion Ciara Mageean died surrounded by her loved ones at the weekend
The Mass booklet included an image of Mageean's greatest achievement on the track, the moment she crossed the line at the 2024 European Championships.
In his homily, Father Martin Kelly, who knew Mageean from her childhood, spoke of her accomplishments, her love for her husband and the joy and pride she had brought to her hometown.
Kelly recalled visiting her in hospice shortly before her death, when she suggested they go for a walk.
Despite her illness, Mageean noticed he was struggling and offered to link arms with him.
"On the way down, she knew I was struggling and she said, 'Let me link you'," he told mourners.
"One of my happiest moments and memories is that of Ciara Mageean linking my arm as we walked back to her room."
The athlete represented Ireland at the 2016 and 2020 Olympics and won gold in the 1500m at the European Athletics Championships in Rome in 2024.
She also represented Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Games, winning silver in Birmingham in 2022.
Noticing blood in your poo - which may appear black or dark red in the toilet bowl - can be a sign of bowel cancer.
If there is no other obvious cause for the bleeding, such as piles, the NHS recommends that you ask for an appointment with your GP , external .
The NHS also advises a check-up if you notice changes in your regular toilet habits, such as having to poo more often, or a pattern of diarrhoea or constipation.
Abdominal pain or lumps, stomach bloating and unexplained weight loss are also among symptoms which should lead to a bowel cancer test.
Bowel cancer can also cause anaemia, the features of which include extreme tiredness and shortness of breath.
The earlier bowel cancer is detected, the easier it is to treat.

sources.title: Benetton sells 900,000 hectares of farmland to Adecoagro executives | Buenos Aires Times
sources.text:
A group of partners and executives from agricultural firm Adecoagro has acquired two businesses belonging to the Benetton family's holding company in a deal involving more than 900,000 hectares of land across four Argentine provinces.
The transaction effectively marks the end of the Italian family's 35-year presence in Argentina, where it built up a major agricultural and livestock business.
The Benettons were among Argentina's largest landowners, with holdings that placed them prominently on rankings of the country's biggest private landholders. Their vast Patagonian estates have featured in debates over land ownership and foreign investment in Argentina.
Mariano Bosch, Adecoagro's chief executive, led the acquisition of Compañía de Tierras Sud and Ganadera Cóndor, a deal that had been in the works for around a year, sources close to the transaction confirmed to the Noticias Argentinas (NA) news agency.
The purchase was made by the investors in their individual capacity, rather than by Adecoagro itself, reported NA. The agency said Agustín Dranovsky would remain on as CEO of Compañía de Tierras Sud.
The two companies operate agricultural and livestock establishments in the provinces of Buenos Aires, Río Negro, Chubut and Santa Cruz, with activities focused primarily on sheep farming, wool production and agriculture.
The Patagonian operation comprises around 250,000 sheep and produce more than 880,000 kilos of wool, according to reports. In Buenos Aires Province, the agricultural business grows potatoes, maize and wheat.
Compañía de Tierras Sud Argentino was the main vehicle through which the Benetton family developed its Argentine agricultural and livestock operations under the Edizione holding group.
The family acquired the company in 1991, when it held around 360,000 hectares across the Leleque, Maitén, Pilcaniyeu and Montoso estates in Chubut and Río Negro.
The companies have also operated in cattle farming, forestry and meat processing.
The sale comes amid Adecoagro's wider expansion. The company recently joined the Asociación de Cooperativas Argentinas (ACA) in acquiring fertiliser producer Profertil in a deal valued at US$1.2 billion.
Adecoagro was not directly involved in the Benetton transaction. Its value and terms were not disclosed, NA reported.

sources.title: A reclusive billionaire, a ‘fearless’ dealer and a globe-spanning feud over priceless art - ICIJ
sources.text: Skip to content Before everything turned sour, Russian billionaire Dmitry Rybolovlev and Swiss art world figure Yves Bouvier had a flourishing partnership. Bouvier, a self-proclaimed “fearless” wheeler-dealer, was pioneering the freeport model — a kind of free-trade zone for art, where the ultra wealthy could stash and trade expensive pieces without the art ever leaving the building. Rybolovlev, a reclusive potash mogul and art collector, was looking to expand his portfolio — and Bouvier was happy to help. For more than a decade, Bouvier worked to help Rybolovlev amass one of the world’s great art collections. Then, their relationship fell apart. Their globe-spanning, multi-billion-dollar feud is at the heart of “ The Oligarch and the Art Dealer ,” a new documentary from Danish director Andreas Dalsgaard, which dives deep into the shadowy trade in priceless masterpieces. The film explores the series of lawsuits, criminal cases (that were eventually dropped), dirty tricks-style surveillance operations, and dramatic press coverage that played out after Rybolovlev accused Bouvier of swindling at least $1 billion by lying about the purchase prices of major works and pocketing the difference. (After a drawn-out battle, Rybolovlev and Bouvier eventually settled their dispute, with the terms undisclosed.) It also draws on ICIJ’s Panama Papers investigation, which helped expose how Bouvier used a vast network of offshore companies to move billions of dollars worth of art for his many clients, including Rybolovlev. The film is showing as part of the Double Exposure Investigative Film Festival and Forum in Washington, D.C. this week. ICIJ spoke with Dalsgaard about how art has become one of the most efficient vehicles for hiding huge amounts of wealth, the challenges of documenting a billionaire oligarch, and how certain U.S. states have become magnets for dark money. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. Let’s start with the oligarch of the title of the film. You interviewed people who worked with Dmitry Rybolovlev. He’s a major part of the film, but ultimately, he’s not really there to speak for himself. What kind of character is he to you, beyond just a Russian oligarch? What was unique in this story is that he never talks – literally never. He’s made one very short interview about the AES Monaco Football Club that he owns. That’s pretty much it. The story is about the dispute between the oligarch Rybolovlev and the Swiss art dealer and freeport magnate Bouvier. And they’ve been fighting it out in courts in eight countries. They’ve had PR teams. They’ve had spies. So much has been made available to the public and to us through these court cases, everything from years of emails, years of text messages, invoices, whatnot. And to be allowed to look into a world they occupy — which is both the world of the ultra rich and the top echelon of the art market — and see how those deals were made, see how those negotiations take place, see how they communicate with each other, it’s just unique. I don’t know of any other case where that’s been so accessible. It’s very interesting to me about how art stops being art. You use the phrase “wealth laundering,” and I’m wondering what it was like visiting the Swiss freeport, where thousands of pieces of priceless art are stored but almost never seen. On one level, it’s just a warehouse. It’s a very, very dull warehouse sitting in this suburban area of Geneva, right next to the highway, close to the airport. It’s just a building. It’s got high security, sure. But it’s really just a building, and from the outside, it looks like any other building, more or less, with the fence. When you go inside, and you walk around there, then it’s still very dull. It’s just storage. The security there is pretty much on par with Fort Knox. So, on that level, it’s an extremely secure place. It’s basically still in the opaque international territory we can call offshore, which is the same thing you’re in

sources.title: Western Pharma Giants Paid Millions to Russian Distributors Linked to Fraud, Whistleblower Report Says - The Moscow Times
sources.text:
Four major Western pharmaceutical companies paid tens of millions of dollars in unusually high bonuses to Russian middlemen to supply cancer drugs to state hospitals, according to whistleblower documents submitted to U.S. financial regulators.
The payments by Merck, Eli Lilly, Novartis and AstraZeneca allegedly helped fund a corruption scheme that kept drug prices high and limited competition across Russia’s public healthcare system.
The pharmaceutical companies were alleged to have provided “excessive” sales bonuses and rebates ranging from 15% to 35% to Russian distributors, with the international average rarely exceeding 10%.
The whistleblower report and other details were laid out in a joint investigation published Monday by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ), the exiled Russian news outlet Proekt and the Swiss publication Republik.
According to the report, Merck’s Russian distributor R-Pharma won $360 million in state contracts for the cancer drug Keytruda, winning 2,400 out of nearly 5,000 bids between 2020 and 2022. Procurement data reportedly showed 96% of the bids had no competitors, allowing sanctioned oligarch Alexei Repik’s R-Pharm to maintain a virtual monopoly on Keytruda supplies to state hospitals.
R-Pharm CEO Vasily Ignatyev denied “any involvement” in improper payments or non-competitive practices, telling ICIJ that its commercial rebates were legitimate and defending Russia’s state auction procedures as transparent.
Separately, Eli Lilly was alleged to have budgeted a 34% bonus for sales of its advanced cancer drug Cyramza in 2022. The year before, Moscow’s health department awarded more than $5 million in Cyramza contracts to distributor Pharmstandard, the sole bidder for most of those contracts.
In another example, AstraZeneca’s drug Tagrisso was sold to Russian state hospitals at or above its official list price of at least $3,000 per box after single-participant bids in 95% of state tenders between 2020 and 2023. The company used distributor Pharmimex, which won $114.3 million out of nearly $129 million in state contracts for another drug, Koselugo, between 2022 and 2024 without competition.
AstraZeneca, Merck and Eli Lilly either declined to comment or did not respond to requests from ICIJ for comment.
Novartis, a Swiss multinational pharmaceutical corporation, was alleged to have identified examples of bid-rigging in government auctions for the drug Kisqali by distributors like Pharmimex and their affiliated front companies.
A Novartis representative said the company conducted an internal investigation into the allegations without disclosing its findings.
While the whistleblower reports do not contain direct financial records of bank transfers between distributors and officials, they allege that Western drugmakers were “willfully blind” to how their profit margins were being used.
U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act holds parent companies legally responsible for ignoring signs that third-party distributors are using company margins to fund kickbacks.
The SEC and the Justice Department both declined to comment on the filings to ICIJ.

“There’s going to be an agreement. It’s going to be a big agreement, and it’s going to involve more than Ukraine,” Trump said, adding that the effort could include “all of Europe”.
Trump has frequently predicted that an agreement to end Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II was close. Negotiations have, however, picked up in recent weeks.
Trump said he did not meet the Ukrainian delegation on Thursday.
The meeting between the US president and Dmitriev came after a diplomatic gathering hosted by First Lady Melania Trump, which brought Russian and Ukrainian representatives together to mark and build on the localised six-day truce she helped broker in the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky in October. The US president did not attend the event.
The temporary ceasefire ran from October 27 to November 1 and allowed for the evacuation of nearly 800 civilians from the besieged, Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region, as well as the delivery of critical food and medical supplies.
Senior officials from both countries attended on Thursday, including Dmitriev; Yana Lantratova, Russia’s human rights commissioner; David Arakhamia, leader of the Servant of the People party in Ukraine’s parliament; and Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s parliamentary human rights commissioner.
Melania Trump also spoke at the event, which the White House described as “the first time in American history that a First Lady has personally brought representatives of two nations at war to the White House for diplomacy”.
“Together, we can create something more enduring than a temporary ceasefire,” she said, urging both sides to see the humanitarian truce in Oleshky “as a spark in a world of darkness”.
The first lady presented Putin’s and Zelenskyy’s representatives with large white envelopes and asked them to deliver her personal letters to each leader. Dmitriev presented her with a painting by an 11-year-old girl, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy sent her the Order of Princess Olga, a Ukrainian award recognising her role in the ceasefire.

The [US State Department](https://www.scmp.com/topics/us-department-state?pgtype=search?module=inline&pgtype=article) said on Thursday that China National Electronic Import and Export Company, or CEIEC, and Beijing H&C Technologies had worked with Cuban arms procurement company Sociedad Mercantil Duna to supply military-related goods in 2026.

Secretary of State [Marco Rubio](https://www.scmp.com/topics/marco-rubio?pgtype=search?module=inline&pgtype=article) said Cuba’s foreign backers supplied military equipment that sustained its armed forces and enabled repression.

He also accused Havana of serving as a “staging ground for a global coalition of hostile anti-American actors to threaten, spy on, and plot against the United States and its interests”.

The Chinese embassy in Washington rejected the sanctions, saying Beijing would defend Chinese companies’ interests.

“We stand firmly against illicit unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law or the authorisation of the UN Security Council,” the embassy said in response to questions from the South China Morning Post. “We will firmly protect Chinese businesses’ legitimate and lawful rights and interests.”

CEIEC, founded in 1980 and headquartered in Beijing, is a subsidiary of state-owned China Electronics Corporation. According to its website, it works in defence and dual-use technology, public security, cybersecurity, and information technology systems.

Beijing H&C Technologies, which Washington identifies as a subsidiary of CETC International, part of China Electronics Technology Group Corporation, worked with Duna to export military equipment to Cuba, the department said.

At the centre of the crisis is Ueno Bank, which in just a few years under Peña went from an obscure digital bank to one of the country’s largest lenders, claiming to have about 60% of Paraguay’s adult population as customers. Last Monday, the central bank ordered Ueno into resolution over insolvency, freezing the deposits of 3 million customers, leaving hundreds of thousands of families without access to money for food and basic daily expenses. Bank executives were arrested, and people took to the streets in massive protests. With my heart set on Paraguay and with the conviction that our republic must always come before any person or circumstance, I have decided to submit my resignation as president of the republic,” said Peña in a video. Ueno Bank began as a finance company in the 1970s and, in 2021, was bought by Grupo Vázquez, one of Paraguay’s largest business and industrial conglomerates. At the end of 2023, it received authorisation from the central bank, already under Peña’s administration, to operate as a digital bank. The bank rapidly expanded its operations, attracting customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries and sponsoring Paraguay’s national football team. On Wednesday, the players released a letter “demanding” a “forceful response” from the government and the justice system. The bank came to manage between $800m and $850m in deposits from state and pension entities, including retirement funds, prompting criticism over conflicts of interest because of Peña’s previous shareholding ties to Ueno Holding. Peña said that, as an economist, he had merely made an “investment”, but that he had already disposed of all his shares. When the local press pointed to possible improper favouritism in directing state and pension funds to the bank, he called it a “false media campaign” aimed at weakening his government. On Wednesday, opposition lawmakers and even members of Peña’s Colorado party filed an impeachment motion holding the president responsible for the collapse. Melania Trump calls for peace at meeting with Russia, Ukraine officials | Russia-Ukraine war News | Al Jazeera Listen (2 mins) Save Share Melania Trump calls for peace at meeting with Russia, Ukraine officials on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google US First Lady Melania Trump shakes hands with Russian and Ukrainian presidential representatives at the White House in Washington, DC, on November 5, 2026 [Saul Loeb/AFP] By Al Jazeera Staff Published On 5 Nov 2026 5 Nov 2026 United States First Lady Melania Trump has urged Russia and Ukraine to build on a recent localised ceasefire and seek a more “enduring” peace, as she hosted officials from both countries at the White House. Melania Trump spoke on Thursday at an event that the White House said is believed to be “the first time in American history that a First Lady has personally brought representatives of two nations at war to the White House for diplomacy”. Those attending included Kirill Dmitriev, a special envoy of Russian President Vladimir Putin; Yana Lantratova, Russia’s human rights commissioner; David Arakhamia, leader of the Servant of the People party in Ukraine’s parliament; and Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s parliamentary human rights commissioner.
“Together, we can create something more enduring than a temporary ceasefire,” Mrs. Trump said, urging both sides to see the humanitarian truce in Oleshky “as a spark in a world of darkness”.
She said her role as “exclusive intermediary” was set out in written agreements signed by both countries, and that she was involved in every stage of the planning, including reviewing de-mining plans and evacuation routes.
Ukrainian representatives presented the US first lady with the Order of Princess Olga, first class, which President Volodymyr Zelenskyy awarded her earlier this week. She also gave the most senior officials present letters she had written to Putin and Zelenskyy.
The six-day truce covered the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region and the surrounding area, and allowed aid deliveries and the evacuation of nearly 800 people.
An estimated 2,000 civilians had been left in the city. It was the longest multi-day truce between Russia and Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, and the first joint relief operation in four years and eight months.
The White House said Melania Trump mediated the truce, though Pope Leo XIV also pressed both sides to allow aid and evacuations, and that the two accounts of who brokered it have diverged.
The truce expired last Sunday with no extension, a day before a Russian bombing of an aid distribution point in Komyshuvakha, in the Zaporizhia region, killed at least 40 people, according to Ukrainian President Zelenskyy.
New US-brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine are expected to take place in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11.

sources.title: Tankers carrying Russian diesel to the US change course
sources.text:
Tankers carrying Russian diesel to the US change course Skip to content
In October, Trump said 300,000 metric tons of Russian diesel would be released to global markets Image: Yoruk Isik/REUTERS Advertisement Several sanctioned tankers headed for the US carrying Russian diesel are said to have changed course, one toward Brazil and the other into the Mediterranean, according to data from marine data company Kpler and vessel traffic site MarineTraffic.com.
The tankers reportedly departed from the Baltic Sea port of Primorsk last month and had declared their destinations as the US east coast.
This all comes after US President Donald Trump eased sanctions on Russian oil last month , in a deal with with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to secure a large amount of diesel directly to the US at a time when diesel prices have skyrocketed across the country.
The agreement caused shock and drew criticism in Ukraine and Europe. But it also was a logistical challenge, given that sanctions against Russia still remain in place.
It was also widely reported at the time that the amount of diesel in question was a fraction of the US daily demand.
UK newspaper The Financial Times (FT) reported Wednesday that two of the tankers appeared to have changed their destination and were no longer headed to the United States.
Russian envoy and negotiator Kirill Dmitriev said on Thursday that the US-bound diesel tankers were still on course.
"Fake. Tankers destined for the US continue on course," Dmitriev said on X, linking to the FT story.
Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov said detail of shipments were a "commercial" matter that could not be made public.
"All diesel will find its buyers," he added, without elaborating.
A third vessel was still in the North Atlantic headed toward the US but changed its destination from New York to a vague "for orders," without listing an unloading point.
Can Trump’s diesel deal bring down US fuel prices?
Despite the fact that the US Treasury Department temporarily authorized Russian diesel transactions, New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill warned port and terminal operators to turn away ships carrying the fuel.
In a letter earlier this week, she warned that "any effort to profit from the illegal trade in Russian fuel will be met with harsh penalties.”
Sherrill accused the Trump administration of lacking authority in overriding the import ban enacted by Congress more than four years ago.
She said New Jersey would act to prevent state facilities and companies from handling Russian fuel.
In a letter dated October 27, Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal warned shipping companies against violating US sanctions forbidding imports of Russian fuel.
"No president can unilaterally override a statute. Trump's license will not absolve you of legal and moral accountability," the letter read.

sources.title: Russian strikes leave 600,000 in the dark in eastern Ukraine – POLITICO
sources.text:
Russian attacks on Ukraine’s power grid on Saturday left more than 600,000 without electricity in the Dnipropetrovsk region in southeast Ukraine, electricity provider DTEK said on social media.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday morning denounced “an overnight attack on the Dnipro region” that left energy infrastructure damages, also pointing out wider attacks across the country.
“There are widespread power outages across the country … Repair work is underway in virtually every affected city and community.”
“Power company workers are already working to restore electricity. Their efforts are being hampered by constant Russian shelling,” said the region’s governor Oleksandr Hanzha, adding that hospitals and critical infrastructure are now relying on generators for power.
The blackout follows shelling in the region on Nov. 3 that damaged infrastructure in a key industrial region bordering active combat areas, and a wider attack the same day across Ukraine targeting energy facilities.
The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant also lost power overnight, with the International Atomic Energy Agency saying on Sunday morning it is now relying “on emergency diesel generators for reactor cooling and other essential nuclear safety and security functions.”
The attack comes as Kyiv and Moscow gear up for another round of US-brokered peace talks in Abu Dhabi next week. Following the new wave of attacks on Saturday night Zelenskyy called on international partners to ramp up sanctions on Russia to hamper its capability to acquire or build more missiles.
“It is very important that they be synchronized across Europe and G7 jurisdictions. If the world does not have enough anti-ballistic capabilities to protect Ukrainian skies, then the missiles must be stopped on the production lines,” he said.

Artificial intelligence models will soon be powerful enough to master biology, presenting both benefits and serious risks, Tencent Holdings’ chief AI scientist and former OpenAI star researcher Vinces Yao Shunyu said during a rare public appearance on Saturday.

The assessment comes as frontier AI systems are increasingly being applied to medicine and biology, which could [accelerate discovery of new drugs](https://www.scmp.com/business/china-business/article/3360395/chinas-drug-industry-pivots-ai-powered-candidates-drive-next-wave-deals?module=inline&pgtype=article) and other treatments. However, experts also warn that malicious actors could use AI to produce bioweapons or potentially start the next pandemic, especially if they are released as open-weight software.

“The cyber abilities of [AI] models and soon [the] bio ability of models will reach a threshold where it’s actually possible to do harm,” Yao said at a science symposium co-hosted by the Hong Kong Academy of Sciences and the Future Science Prize.

sources.text:
URL Source: https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/health-environment/article/3373668/cant-be-inaccurate-how-two-tiny-robot-arms-could-halve-digestive-cancer-surgery-time

Markdown Content:
_In the final instalment of a four-part Health Matters wellness series on frontier medicine in Hong Kong, Elizabeth Cheung examines a dual-arm surgical robot that could remove gastrointestinal tumours in about half the usual time, and the hurdles between its first human trials and wider patient access._

Ho Man-wai underwent a colonoscopy in late August, during which doctors identified three polyps that needed to be removed before they could develop into cancer.

Two were removed during the initial examination, but the third was more deeply rooted and required a more complex procedure.

Ho, a 52-year-old property management worker, returned to hospital in September for an endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD), a technique used to remove larger or more difficult polyps through an endoscope.

His polyp was relatively small, so the procedure took about an hour and Ho was discharged the following day.

But removing a polyp or a lesion measuring 3cm (1.2 inches) to 4cm can take up to two hours, according to Professor Philip Chiu Wai-yan, dean of medicine at the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), who performed Ho’s procedure.

A new surgical device, developed under Chiu’s leadership, could cut the operating time for lesions of a similar size by half, to an average of 49 minutes.

Chiu, an internationally renowned surgeon, performed the world’s first robotic ESD in the stomach in 2011 and the world’s first such procedure in the colorectum in 2020.

[Video 5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kw_ohPAO_Zc)

CUHK team demonstrates new EndoR Surgical System

The new device, known as the EndoR Surgical System, is designed to carry out the procedure more quickly and safely. It primarily targets patients with early-stage gastrointestinal cancers, or those with polyps that are difficult to remove.

The system consists of a long, thin tube that enters the body through a natural orifice, such as the anus or mouth, and performs surgery inside the gastrointestinal tract without making any incisions.

At present, it is the world’s only surgical robotic system equipped with two arms that can work throughout the entire gastrointestinal tract, and it has entered clinical trials.

Other surgical robots that enter through the body’s natural openings may not be able to reach some parts of the gastrointestinal system.

Chiu said the system’s robotic arms were what set it apart.

“The EndoR has two robot arms and they are really small,” Chiu said. “They have to perform this dissection with one arm for traction, the other arm is for dissection.”

The two arms, fitted with knife tips measuring just 1.5mm to 2mm, are housed inside the long, thin tube that also contains an endoscopic camera. The device enters the body and navigates the tortuous pathways of the gastrointestinal tract, sometimes travelling 70cm to 80cm from the entry point to reach the lesion.

The surgeon controls the robotic arms using two hand controls at a console.

Chiu said such precise, delicate arms were necessary because early-stage tumours were usually located in the mucosa, the innermost layer of the gastrointestinal tract.

To remove a tumour thoroughly, doctors must cut through the layer beneath it, known as the submucosa.

The procedure allowed doctors to remove cancerous cells while preserving the patient’s organ, helping to maintain their quality of life, Chiu said.

ESD was first developed in Japan in the late 1990s, but the procedure can be lengthy because the endoscopic camera and knife are attached to the same instrument in the earlier generation of devices.

People walk in front of garages destroyed in a Russian missile strike on Vyshhorod, Kyiv region, Ukraine, Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. (AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka)
PARIS: Europe will be represented at upcoming United States-mediated talks with Moscow and Kyiv in Abu Dhabi aimed at ending the Ukraine war , France said Sunday (Nov 8).
"The Europeans will be represented and France will be in Abu Dhabi to participate in these talks," French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told RTL radio.
His comment came after President Donald Trump stoked fears of a US pivot toward the Kremlin by predicting a "very big" deal with Russia involving not only the Ukraine war but "all of Europe".
Up to now, the talks scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday had been framed as a trilateral format at the level of officials, not leaders, from Ukraine, Russia and the United States.

Barrot said that, in the past, "there have been discussions, sometimes without the Europeans and sometimes with" but "this time they will participate".

On Thursday, US, European, Ukrainian and North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) officials met in Brussels ahead of the Abu Dhabi talks.
A NATO spokeswoman said they "sought to advance a just and sustainable end to the war in Ukraine".
Jared Kushner, the US president's envoy and son-in-law, participated in the Brussels meeting by video link. He said the UnS was working on "a broader European security architecture that can help establish the conditions for lasting peace".
The American approach is being treated warily by European allies, which have long rejected Moscow's desire to rewrite the European security architecture.
Before launching the war in Ukraine in 2022, the Kremlin delivered an ultimatum to NATO which included a demand that the alliance's troops be withdrawn from eastern Europe.
That was rejected by the Western military alliance.
Kushner on Thursday said that Washington will "consult closely with our European partners on the sidelines" of the Abu Dhabi talks and "if progress is made, aim to move toward a broader multilateral format with their direct participation".

sources.title: Rosstat hack: data obtained suggests over 390,000 Russian deaths in Ukraine war | Euronews
sources.text: Advertisement By&nbsp Euronews Russian Published on 8 November 2026 - 18:04 GMT+1 Share Comments Add Euronews on Google Share Facebook Twitter Flipboard Send Reddit Linkedin Messenger Telegram VK Bluesky Threads Whatsapp Hacker groups Cyberpartisans BY and Silent Crow say they hacked Rosstat and counted Russian losses since the invasion of Ukraine. Their tally: between 393,000 and 450,000 killed. The hacker groups Kiberpartizany BY and Silent Crow claim to have carried out a large-scale breach of Russia's Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat). ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT According to the hackers, they managed to steal about 23 terabytes of data, including internal documents, demographic and economic statistics, as well as information on Russian losses in the war against Ukraine. The data obtained enabled the groups to make their own calculations of the number of people killed since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. According to Kiberpartizany BY, as of 27 August 2026 at least 393,881 Russian citizens have been killed in the war. Silent Crow gives an even higher figure of 450,100 dead. This significant difference in estimates is due to the use of different methods of counting losses. Kiberpartizany BY counted deaths in which military action or its consequences were listed as the cause. Silent Crow, by contrast, not only included those killed in combat, but also added several other categories of deaths: non-combat losses among military personnel, deaths marked as terrorist acts, and deaths of people registered in Russia but who died in occupied territories or in Ukraine where the exact cause of death was not established. Why these figures are particularly important Russia has not released official statistics on combat losses since September 2022. In addition, from 2024 Rosstat stopped publishing annual data on causes of death, which has made an independent assessment of the demographic impact of the war much more difficult. Against this backdrop, access to the agency's internal statistical materials may make it possible to assess the scale of human losses more accurately. For comparison, as of 8 November the joint database of BBC News Russian Service and Mediazona, which collects a list of dead Russian servicemen identified by name, contained around 286,000 names. However, this list is known to be incomplete, especially for the most recent months of the war. In a joint study by Meduza and Mediazona, based on analysis of inheritance registry data, the number of fallen Russian servicemen by the end of 2025 was estimated at roughly 350,000. In this way, the hackers' estimates are in line with figures from previously published independent studies, although this does not yet prove the accuracy of each individual number. Verifying the authenticity of the data Meduza and Mediazona have said they obtained access to the data published by the hackers and have begun checking it. The journalists aim to establish not only whether the materials are authentic, but also how complete the information is they contain. In particular, they need to rule out the possibility of deliberate data falsification. Moreover, causes of death given in medical documents do not always reflect the actual circumstances of a person's death. It should also be noted that Rosstat's internal databases do not contain up-to-date information on people listed as missing. Such individuals may be declared dead only after a long period of time. Therefore even data from the state statistics agency cannot automatically provide a definitive figure for Russian military losses. If the authenticity and completeness of the leak are confirmed, the materials obtained could become one of the largest sources of information on the demographic consequences of the war for Russia. Ukraine: Russian strikes hit Kyiv region, damaging infrastructure
Footage released by Ukraine's emergency services shows crews directing powerful jets of water towards burning industrial structures, with firefighters working among the wreckage as flames spread through the site. The attacks also damaged energy facilities and a major bridge in Kyiv. In the capital, a kindergarten was left severely damaged, with a large crater in its grounds, shattered walls and children's toys scattered among the rubble. Workers began clearing debris from the destroyed building, while nearby residents inspected the damage. Five people were reported wounded in the strikes. The latest attacks come as Ukraine prepares for another difficult winter, with its energy infrastructure repeatedly targeted by Russian forces. Damage to power facilities threatens to disrupt electricity and heating supplies as temperatures fall, placing further pressure on an already strained network. The renewed bombardment also comes amid diplomatic efforts to bring the war to an end, with talks involving Ukraine, Russia and the United States under discussion. Despite these initiatives, strikes on civilian areas and critical infrastructure continue, highlighting the challenges facing Ukrainians as the conflict enters another winter.

sources.text: Advertisement By&nbsp Nathan Rennolds Published on 8 November 2026 - 15:48 GMT+1 • Updated 15:51 Share Comments Add Euronews on Google Share Facebook Twitter Flipboard Send Reddit Linkedin Messenger Telegram VK Bluesky Threads Whatsapp Zelenskyy said Russia had launched a drone strike on the site of a recent attack on Komyshuvakha, where rescuers have been carrying out search operations following a bombing that killed at least 55 people on Monday. Russian strikes on Ukraine overnight reportedly left more than 850,000 people without power across the country. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Ukrainian energy firm DTEK said Russian forces had launched a "massive attack" on Ukraine's energy sector, targeting key facilities in the eastern Dnipropetrovsk region. "Over 600,000 residents of the region in the Pavlohrad, Samar, Kamianske and Dnipro districts, as well as in the city of Dnipro itself, have been left without power," the company said. Power is gradually being restored in the region, authorities later announced. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy added that there were widespread power outages across the nation, including in Kharkiv Oblast in the northeast and the Zhytomyr region in the northwest, where he said 140 apartment buildings were without heating following a Russian strike. Local authorities in Kharkiv reported that around 250,000 customers in the region had been left without power but that it had since been restored. Russia has once again begun to ramp up attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure as winter draws nearer, capitalising on Kyiv's shortage of interceptor missiles as it seeks to break Ukraine's resistance. Over the past week, Zelenskyy said Russian forces have fired 115 missiles, almost 1,900 guided aerial bombs, and more than 3,000 attack drones against Ukraine. Komyshuvakha On Sunday morning, Zelenskyy said Russia had also launched a drone strike on the site of a recent attack on Komyshuvakha, where rescuers have been carrying out search operations following a bombing that killed at least 55 people on Monday. "Unfortunately, more people may still be under the rubble. Absolute cynicism and brutality," the Ukrainian leader wrote on X. Ukraine's State Emergency Service said Russia had "deliberately attacked" emergency service workers at the site but that no one had been injured. The Monday strikes, which hit a school Kyiv said was used for humanitarian purposes, followed a rare localised truce between Kyiv and Moscow that had allowed evacuees to leave the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine's southern Kherson region. One person was also killed and three others were injured in a strike on a residential area of Dnipro on Sunday, per Oleksandr Hanzha, the head of the regional military administration. "A fire has broken out. At least one private house has been destroyed. It is believed that people may be trapped under the rubble," he said. Zelenskyy has accused the Kremlin of intensifying attacks in a bid to put additional pressure on Ukraine's negotiating position ahead of planned trilateral talks between Kyiv, Moscow and Washington in Abu Dhabi. sources.title: Keytruda After Kidney Cancer Surgery Lowers Risk of Death by 30% | CURE
sources.text:
Keytruda After Kidney Cancer Surgery Lowers Risk of Death by 30%
Final KEYNOTE-564 data show Keytruda after kidney cancer surgery lowered the risk of death by 30%. Dr. Toni Choueiri explains what it means for patients.
Receiving Keytruda (pembrolizumab) after surgery for kidney cancer continued to help patients live longer and lowered the chance of their cancer coming back, according to the final analysis of the phase 3 KEYNOTE-564 trial presented at the 2026 ESMO Congress.
The trial included 994 patients with clear cell renal cell carcinoma at increased risk of recurrence after surgery to remove the kidney. After a median follow-up of about seven years, patients who received Keytruda had a 30% lower risk of death than those who received placebo. At seven years, 82.3% of patients who received Keytruda were alive, compared with 76.6% of those who received placebo. Keytruda also lowered the risk of the cancer coming back or death by 32%.
Keytruda, an immunotherapy that helps the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells, was approved by the Food and Drug Administration in 2021 for this use. Treatment is given as an infusion every three weeks for up to about one year. No new safety concerns were identified with longer follow-up.
In an interview with CURE, Dr. Toni K. Choueiri, [title — verify], Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, explained what these findings mean for patients.
Choueiri: In an unselected population, because we do not have a biomarker yet despite our 20 years of shots on goal, [there are] patients who have a chance that the cancer comes back after [removing] the kidney because of micrometastatic disease that we cannot detect. Pembrolizumab will allow [these] patients to live longer by 30% and reduce the chance of the cancer coming back.
It’s not for everyone. We don’t know who it’s for, because surgery sometimes can cure patients alone. But with pembrolizumab, the chances of that cure are higher.

sources.title: Sac-TMT Plus Keytruda Improves Outcomes in PD-L1-Negative Lung Cancer | CURE
sources.text: Sac-TMT Plus Keytruda Improves Outcomes in PD-L1-Negative Lung Cancer | CURE Advertisement News | Articles | November 4, 2026 Sac-TMT Plus Keytruda Improves Outcomes in PD-L1-Negative Lung Cancer Fact checked by: Kaitlyn M. Le Patients with PD-L1-negative non-small cell lung cancer experienced longer progression-free survival with sac-TMT plus Keytruda compared with chemotherapy plus Keytruda in a phase 3 trial. Advertisement Patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who received sacituzumab tirumotecan (sac-TMT) plus Keytruda (pembrolizumab) had longer progression-free survival than those receiving chemotherapy plus Keytruda, according to findings from the phase 3 OptiTROP-Lung06 trial. The study, published in The New England Journal of Medicine , found that median progression-free survival was 15 months with sac-TMT plus Keytruda compared with 5.7 months with chemotherapy plus Keytruda. Progression-free survival refers to the length of time patients live without their cancer worsening or death from any cause. The combination reduced the relative risk of disease progression or death by 51%. However, overall survival data were not yet mature, meaning researchers have not determined whether the combination helps patients live longer overall. How Did Sac-TMT Plus Keytruda Affect Cancer Progression? The trial included 455 patients with previously untreated, locally advanced or metastatic nonsquamous NSCLC. All patients had PD-L1-negative tumors, meaning fewer than 1% of their tumor cells expressed PD-L1, and lacked targetable genomic alterations. PD-L1 is a protein that can help cancer cells avoid detection by the immune system. Patients with PD-L1-negative tumors may be less likely to benefit from immunotherapy alone. Chemotherapy plus Keytruda is a commonly used first-line treatment for these patients. Researchers evaluated whether replacing chemotherapy with sac-TMT, an antibody-drug conjugate designed to deliver cancer-fighting medication to cells expressing the protein TROP2, could improve outcomes. Of the patients enrolled, 229 received sac-TMT plus Keytruda and 226 received chemotherapy plus Keytruda. astro-island:empty]:hidden [&:has(>astro-island:empty)+*]:-mt-8"> After a median follow-up of 9.7 months, patients receiving sac-TMT plus Keytruda experienced significantly longer progression-free survival compared with those receiving chemotherapy plus Keytruda. How Long Did Patients Respond to Treatment? Researchers also evaluated the percentage of patients whose tumors shrank or disappeared following treatment and how long those responses lasted. Tumor responses occurred in 50.2% of patients receiving sac-TMT plus Keytruda compared with 47.3% receiving chemotherapy plus Keytruda. Among patients whose tumors responded to treatment, the median duration of response was 13.6 months with sac-TMT plus Keytruda compared with 6.8 months with chemotherapy plus Keytruda. Duration of response refers to the length of time a tumor continues responding to treatment before the cancer progresses. What Side Effects Were Reported? Grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 47.6% of patients receiving sac-TMT plus Keytruda compared with 60.6% receiving chemotherapy plus Keytruda. Anemia, or a low red blood cell count, was the most commonly reported adverse event in both groups, occurring in 82.5% and 84.5% of patients, respectively. However, stomatitis, which can cause inflammation and sores in the mouth, occurred more frequently among patients receiving sac-TMT plus Keytruda (51.1%) compared with chemotherapy plus Keytruda (8.4%). The assessment, seen by Reuters, offers an insight into how external actors have been exploiting France's domestic turmoil for their ⁠own political ends. Issued on: 09/11/2026 - 16:38 4 min Reading time Share By: FRANCE 24 Protesters react among tear gas during a demonstration in Paris, France, on November 7, 2026. © Stephanie Lecocq, Reuters A covert Russian network sought to exploit ​last month's riots in France by using social media to blame the unrest on uncontrolled immigration and portray the government as having lost control, according to an internal EU assessment seen by Reuters. A separate internal assessment – compiled by France's foreign ministry and also seen by Reuters – found that social media accounts linked to Israel and to the US MAGA movement also pushed "hostile narratives" around ​the riots, linking them ‌to radical Islamism and migration. Taken together, the assessments offer insight into how external actors have been trying to use France's domestic turmoil for their ⁠own political ends, according to analysis by European disinformation specialists. The European Union analysis found that a covert Russian network known as "Operation Overload" spread videos impersonating Western media outlets to target French audiences – some falsely claiming migrants had raped protesters or terrorist attacks were imminent. The Russian foreign ‌ministry did not respond to a request for comment. In August, ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova rejected allegations by a French state watchdog agency of spreading ⁠disinformation about France's 2027 elections and said they would "not be the last concoction which the authorities will use to manipulate public opinion". Rioting erupted in cities across France last month as demonstrations against rising living costs and declining public services spiralled out of control in some of the worst violence the country had witnessed for ​decades. sources.text:
Advertisement By&nbsp Serguei Doubine &nbsp&&nbsp Euronews Russian Published on 9 November 2026 - 17:28 GMT+1 Share Comments Add Euronews on Google Share Facebook Twitter Flipboard Send Reddit Linkedin Messenger Telegram VK Bluesky Threads Whatsapp The IIHF has moved Norway, ranked 10th, to Division 1A to free a place for Russia at the tournament in Alberta, after the Court of Arbitration for Sport ordered Russian teams reinstated. The change is not yet confirmed, and Russia has not been guaranteed Canadian visas. Norway's junior ice hockey team has been dropped from the World Junior Championship in Canada to make room for Russia, following a Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling ordering Russian teams to be reinstated in international competition. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Norway, which ranked 10th, has been moved to Division 1A to free a place for Russia at the tournament, which runs from 26 December to 5 January in Alberta. Tickets for the event, including for Norway's matches, are already on sale. The International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) has yet to formally confirm the change. Norway remained listed as a participant on the IIHF website on Monday. Russia's participation is also uncertain. The Russian team has not been guaranteed visas to enter Canada, which could restore Norway's place. "The situation is still unclear," Norwegian Ice Hockey Federation general secretary Petter Salsten said in a statement. "That gives us hope that the question of our participation in the tournament in Canada has not yet been finally settled." Related Hockey nations refuse to play Russia as Germany weighs pulling out as host
Salsten said the federation disagrees with the CAS ruling but is obliged to comply. He added that the situation "clearly illustrates all the practical difficulties and immediate consequences for everyone involved if countries are immediately reinstated in full."
The IIHF has flagged serious problems with scheduling, participant safety and tournament logistics that Russia's potential return would create.
Six countries, including Norway, have pledged to boycott matches against Russia for as long as the war in Ukraine continues. Several long-standing corporate sponsors of ice hockey have also said they will withdraw support if Russia is allowed to compete.
The CAS ruling covers five world championships in 2027, including the senior men's tournament scheduled for May in Germany.
Ukraine, which qualified for the senior men's championship for the first time since 2007, could be displaced if Russia is reinstated, as the lowest-ranked team would have to give way.
The German government said on Friday that holding the championship in Germany with Russia participating was "virtually impossible," following consultations with the IIHF, the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) and the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB).
DEB chief executive Frank Lutz has said Germany may consider relinquishing its hosting rights.
Russia has been suspended from international ice hockey following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022. At its last world championship in 2021, the Russian team finished fourth.

sources.title: Russia: Independent Novaya Gazeta shuts its Moscow newsroom
sources.text:
Russia: Independent Novaya Gazeta shuts its Moscow newsroom Skip to content
Launched in 1993, Novaya Gazeta often took on Russia's criminal and political elites Image: AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement The Novaya Gazeta newspaper closed its Moscow office on Monday, saying it was not able to continue reporting amid a campaign of state pressure in Russia .
The investigative outlet, co-founded by late USSR chief Mikhail Gorbachev, had long been a thorn in the Kremlin's side. In recent years, it ran into increasing roadblocks amid its critical coverage of the Russian invasion of Ukraine .
It was branded a "foreign agent," a Soviet-era term resuscitated by President Vladimir Putin 's administration, with officials ordering it to vacate its Moscow offices.
Russian banks were also forbidden from processing donations from readers and supporters. The paper had been heavily dependent on this income stream after moving wholly into online publishing, with the transition taking place shortly after the invasion of Ukraine. Russian authorities introduced new wartime censorship rules in the wake of the full-scale invasion.
Nobel Prize winner Muratov calls for free speech
2021 Nobel Peace Prize -winning founding editor Dmitry Muratov issued an appeal for free speech in wartime Russia as journalists gathered in the Novaya Gazeta offices to witness its closure.
"Those in our country who advocate for peace have been denied the right to read what they choose, as we see happening today," he said. "We are currently at a point where the section of the Russian constitution that guarantees political and civil rights has ceased to function."
Russia's government meanwhile sought to play down the significance of the closure, with Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying it was part of a "rotational process" in a fiercely competitive media landscape.
Novaya Gazeta was a flagship for post-Soviet democratic Russia and the era of "glasnost" or openness, also launched by Mikhail Gorbachev. The reformist Soviet leader used some of the prize fund for his 1990 Nobel Peace Prize as seed money for the publication.
The paper has built a reputation for fearless reporting, which has also put it in the crosshairs of Russia's wealthy and powerful. Six of its journalists were murdered since the paper was launched in 1993.
They included Anna Politkovskaya , who spent years investigating allegations of abuses by Russia's military during its campaigns in Chechnya. An early critic of Putin, she was found dead in her apartment bloc on the president's birthday in 2006.
Images published in Russian media on Monday showed the paper's editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, taking down photographs of Polikovskaya and other reporters murdered in what's thought to be retribution for their work.
Last month, when first announcing that the paper would close, Sokolov said the outlet had "been killed." The paper was shutting down after "the Russian authorities — the Russian special services — have forced the editorial team to end its work," he said.
Will closure in Moscow mark a definitive end?
Muratov called for a ceasefire in Ukraine and urged foreign observers to remember the strength of dissent that endured in Russia, even if it was being pushed underground by censorship laws and other repression or intimidation.
"We canot blame the citizens themselves for this," Muratov said, "especially the wonderful, truly remarkable younger generation."
"I urge you to distinguish between the Russian authorities and the Russian people," he added.
Muratov also called for the release of around 4,000 people he termed political prisoners in Russia.
Novaya Gazeta 's leadership has not made it entirely clear whether its closing down in Moscow marks a defeinitive end to the outlet's reporting, or whether they might perhaps seek to regroup and begin operating in some form from outisde Russia , as several other publications including DW have been forced to in recent years.

sources.title: New trilateral talks on Ukraine war: What to expect?
sources.text:
New trilateral talks on Ukraine war: What to expect? Skip to content
Observers don't expect quick progress from the fresh talks Image: Dmytro Smolienko/Avalon/Photoshot/picture alliance Advertisement A new round of trilateral talks between Russia , Ukraine and the United States are scheduled to take place in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, months after a flurry of US-mediated peace talks earlier this year in January and February went nowhere .
When announcing the new trilateral talks last week, US special envoy Steve Witkoff said the discussions would focus on "post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has named security guarantees, an energy ceasefire, unblocking the Black Sea, extended prisoner exchanges, and preparations for a meeting of the leaders of Ukraine, the United States and Russia as his key topics.
Lawmaker Davyd Arakhamia, a member of Ukraine's delegation, told DW he was not expecting quick progress.
"I don't think there will be a breakthrough, after there was such a long break in the negotiation process," he said. "Simply the fact that trilateral talks are being resumed can be counted as a success."
Witkoff will be joined by US President Donald Trump 's son-in-law, real estate developer Jared Kushner, who serves as special envoy.
The Kremlin has sent Vladimir Medinsky, an aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin , to act as chief negotiator, along with a delegation including high-ranking Russian military and intelligence officials.
The Ukrainian delegation will be led by Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, along with Arakhamia, and diplomatic and military officials.
Separate formats are planned with several European representatives.
These include Günter Sautter, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's foreign and security policy adviser, Emmanuel Bonne, head of the Elysee Palace's diplomatic service and Jonathan Powell, the UK's national security advisor, and Fabrizio Saggio, diplomatic adviser to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.
Björn Seibert, Chief of Staff for the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and Geoffrey van Leeuwen, Chief of Staff for NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, will also attend.
It's doubtful, however, whether European representatives will be formally involved in talks on a potential peace deal.
Hanna Shelest, a security studies director at the foreign policy network Ukrainian Prism, told DW she believed they'd play "an observing role, at best."
She added that, until now, Russia had been reluctant to have European representatives at the table to uphold the impression that talks were "a matter between two superpowers" — namely, Russia and the United States — and to increase pressure on Washington.
"I doubt the Russian delegation will let the Europeans have a say," she told DW.
"Experience from the past years has taught us that as soon as Medinsky heads negotiations, the point becomes demonstrating to the US that Russia is willing to talk, but in reality, they won't reach an agreement," she explained. "Instead, there will be a long sermon about history and all sorts of other things."
However, she said Moscow sending high-ranking intelligence officers as part of the delegation was a "fairly positive aspect" of Russia's intentions.
She believed that additional negotiations were possible at this level.
This could include over prisoner exchanges or humanitarian pauses in villages near Oleshky, a town in the Russian occupied Kherson region in Ukraine's south, where US First Lady Melania Trump was credited with arranging a temporary truce in late October that secured humanitarian aid and allowed civilians to evacuate.
But despite these "positive signals," Shelest cautioned against hoping for concrete results, and suspected Russia was using the talks to stall.

sources.text:
Nvidia shareholders sue Jensen Huang over alleged spy ties Skip to content
Huang led Nvidia's transformation from a gaming chipmaker into a central supplier of AI technology (FILE: 21/10/2026) Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Shareholders sued chipmaker Nvidia and its chief executive, Jensen Huang, on Monday, accusing them of concealing his alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset .
The proposed class action adds to investigations into whether Huang was targeted by foreign intelligence, raising questions about the security of sensitive information at the world's most valuable chipmaker.
The complaint, filed in federal court in San Jose, California, alleges that Nvidia and Huang misled investors about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who is not related to him.
Shareholders say the defendants failed to disclose national security concerns that threatened Nvidia's reputation and business prospects. They are seeking unspecified damages.
The New York Times reported last month on the alleged relationship and said US authorities had concluded that Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset.
Nvidia announced an independent investigation Sunday into reports that Huang had been the "target of a foreign intelligence effort."
Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in an open letter, but did not identify the woman.
Nvidia investigates CEO after reports of affair with Chinese spy
"I support the investigation and will cooperate fully," he said. "I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security."
Nvidia shares closed down 4.3% Monday. The lawsuit was filed five minutes after US markets closed.
How have Washington and Beijing responded?
US President Donald Trump said Monday that the FBI was investigating the matter, while expressing support for Huang.
Trump said he had spoken to the executive earlier that day.
"He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy," Trump told reporters.
China denied conducting an intelligence operation targeting Huang.
"The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.
Why does the case matter for the AI industry?
Huang co-founded Nvidia and led its transformation from a maker of gaming chips into a leading supplier of the computing technology powering artificial intelligence .
Its advanced chips have become a focus of US-China competition, with Washington restricting exports to limit Beijing's access to the technology.
Huang has pushed for looser restrictions on sales to China. The investigations have intensified scrutiny of his leadership and whether confidential company information was compromised.

Russian and Ukrainian officials met on Tuesday for their first US-brokered talks since February, after President Donald Trump suggested last week that a broad deal was possible on ending the war in Ukraine and guaranteeing security in Europe.

Russian state news agency RIA reported the start of what is scheduled to be two days of talks, in which Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are to mediate between the two ‌warring sides.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, and with Russian forces holding about a fifth of the country, Moscow and Kyiv remain far apart – despite Trump’s optimism – on terms for a possible settlement.

The new American drive for a deal has galvanised European officials into pushing for a place at the table to seek an end to the continent’s deadliest conflict since World War II.

![Image 1: United Arab Emirates Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan (R) speaks to United States envoy Jared Kushner during trilateral talks between Russia and Ukraine mediated by the US in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday. “We are doing everything to ensure that Europe is a participant in ⁠the diplomatic process,” Umerov said before the meeting.

France said there could be no lasting peace in Ukraine without addressing European security, and that this required the involvement of the ‌Europeans.

Russia had made clear it did not see a place for Europeans at the meeting with the Ukrainians and Americans.

![Image 2: Representatives of the US, Ukraine and EU member states hold consultations ahead of trilateral negotiations involving Ukraine, the US and Russia in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday. Photo: EPA](https://img.i-scmp.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=contain,width=1024,format=auto/sites/default/files/d8/images/canvas/2026/11/10/7ee6f813-3ffe-4653-9e34-dac74dda9eaf_32afda76.jpg)

Representatives of the US, Ukraine and EU member states hold consultations ahead of trilateral negotiations involving Ukraine, the US and Russia in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday. Photo: EPA

On the eve of the talks, Trump said Washington was seeing a “very strong inclination” towards ending the ‌war, and that both sides were “tired of fighting”.

After meeting privately with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s envoy last week at the White House, Trump predicted ⁠that a peace deal could emerge ⁠soon.

Trump has frequently said an agreement to end Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II was close, without a deal emerging.

However, negotiations have picked up again in recent weeks after months in which Washington’s ‌attention was focused on the war in Iran.
