Advertisement By&nbsp Simon Ormiston Published on 10 November 2026 - 13:53 GMT+1 • Updated 15:53 Share Comments Add Euronews on Google Share Facebook Twitter Flipboard Send Reddit Linkedin Messenger Telegram VK Bluesky Threads Whatsapp The Copenhagen talks coincided with the start of US-mediated negotiations between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held security talks with Nordic leaders in Copenhagen on Tuesday, as Denmark unveiled a new military aid package for Ukraine worth 4.8 billion kroner (€643 million). ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen told reporters that Denmark would also give 150 million kroner (€20 million) to support Ukraine’s energy sector. Television footage showed Zelenskyy’s plane landing in the Danish capital. On the same day, direct talks between Ukraine and Russia, mediated by the United States, got under way in Abu Dhabi. “I am proud to welcome President Zelenskyy and the Nordic leaders to Denmark. The Ukrainians’ fight for a free Ukraine and a free Europe continues,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said in a statement. Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, Norway’s Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo were also expected in Copenhagen. “Almost five years after the full-scale invasion, the rain of bombs targeting civilians, relief centres, and water and heating plants continues. That is why we must stand firm,” Frederiksen said. Nordic tensions over Putin call The Nordic countries are among Ukraine’s strongest backers. At the end of October, Zelenskyy travelled to Oslo to meet US envoys. After that meeting, Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin by phone for 90 minutes. Stubb described the conversation as “frank and substantive”. Related Ukraine and Russia reportedly show 'a little bit of flexibility' on territory as Abu Dhabi talks begin
Frederiksen criticised the call, saying it had not been coordinated with the other Nordic countries.
There was a heavy police presence outside the Danish prime minister’s office during the visit. Copenhagen police said security would be tightened over the coming days and drones would be banned over the capital until 12 November.

Fresh round of Ukraine-Russia talks held as Trump insists peace close
There is no sign of an end to fighting in Ukraine despite US-brokered talks being held for the first time since February. ( AP: Evgeniy Maloletka )
Envoys from Kyiv, Moscow and Washington DC discuss security guarantees, territorial concessions and a Europe-wide security framework at their first meeting since February.
Despite Donald Trump insisting a deal can be done, the trilateral failed to provide any breakthroughs.
There remain major gaps between Ukraine and Russia on the terms of any possible agreement.
Russian and Ukrainian officials have met in Abu Dhabi for their first US-brokered talks since February, after Donald Trump suggested last week that a broad deal was possible on ending the war in Ukraine and guaranteeing security in Europe.
US envoy Jared Kushner told delegates that recent contacts with both sides had "really identified, narrowed the gaps", and the US side had "some good ideas" on how to bridge their differences.
Mr Trump, he said, was committed to achieving peace.
"He really has asked us to put extra effort into trying to find a solution that hopefully ends the war but also leaves both sides in a much stronger position" to realise their full potential, Mr Kushner said.
Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, is leading the trilateral talks with Russia and Ukraine. ( Reuters: Rula Rouhana )
But more than four and a half years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and with Russian forces holding about a fifth of the country, Moscow and Kyiv remain far apart — despite Mr Trump's optimism — on terms for a possible settlement.
Ukraine's chief delegate, Rustem Umerov, said in his opening remarks that Kyiv was focused on achieving security guarantees and a lasting peace.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov underlined Moscow's preference for negotiating a broad European security framework before tackling the specifics of the war.
"The idea of defining clear parameters for a future security architecture, and only then moving on to resolving the actual Russia-Ukraine conflict, is absolutely reasonable," he told reporters in Moscow.
A day before the talks, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen voiced the opposite view, saying wider security talks should come only after a ceasefire in Ukraine.
Mr Lavrov again rejected the notion of a truce, saying the Europeans were trying to buy breathing space for Ukraine.
The new American drive for a deal has galvanised European officials into pushing for a place at the table to seek an end to the continent's deadliest conflict since World War Two.
Before the start of the main meeting, the Ukrainians met separately with European, NATO and EU representatives and the two American envoys, Mr Kushner and Steve Witkoff.
France said there could be no lasting peace in Ukraine without addressing European security, and that this required the involvement of the Europeans.
Rustem Umerov says Ukraine is unwilling to concede territory without serious security guarantees from allies. ( Reuters: Rula Rouhana )
Russia had made clear it did not see a place for Europeans at the meeting with the Ukrainians and Americans.
Describing the talks in Abu Dhabi as "very productive", US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the goal at some point was to expand the trilateral talks to include the Europeans.
The US president has frequently said an agreement was close, without a deal emerging.
However, negotiations have picked up again in recent weeks after months in which Washington's attention was focused on the war in Iran.

sources.text:
South Africa: Ministers Pocket Pay Hikes As Millions Battle to Survive - allAfrica.com South Africa: Ministers Pocket Pay Hikes As Millions Battle to Survive GovernmentZA/Flickr President Cyril Ramaphosa delivers his SONA 2025 speech. 11 November 2026 Scrolla (Johannesburg) By Palesa Matlala The increase adds about R97,725 a year to a minister's remuneration package and R46,304 to an ordinary MP's package.
The announcement came on the same day Stats SA reported that unemployment had risen to 33.7%, with 8.6 million people officially unemployed.
Ministers will get nearly R98,000 more a year after President Cyril Ramaphosa approved salary increases for politicians, a decision unions have condemned as millions struggle to make ends meet.
The South African Federation of Trade Unions (Saftu) wants the 3.5% increase reversed, arguing that political leaders should put struggling households first.
AdvertisementThe Presidency announced the increases on Tuesday, 10 November. They are backdated to 1 April 2026.
Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn
The 3.5% adjustment covers ministers, deputy ministers, members of Parliament, premiers, members of provincial executive councils and provincial legislators.
Based on previously gazetted remuneration, the increase adds about R97,725 a year to a minister's package and R46,304 to an ordinary MP's.
AdvertisementThese are increases in total remuneration packages, which include pension contributions, rather than additional take-home pay.
Saftu general secretary Zwelinzima Vavi said the decision could not be justified against the country's unemployment crisis.
"This decision is indefensible in a country where, in the second quarter of 2026, 8.5 million people were officially unemployed and another 4.6 million formed part of the potential labour force. That means 13.1 million people were unemployed or part of the potential labour force," Vavi said, according to The Citizen.
Those figures refer to April to June. Newer figures released by Statistics South Africa on Tuesday show that official unemployment rose to 33.7% in the third quarter, with 8.6 million people unemployed.
The number of unemployed people increased by 97,000, even though employment also grew by 101,000 to 16.8 million.
The potential labour force is counted separately from official unemployment. It includes discouraged jobseekers and others who meet some, but not all, of the criteria for being officially unemployed.
Ramaphosa also approved a separate 4% increase for judges, magistrates, traditional leaders and members of national and provincial houses of traditional and Khoi-San leaders.
AdvertisementThe Presidency said the decision followed recommendations from the Independent Commission for the Remuneration of Public Office-Bearers.
The commission considered factors including inflation, the affordability of increases for the state, previous pay decisions and average annual wage increases.
The Presidency said Ramaphosa urged public office-bearers to uphold their responsibilities and honour the public's trust.

"At a time when millions are unemployed, and households are being pushed deeper into hardship, leadership must be measured by service to the people, not by higher pay for those already entrusted with governing them," Vavi said.

sources.text: Skip to main content Skip to navigation Tomás Beltrán Photograph: Inter American Press Association View image in fullscreen Tomás Beltrán Photograph: Inter American Press Association Killing of journalist underscores deteriorating conditions in Ecuador Tomás Beltrán was shot dead amid gang warfare that has turned Latin American country into one of its most violent Tomás Beltrán was manoeuvring his car into his garage on Sunday night when the Ecuadorian journalist was shot dead. Beltrán ran a Facebook page with news about Calceta, a small city in the province of Manabí, whose Pacific coastline has made it a key flashpoint in the gang warfare over drug trafficking routes that has transformed one of Latin America’s safest countries into one of its most violent . Police and the public prosecutor’s office have not said much about the case, and little was known about the killers except that they were armed and then fled the scene. It was also unclear whether the crime was linked to Beltrán’s work, though he had previously reported allegations of corruption involving local authorities. Regardless, many press freedom groups already cite his murder as the latest example of how conditions for journalists have deteriorated dramatically in Ecuador. Six journalists were killed in the country last year alone. Artur Romeu, Reporters Without Borders’ Latin America director, said in a statement that months ago Beltrán had told the organisation “about his fears and the threats he was receiving”. “We took part in efforts to get him to safety,” he said, adding that Beltrán had been placed in a protection programme run by the public prosecutor’s office, although it was not known whether that protection was still in place when he was killed. “Reporters Without Borders calls on the public prosecutor’s office to investigate as a priority whether there is a link to his journalistic work, identify any possible masterminds and protect his family and colleagues,” said Romeu. The Ecuadorian civil society organisation Fundación Periodistas Sin Cadenas (FPSC) reported that at least 19 journalists have had to go into exile since gang violence exploded in 2023. Although Ecuador does not produce cocaine like neighbouring Colombia and Peru, it has become a major trafficking hub , particularly through the Pacific. Journalists have received death threats with photographs of their homes and details of their routines and families. “Practising journalism in Ecuador is now an extremely high-risk job,” said María Fernanda Almeida, a project coordinator at FPSC, adding that all of last year’s killings of journalists “remain completely unpunished”. “And one of the many terrible effects of this violence is self-censorship: at least in the coastal provinces, colleagues no longer want to report on violence,” she added. Almeida said another problem for journalists has been the stance of the government of the far-right president Daniel Noboa, who has responded to the surge in crime with a controversial “iron-fist” approach to the gangs, repeatedly declaring states of emergency and expanding the role of the armed forces in measures that have been widely criticised by human rights groups. While covering military operations, reporters have had their phones confiscated , a search warrant was executed at a reporter’s home and a journalist was threatened by soldiers simply for filming them stopping university students. There have also been several reports that Noboa, one of US president Donald Trump’s key allies in Latin America, has pressured media organisations to dismiss journalists critical of him, including the columnist Roberto Aguilar, who said he was fired from the newspaper Diario Expreso after the government reportedly threatened private advertisers with audits if they continued advertising with the outlet. sources.text:
ASIC accuses Commonwealth Bank of overcharging tens of thousands of business customers - ABC News Skip to main content Skip to news navigation, settings and search Explore the ABC news
ASIC accuses Commonwealth Bank of overcharging tens of thousands of business customers
The CBA faces allegations it failed to report cash transactions made through intelligent deposit machines. ( ABC News: Margaret Burin )
Commonwealth Bank allegedly overcharged millions of dollars in fees to tens of thousands of business customers, many of them small businesses, according to the corporate regulator.
ASIC has started civil penalty proceedings against Australia's biggest bank, alleging customers have been overcharged fees they were never told about.
ASIC alleged CBA's CommBiz terms and conditions were misleading because they failed to clearly and accurately disclose all the fees business customers would be charged for direct debit and direct credit payments.
Business customers were told they would be charged a fee for a payment to or from a third-party account.
However, ASIC alleges CBA also charged an additional, undisclosed fee for the corresponding movement of money into or out of the customer's CommBiz account.
ASIC alleges that between November 2020 and May 31, 2025, about 42,000 CommBiz customers were overcharged about $8.5 million in fees.
ASIC alleges that in one example a small business paying the fortnightly wages of 10 employees from two CommBiz accounts was charged 12 fees: 10 for the payments to its employees and another two undisclosed fees for the money being withdrawn from its own accounts.
"We allege Commonwealth Bank broke a basic promise to its business customers," ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland said.
"Small businesses are busy enough. They should not have to scrutinise every transaction to make sure that their bank is charging them the right fees."
ASIC says customers were overcharged for years
ASIC alleges business customers were overcharged for about 19 years, with the allegedly misleading terms and conditions in place from the launch of CommBiz in 2006.
ASIC further alleges CBA received customer complaints about the issue from at least 2015, while a 2016 internal audit identified overcharging of direct debit fees and required corrective action.
ASIC also alleges governance failings at CBA meant the alleged misleading statements were not identified and corrected, and that CBA allegedly failed to act efficiently, honestly and fairly.
"What makes this particularly concerning is how long the alleged conduct went on, despite customer complaints to Commonwealth Bank pointing to a problem years earlier," Mr Kirkland said.
ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland says "Commonwealth Bank broke a basic promise to its business customers". ( ABC )
CBA temporarily ceased charging the relevant fees in June 2025 and amended the CommBiz terms in August 2025.
Since February 2026, the bank has waived the "contra leg" fees for processing direct debits and direct credits.
CBA has completed a remediation program covering December 1, 2006, to present for past and current CommBiz customers.
This has resulted in more than $26.4 million in remediation payments to about 93,000 CommBiz customers, including about 40,000 small businesses.
The case was filed in the Federal Court on late Wednesday afternoon. However, the court has not yet listed the matter for a case management hearing.
It is the second legal action ASIC has taken against a big bank in as many days, with Macquarie Bank on Monday admitting to failures in the promotion of its "welcome" interest rate for new savings account customers, which could result in a $14 million penalty.
CBA apologises but says it will defend aspects of litigation
The Commonwealth Bank said in a statement to the ASX that it intended to defend aspects of the litigation.
"While CBA charged the fee consistently over time, the issue arose from changes made to certain Terms and Conditions intended to simplify them

MOSCOW: Russia's ambassador to the United States, Alexander Darchiev, has died suddenly at age 66 after one and a half years in the job, Moscow's foreign ministry announced Wednesday (Nov 11).
The ministry called Darchiev an "outstanding diplomat, an experienced leader and a kind colleague". He was appointed in March 2025.
Moscow did not give more details on the death.
The US State Department said Darchiev died Wednesday in Moscow.

sources.title: German ministries spend €5.8 million on office décor, drawing taxpayers' criticism | Euronews
sources.text: Advertisement By&nbsp Nela Heidner Published on 11 November 2026 - 21:58 GMT+1 Share Comments Add Euronews on Google Share Facebook Twitter Flipboard Send Reddit Linkedin Messenger Telegram VK Bluesky Threads Whatsapp Citizens face burdens and service cuts, while the federal government spends millions on furniture, lamps and decor, claims the Taxpayers' Association. Since the start of the current legislative term in May 2025, the federal government has spent around 5.8 million euros on new furniture, furnishings and decorations. This emerges from a government response to a parliamentary question from the AfD group in the Bundestag. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT The figures have now triggered sharp criticism from the German Taxpayers' Association. Its president, Reiner Holznagel, is particularly critical of what he sees as a contradiction between calls for savings directed at the public and the spending within the machinery of government. "There is supposedly no room to relieve the burden on citizens, but when it comes to their own government apparatus, the belt is pretty loose - for decor and the like!", Holznagel told the German newspaper Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung. Foreign Office, Defence and Finance most spending Spending by the 16 federal ministries has totalled about 5.8 million euros since May 2025. The figures cover not only classic items of furniture but also lamps, carpets, curtains, paintings, sculptures and ornamental plants. The Foreign Office was particularly free with its money. There, spending on furniture, lamps, carpets and decoration has added up to €840,062 since the start of the legislative term. In 2026 alone, around €256,000 went on lamps, carpets and curtains. In second place comes the Defence Ministry with around €813,000. The Federal Finance Ministry has also recorded substantial expenditure. Since May 2025, the department led by Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil (SPD) has invested more than half a million euros in furniture, equipment and decoration. Finance Ministry tops the league Particularly striking is a look at decoration costs alone. Here, the Finance Ministry heads the list. Since May 2025, it has spent a total of €45,077 on decorations. That means more than a quarter of the federal government's total decoration spending is accounted for by this ministry. The Finance Ministry has also incurred substantial costs for office furnishings at the senior management level. In 2026 alone, 47,737 euros have so far been spent on refitting the relevant offices. Taxpayers' association calls for more responsible spending policy For the German Taxpayers' Association, the figures are a reason to question the federal government's spending policy in principle. Holznagel argues that anyone demanding thrift from citizens must apply the same standards within their own authorities and ministries. He sees the Bundestag's budget committee as having a particular responsibility. It can now demonstrate how seriously politicians take the savings measures they have announced. The debate is likely to raise the broader question of how responsibly the federal government handles taxpayers' money. Especially at a time of strained public finances, the public is likely to watch closely how politicians spend their money. sources.text:

Published Time: 2026-11-12T04:55:07+08:00

Markdown Content:
Joe Biden says he did not know he had cancer while he was US president and would not have sought a second term if he already had been diagnosed.

The former Democratic president’s comments came in an interview with People magazine before the release of his White House memoir on Tuesday.

“If I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer,” said Biden, who turns 84 on November 20, “I would’ve not gone forward” with a 2024 re-election bid that ended after a disastrous debate performance against Republican Donald Trump.

Biden was diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer months after leaving office in 2025.

“I don’t think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running” for president, Biden said in the interview.

[Video 5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jzcOamcLQjI)

02:24

Trump ‘surprised’ public wasn’t notified of Biden’s cancer diagnosis ‘long ago’

Still, he argued that the June 2024 debate, less than five months before Election Day, was not a seismic event even if it accelerated Democrats’ concerns about his age – he was 81 at the time – and his ability to defeat Trump.

“First of all, I thought there’d be another debate, which there wasn’t,” Biden said. “But notwithstanding the fact that there wasn’t another debate, it didn’t disturb me because it wasn’t consequential.”

Within weeks, Biden announced he was ending his campaign and endorsing his vice-president, Kamala Harris, who secured the nomination and lost to Trump in the general election.

Biden insisted he was able to perform his duties while he was in office. He said age itself was not disqualifying and meant he had experience and deep personal relationships with world leaders.

“I believe that on an objective basis, I was the best-equipped person to do the job,” he said.

His son Hunter told the BBC in August that the cancer had spread and was causing his father pain. “It’s very painful and it’s very debilitating in many respects,” he said.

Since Joe Biden left office, his son has become a higher-profile public presence, sparring with Republicans on social media, posting lengthy thoughts on the nation’s direction and launching his own cryptocurrency.

![Image 1: Former US president Joe Biden (centre right) and Hunter Biden (centre left) are seen at the College Historical Society in Dublin, Ireland, on Tuesday. Photo: PA via AP](https://img.i-scmp.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=contain,width=1024,format=auto/sites/default/files/d8/images/canvas/2026/11/12/91f16524-c8c7-45f7-be1b-195718570e36_eeb754c2.jpg)

Former US president Joe Biden (centre right) and Hunter Biden (centre left) are seen at the College Historical Society in Dublin, Ireland, on Tuesday. Photo: PA via AP

Joe Biden defended his son’s public persona and his decision to pardon Hunter Biden after the younger Biden’s 2024 conviction on federal felony gun charges and his guilty plea to federal tax charges.

Hunter Biden also had faced years of scrutiny and withering Republican attacks over his international business dealings.

Hunter Biden has said the pardon damaged his father’s legacy, but the former president said Trump’s penchant for vengeance made it necessary.

“He goes after people without any basis, whether they’re viewed as an enemy. I knew what he would do,” Joe Biden said.

“If I hadn’t pardoned – not just some of my family members, anyone who’s dealt with me – he would go back and try to do harm to them.”

Biden called his son “one of the brightest men I know”, adding: “I’m really proud of him.”

MOSCOW — U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys met Thursday with President Vladimir Putin as Washington sought new momentum in peace efforts after two days of U.S.-mediated negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian delegations.

Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also Trump's son-in-law, brokered the talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates. Those were the first direct discussions between representatives of Moscow and Kyiv in nine months as the push for peace stalled.

The two days of talks that ended Wednesday produced no major breakthrough, aside from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners, with the exact figure still to be announced.

Kushner and Witkoff went straight to the Kremlin to brief Putin in a meeting that lasted about two hours and are scheduled to fly to Dublin, Ireland, for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as the conflict stretches toward the five-year mark.

### U.S. envoys want Europe at the negotiating table, too

Kushner said that one of the goals of the meeting with Putin was to get the Russian leader's blessing for European representatives to be part of the talks, which are looking at the continent's broader security arrangements.

The U.S. and Zelenskyy want Europe to appoint a single person to negotiate with Moscow.

sources.title: Ukraine captures first Indonesian prisoner of war amid surge in Russian recruitment | Ukraine | The Guardian
sources.text: Skip to main content Skip to navigation Rescue workers at the scene of a Russian drone attack in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on Tuesday. An Indonesian national has been captured by Ukraine after being recruited by Russia in Zaporizhzhia. Photograph: Ukrinform/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Rescue workers at the scene of a Russian drone attack in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on Tuesday. An Indonesian national has been captured by Ukraine after being recruited by Russia in Zaporizhzhia. Photograph: Ukrinform/Shutterstock Ukraine captures first Indonesian prisoner of war amid surge in Russian recruitment Capture of man from Java follows reports that hundreds are being recruited from the south-east Asian country as Moscow seeks to boost its war effort Ukraine says it has captured its first Indonesian prisoner of war, amid what it says is a spike in recruitment by Russia from the south-east Asian nation. The 49-year-old man from Java was taken to Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region to take part in a Russian assault, but managed to reach Ukrainian-held territory after the group came under drone attack, according to Ukraine’s state-run I Want to Live project. He was then captured by the Ukrainians. According to the project, some 283 Indonesians were recruited in the first nine months of this year to fight for Russia against Ukraine. It said recruitment from Indonesia was no more than 10 in the previous three years. ‘I made the biggest mistake’: the young Yemeni men lured into the Russian army with empty promises Read more The Russian embassy in Jakarta did not immediately respond to questions about the alleged recruitment effort but it is not the first time Russia has sought foreign mercenaries for its war effort. In February, Kenya’s intelligence services reported that more than 1,000 Kenyans had been lured to fight for Russia. A growing number of people from African countries – including Kenya, Uganda and South Africa – and elsewhere have been lured to the frontline as Russia seeks help to sustain its more than four-year war after invading Ukraine in February 2022. This month Jakarta urged Moscow to ensure no Indonesians were drafted into its military, following the reported death in October of an Indonesian national serving with the military. Indonesian foreign ministry spokesperson Yvonne Mewengkang said: “The Indonesian government asked the Russian government to take all necessary steps to ensure that no Indonesians will be recruited into the Russian military or any other military-related position in Russia through any avenues.” Indonesia, she added, was particularly concerned about recruitment practices that could constitute human trafficking. Days later, Indonesian police said they had identified a human trafficking syndicate targeting its nationals that used social media and messaging apps to recruit victims. The posts promised lucrative jobs in logistics, border security and defence construction, but after the applicants travelled to Russia they were directed to sign contracts to serve as mercenaries, with some deployed to conflict zones, police said. The ‘I Want to Live’ governmental initiative was established in September 2022 by the coordination headquarters for Prisoners of War with support from Ukraine defence ministry and defence intelligence (HUR). It was designed to allow active-duty troops, including Russian servicemen and foreign nationals recruited into the Russian military, to safely surrender and exit the battlefield. The court imposed the sentence on Thursday on Maria Bontsler, according to the rights group Slovo Zashchite, which said she had worked with a number of defendants accused of political offences in Kaliningrad. list 2 of 3 What is northern Europe’s new drone and warship plan to counter Russia?
list 3 of 3 US soldier arrested for Russia spying: What we know
The territory sits on the Baltic Sea between Lithuania and Poland.
A court statement posted on Telegram did not name her, but said she had been detained by the FSB intelligence agency on allegations of passing information to Ukraine beginning in 2024 about security officers in Kaliningrad.
Prosecutors also alleged she gave Ukraine information on criminal cases in the exclave that were of interest to Kyiv, the statement said.
She was also given an extra year of restrictions on her activity. Prosecutors had sought 15 years, according to Slovo Zashchite.
Slovo Zashchite said the trial was held behind closed doors, with Bontsler and her lawyers prevented from attending, and that she was allowed only to make a closing statement. It said her lawyers argued that none of the information cited by prosecutors was secret, and that she had been in ill health in detention.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, parliament has approved laws that make public actions aimed at “discrediting” the army illegal and ban the spread of “fake news” about the armed forces.
Russian courts have also jailed lawyers who took on politically sensitive cases. In January 2025, a court sentenced three lawyers of the late opposition leader Alexey Navalny to between three and a half and five and a half years on “extremism” charges, in a case widely seen as an effort to discourage defence lawyers from taking political cases.

sources.title: Antibiotic-resistant infections hit 400 a week in England despite falling drug use | Euronews
sources.text:
Advertisement By&nbsp Giedre Peseckyte Published on 12 November 2026 - 17:48 GMT+1 Share Comments Add Euronews on Google Share Facebook Twitter Flipboard Send Reddit Linkedin Messenger Telegram VK Bluesky Threads Whatsapp New figures show drug-resistant bloodstream infections rose by nearly 17% since 2019, highlighting the challenge facing the UK’s efforts to tackle antimicrobial resistance. More than 400 people a week developed antibiotic-resistant infections in England last year, according to surveillance data published by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) on Thursday, highlighting the growing threat of antimicrobial resistance despite efforts to reduce antibiotic use. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT A total of 21,129 cases of antibiotic-resistant bacteraemia – a potentially life-threatening infection where bacteria are present in the bloodstream – were recorded in 2025, up 16.8% from 18,086 in 2019. The continued upward trend comes despite a reduction in antibiotic consumption across the NHS. Total antibiotic use fell by 10.7% between 2019 and 2025, from 17.8 to 15.9 defined daily doses per 1,000 inhabitants per day. "We can’t rely on reducing antibiotic use alone," Shona Arora, interim chief medical adviser at UKHSA, said in a press release , calling for greater efforts to prevent infections and develop new treatment options. “We need to continue our work with partners globally to prevent infections from occurring in the first place, alongside exploring new treatment options.” Related Antimicrobial resistance is outpacing the industry’s efforts to fight it, report finds
When antibiotics stop working: Europe's growing superbug threat
The data also reveal significant inequalities in the burden of resistant infections.
People living in England's most deprived areas had a 44.2% higher rate of antibiotic-resistant bacteraemia than those in the least deprived communities. Older people were also disproportionately affected. Adults over 45 accounted for 89.3% of infections, while almost half of cases were detected in people aged over 74.
The findings point to a wider challenge for policymakers: tackling antimicrobial resistance requires not only responsible prescribing but also stronger infection prevention, vaccination programmes and investment in new treatments.
The UK has set out its ambitions in a National Action Plan for antimicrobial resistance 2024 to 2029 . Its objectives include limiting the spread of resistant infections and reducing the need for antibiotics in the first place.
Diana Johnson, the UK's minister for public health and patient safety, urged people to take antibiotics only when advised by a healthcare professional, complete their prescribed course and avoid sharing or saving medication.
“This will help reduce the spread of resistant infections and keep all of us safer,” she said.

sources.title: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland - BBC News
sources.text:
Image source, Russian military Image caption, The Naro-Fominsk is believed to have headed back to port in St Petersburg after the attack By Paul Kirby Europe digital editor Published 3 hours ago
Finnish officials have confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, although little is known about the strike.
Ukraine's SBU security service said it targeted the ship Naro-Fominsk as part of a broader drone operation against Russia's Ust-Luga oil export depot on the Baltic coast.
The attack, thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic Sea open to civilian maritime traffic, has raised questions about whether Ukraine could expand its strikes.
Helsinki has been one of Kyiv's closest European allies, and Finnish officials have described the incident as a direct result of Russia's continued full-scale war.
Finland's military has given few details of the incident, but it appears to have taken place in a narrow stretch some distance from the Finnish coast.
The country's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen was adamant that the situation in the Baltic Sea remained stable and safe and that there was no threat of any kind to marine traffic.
Defence officials are understood to have stressed to Kyiv that the Gulf is a relatively narrow waterway used by oil tankers and civilian vessels, and is also home to subsea data cables.
Ukraine's SBU described the Russian ship as a Buyan-M type small corvette that carried Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. There were also unconfirmed reports of Russian combat helicopters being destroyed.
Martin Herem, the defence minister of Estonia, which borders the Gulf, told public broadcaster ERR that the ship was hit at about 05:30 (03:30 GMT) on Wednesday but did not say how it was attacked: "We know that smoke came from the ship afterwards. The ship itself went back towards St Petersburg."
The extent of casualties or damage sustained by the Russian navy ship remains unclear, and Moscow rarely gives such details.
"The Baltic Sea fleet has been untouched up to this point but there seemingly was a window of opportunity for Ukraine and they understandably tried to use it," said military analyst Emil Kastehelmi, co-founder of the Black Bird monitoring group.
Russian and Ukrainian vessels have been repeatedly targeted in the Black Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, but even though the latest strike on a ship in the Baltic is unprecedented, Kastehelmi told the BBC he did not consider it a serious escalation.
Ukrainian drones are regularly launched into Russia from northern Ukraine. Several storage tanks at the Ust-Luga terminal are thought to have been hit overnight on Wednesday and fires at the port were visible over the border in Estonia.
Herem said Ukrainian drones attacked the Ust-Luga region from midnight until about 06:00, mostly flying close to the Estonian border but still in Russian airspace.
He added that one drone had entered Estonian airspace briefly from Latvia and then headed towards Russia.
Nato aircraft based in the Baltic states were in the air at the time, but Herem said it had not been considered safe for them to destroy the drones.
Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesman Heorhiy Tykhyy said late on Wednesday that Moscow's allegations that Kyiv had used the airspace of the Baltic states to attack Russia were "baseless", although he acknowledged "incidents might occur when Russia diverts drones from its airspace using electronic warfare".

sources.title: Financial Audit: IRS’s FY 2026 and FY 2025 Financial Statements | U.S. GAO
sources.text:
Financial Audit: IRS’s FY 2026 and FY 2025 Financial Statements | U.S. GAO Skip to main content GAO-27-108909 Published: Nov 12, 2026. Publicly Released: Nov 12, 2026.
IRS collects taxes to fund government operations. In FY 2026, IRS collected about $5.6 trillion in taxes and paid out about $670 billion in refunds, credits, and other payments.
We annually audit IRS’s financial statements and related internal controls —the processes that help ensure its financial information is reliable. In FY 2026, we found that IRS’s statements were reliable and its controls were effective—although some controls over unpaid assessments could be improved.
Such financial statement audits give Congress and taxpayers an independent check on federal spending. They can also lead to better financial practices, helping agencies improve decision-making, efficiency, and public trust.
Entrance sign to the Internal Revenue Service building
In fiscal year 2026, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) collected more than $5.5 trillion in taxes and paid out about $670 billion in tax refunds, credits, and other payments.
Fiscal Year 2026 IRS Collections of Federal Taxes, by Type
In GAO’s opinion, IRS’s fiscal years 2026 and 2025 financial statements are fairly presented in all material respects. In addition, in GAO’s opinion, although internal controls could be improved, IRS maintained, in all material respects, effective internal control over financial reporting as of September 30, 2026. GAO’s tests of IRS’s compliance with selected provisions of applicable laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements disclosed no instances of reportable noncompliance for fiscal year 2026.
System limitations and other deficiencies in IRS’s accounting for federal taxes receivable and other unpaid assessment balances continued to exist during fiscal year 2026. These control deficiencies affect IRS’s ability to produce reliable financial statements without using significant compensating procedures. These control deficiencies are significant enough to merit the attention of those charged with governance of IRS and therefore collectively represent a continuing significant deficiency in internal control over financial reporting. Continued management attention is essential to fully addressing this significant deficiency.
In commenting on a draft of this report, IRS stated that it was pleased to receive an unmodified opinion on its financial statements. IRS also commented that it is dedicated to promoting the highest standards of financial management and accountability and will continue to work to improve internal controls.
In connection with fulfilling GAO’s requirement to audit the consolidated financial statements of the U.S. government, and consistent with its authority to audit statements and schedules prepared by executive agency components, GAO has audited IRS’s financial statements because of the significance of IRS’s tax collections to the consolidated financial statements of the U.S. government. GAO annually audits IRS’s financial statements to determine whether (1) the financial statements are fairly presented and (2) IRS management maintained effective internal control over financial reporting. GAO also tests IRS’s compliance with selected provisions of applicable laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements.
IRS’s tax collection activities are significant to overall federal receipts, and the effectiveness of its financial management is of substantial interest to Congress and the nation’s taxpayers.
For more information, contact Dawn B. Simpson at simpsondb@gao.gov .

sources.title: Kallas says 'Russians don't want me' as EU envoy for peace talks | Euronews
sources.text: Advertisement By&nbsp Jorge Liboreiro Published on 13 November 2026 - 15:13 GMT+1 Share Comments Add Euronews on Google Share Facebook Twitter Flipboard Send Reddit Linkedin Messenger Telegram VK Bluesky Threads Whatsapp Kaja Kallas has made a strong push to be appointed special EU envoy for the peace negotiations. But "Russians do not want me", she added. High Representative Kaja Kallas has pitched herself as the European Union's designated envoy for the negotiations to end Russia's war on Ukraine, arguing it is incumbent upon her, as foreign policy chief, to take on the high-stakes job. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT But, she noted, "Russians do not want me" at the table due to her "strong" views . "But do we have a say in who is representing Russia? No, we do not," Kallas said on Friday morning. "Really, we have to have a strong team." Speaking in Dublin, Ireland, at an informal summit of EU leaders, Kallas said it was those very heads of state and government who named her High Representative, knowing that face-to-face talks with Moscow would have to happen at some point. "In June 2024, there was a decision by the leaders (on) who is representing (the EU) when it comes to security and foreign policy. And it was the discussion that in these five years there is going to be a negotiation with the Russians," she said. "If the leaders want to change that agreement, of course, they may, because it is the leaders' decision, but I think we should focus our energy actually on the substance." Kallas said the EU should not "copy the same pattern" that the United States follows in the negotiations, with two hand-picked envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Instead, it should select somebody with a defined "institutional role". The Treaty of Lisbon leaves foreign policy coordination and execution in the hands of the High Representative, but also envisions a representational role for the president of the European Council, currently António Costa. The European Commission, meanwhile, handles areas such as sanctions, financing and accession that are crucial for the diplomatic track. Costa has quickly overtaken Kallas in the race and is now seen as the frontrunner to be the special envoy. Kallas is considered a divisive figure in Brussels and has become increasingly sidelined in top-level discussions. "I am bound to what the member states say," Kallas said, referring to the unanimity principles that guide EU foreign policy. "I am not representing myself. I am representing 27, as I have done already for two years." Asked if part of the Russian opposition against her stemmed from her being Eastern European, Kallas said Moscow would resist "anybody strong" at the table. "They want to push through their maximum demands, like they have always done," she said, pushing back against "threats and ultimatums". "Of course, if you negotiate with anybody, you want the other side to be as weak as possible so that you can get what you want. That is very clear," she went on. "But it is not up to them to say. Otherwise, if we give them the right (to) this, we are actually really giving them the leverage that they should not have." The topic of special envoy has come to the forefront of the conversation after both Ukraine and the US asked Europeans to appoint one representative for the talks. Leaders discussed the matter while in Dublin. "It's important we focus on the message and not the person who represents Europe," a senior diplomat said, warning that debating potential candidates risks "fuelling divisions among Europeans, which is what Russia wants". So far, the negotiations have unfolded at the technical level, so it is unclear which role the envoy would play and at which table they would sit. sources.text: Advertisement By&nbsp Euronews Persian service Published on 13 November 2026 - 18:46 GMT+1 Share Comments Add Euronews on Google Share Facebook Twitter Flipboard Send Reddit Linkedin Messenger Telegram VK Bluesky Threads Whatsapp A Russian deputy prime minister led a 70-strong Russian delegation to Afghanistan, pursuing deals on transport, logistics, agriculture, and health products with the Taliban. Russian deputy prime minister Alexei Overchuk was welcomed by a guard of honour when he arrived in Kabul on Thursday with a delegation of 70 Russian business people to conduct business talks with the Taliban government, Afghan officials said. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Overchuk met Taliban prime minister Mohammad Hassan Akhund, the deputy prime minister for economic affairs Abdul Ghani Baradar as well as foreign minister Amir Khan Muttaqi. According to a statement by the Afghan government published on X, Abdul Ghani Baradar described to the Russians Afghanistan's potential for economic development and investment, pointing to "strategic location, abundant resources and a workforce of 24 million people". Abdul Ghani Baradar invited Russian companies to invest in agriculture, mining, constructions of roads, railways and factories, and to create a special economic zone in Afghanistan, while expressing his wish to expand exports of Afghan agricultural products to Russia. The deputy prime minister also asked Russia to "provide the necessary facilities for Afghan products to be supplied to Russian markets and to cooperate in reducing transport and transit costs". A Russian news agency quoted Alexei Overchuk as saying that the Russian delegation represent companies that are already operating in Afghanistan and that "many others want to start operating in this country." Overchuk said that the companies represented in the delegation work in the fields of transport, logistics, agriculture and pharmaceuticals and that the Afghan government is interested in Russian chemical fertilisers, as well as in "building fertiliser production plants on Afghan soil". Overchuk estimated that trade between Russia and Afghanistan in the first eight months of 2026 had more than doubled, reaching over 349 million dollars. Russia officially recognised the Taliban government in July 2025, being the only state to have taken such a step since the Taliban seized power in August 2021, after the withdrawal of the United States. Although no country other than Russia has formally recognised the new Afghan regime, the Taliban authorities have so far held high-level talks with many states and have established specific diplomatic and economic relations with some governments. sources.text:
URL Source: https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-states-canada/article/3374414/us-air-force-responds-suspected-drone-activity-over-uk-airbase

Published Time: 2026-11-14T07:47:51+08:00

Markdown Content:
US Air Force personnel at the RAF Lakenheath base in Britain responded to “suspected unauthorised drone activity” on Friday evening, although no personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected, a US Air Force spokesman said.

“We continue ‌to work closely with our host nation counterparts to ensure the safety and security of our US service members, US and host nation civilians, contractors and all of our families,” the spokesman added by email.

The British Ministry of Defence was not immediately available for comment on the incident in the east of England.

The US has in recent weeks moved bombers that had been used to ⁠strike Iran out of Britain, and relocated huge refuelling aircraft from Britain to Germany. A news report ‌later said there had been a threat from Iran.

The bombers left RAF Fairford on security grounds after a group of men approached the base in white vans in ‌the middle of the night on September 27.

![Image 1: An F-15 is towed from the main runway at RAF Lakenheath in April 2010. Photo: AP](https://img.i-scmp.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=contain,width=1024,format=auto/sites/default/files/d8/images/canvas/2026/11/14/60d2ce31-74ea-41a9-b623-818f97fc2561_51715de7.jpg)

An F-15 is towed from the main runway at RAF Lakenheath in April 2010. Photo: AP

Two men were charged last month in relation ⁠to that incident, with ⁠prosecutors alleging one of them had tried to assist Iranian intelligence in Britain.

The US Justice Department said this week that a ‌member of an Iran-backed militia had plotted to attack the Fairford airbase while detained in the US on criminal charges.

The Wall Street Journal ‌has reported ‌that the refuelling aircraft were moved due to a threat from Iran.

Britain’s domestic spy chief said ‌in October that Iran had stepped up attempts to hit harder targets such as military sites in Britain.

Tehran ⁠has rejected accusations of involvement in the Fairford incident or any other accusations of malign activity in Britain, where ⁠the authorities have for a number of years accused it of being involved in plots and attempted assassinations against dissidents and Israeli and Jewish targets.

Germany has blamed Russia for an attempted attack ‌at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August ‌after airport workers found a drone laden with explosives and a detonator at the airport, an important civilian freight and Nato logistics hub in eastern Germany that is also a base for several giant Ukrainian Antonov An-124 cargo planes.

sources.title: Hungary seizes millions in cash found buried in forests amid corruption investigation | Euronews
sources.text: Advertisement By&nbsp Beatrix Asboth &nbsp&&nbsp MTI Published on 14 November 2026 - 12:31 GMT+1 Share Comments Add Euronews on Google Share Facebook Twitter Flipboard Send Reddit Linkedin Messenger Telegram VK Bluesky Threads Whatsapp Investigators uncovered large amounts of cash hidden in a variety of spots: buried in forests, concealed in agricultural buildings and warehouses, stashed inside residential properties and stored in a high-value safe in a remote location. Hungarian authorities said they seized more than €17.5 million in cash buried in forests and hidden in other places across the country this week. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT On 12 and 13 November, the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) carried out coordinated searches at multiple locations across Hungary, including in Budapest and the counties of Pest, Békés and Nógrád, as part of a criminal investigation involving Miklós Seszták, a former minister of national development. During the searches, investigators uncovered large amounts of cash hidden in a variety of spots: buried in forests, concealed in agricultural buildings and warehouses, stashed inside residential properties and stored in a high-value safe in a remote location. Over the course of the two-day operation, investigators recovered a total of 5,071,632,000 forints, €2,658,350 and $1,257,100. On Friday, NVVH staff paid the cash into the Hungarian State Treasury. According to the investigation, there is reason to suspect that between 2015 and 2018, Seszták and the CEO of Hungarian National Asset Management (MNV) received more than 11 billion forints in illicit payments from representatives of companies contracted by Volánbusz, a national bus operator. The NVVH previously announced that an earlier search carried out in October at the Kisvárda home of Seszták had uncovered safes of a type more commonly used by financial service providers and pawnshops. On 30 September, the Buda Central District Court ordered the detention of Seszták at the request of the NVVH. In late October, the court announced that Seszták's detention had been extended until 30 January. It cited the seriousness of the case and the risk that he might flee or go into hiding. sources.title: DW's Abdul Karim, Katja Gloger win top journalism prize
sources.text:
DW's Abdul Karim, Katja Gloger win top journalism prize Skip to content
Jaafar Abdul Karim (left) and Katja Gloger were the proud winners of the award for outstanding international journalism Image: Sven Moschitz Advertisement At a time when press freedom is under pressure and international newsrooms are shrinking, the Werner Holzer Prize celebrates a profession that many consider indispensable to democracy: foreign correspondence.
Presented in honor of Werner Holzer, the veteran reporter and former editor-in-chief of the German daily newspaper Frankfurter Rundschau , this year's award coincided with what would have been his 100th birthday. Holzer spent decades reporting from some of the world's most important hot spots and championing international journalism.
At the award ceremony in Frankfurt's Römer, the city's historic town hall, Mayor Mike Josef recalled that fundamental rights such as freedom of speech and freedom of the press were first enshrined for all Germans by the Frankfurt Parliament in the nearby Paulskirche in 1848.
Germany's public broadcasters under fire from far-right AfD
The 2026 winners reflect the breadth and ambition of the award. First prize went to Katja Gloger, a veteran Russia correspondent who moved to Moscow in 1989 and accompanied Vladimir Putin during the early years of his presidency.
In her recent nonfiction book, "The Failure: An Investigative Report of Germany's Russia Policy," Gloger and co-author Georg Mascolo offer a searing critique of the misjudgments and illusions that shaped German policy toward Russia for decades .
Second prize was awarded to DW journalist and presenter Jaafar Abdul Karim. His talk show JaafarTalk reaches millions of viewers across the Arab world and in Germany. Whether in Tunis, Beirut or Cairo, Abdul Karim tackles subjects that are often considered taboo.
A research grant went to freelance journalist Luise Land, whose current project explores why her German-Namibian family still owns extensive landholdings in Namibia today. By tracing that history, she examines the enduring legacy of the genocide against the Herero and Nama peoples by German colonial forces in the early 20th century.
"Katja Gloger is one of the leading foreign policy reporters. For decades, she has been among the foremost experts on Russia and speaks out on uncomfortable truths," the jury stated on Friday, explaining its decision to honor Gloger. "Like almost no one else, she has gained access to the very heart of the Kremlin's power elite — from Mikhail Gorbachev to Vladimir Putin."
At the prize-giving ceremony, Gloger delivered a passionate plea for more journalism — and more international coverage — in the German press. "We must defend trustworthy, reliable and fact-based journalism with everything in our power," she said.
Why press freedom matters to everyone, not just journalists
Gloger worked for Reporters Without Borders for 12 years. "The latest rankings show that only one in 100 people can get their information from free, independent journalism and a free, independent press . That shows what's at stake," she said.
The prize winner also said she would dedicate the award to journalists in exile and to her colleagues at Novaya Gazeta , the independent Russian newspaper long known for its critical reporting on the Kremlin. Earlier this week, the paper was forced to shut down its operations in Russia and leave its Moscow newsroom .
In his acceptance speech, Jaafar Abdul Karim said journalism has become more challenging and exhausting than ever. The DW host spoke of hatred and incitement, attacks and threats, both online and offline, in the regions he reports on as well as in Germany .
Such pressure, he said, takes a personal toll — yet giving up is not an option. "When I listen to my heart, I know I have to keep going," he said. The answer, he argued, is a form of journalism that fosters dialogue, embraces multiple perspectives and helps bridge divides rather than deepen them.

sources.title: Pope laments poverty-stricken Inca communities as locals leave Peru - France 24
sources.text: Pope laments poverty-stricken Inca communities as locals leave Peru - France 24 Skip to main content Advertising Pope laments poverty-stricken Inca communities as locals leave Peru Pope Leo XIV on Sunday will traverse the length of Peru in what marks the penultimate day of his Latin American tour. The leader of the Catholic church – who underwent cancer surgery just a month ago – warned that Peru's remote Inca communities are under threat as poverty continues to drive locals out of their homeland in search of better futures. Issued on: 15/11/2026 - 11:55 Modified: 15/11/2026 - 13:27 3 min Reading time Share By: FRANCE 24 On November 14, 2026, Pope Leo XIV visited the Santo Toribio de Mogrovejo sanctuary in Zana, located in the Peruvian province of Chiclayo – a place where he had served as bishop from 2015 to 2023. © Yara Nardi, Reuters Pope Leo XIV warned that the heartland of the ancient Inca Empire is "suffering", as the remote, poverty-stricken communities he served as a missionary in Peru shrink dramatically. The head of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics flew by helicopter to the isolated town of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba in the Andes mountains – an area he visited on horseback when he lived in Peru as Robert Francis Prevost. Despite undergoing cancer surgery just one month ago , the 71-year-old pope was determined to visit the town – which sits among green peaks at an altitude of over 2,000 metres (6,560 feet) – during his 12-day tour of South America . Gathered in front of colorful murals of the pope, thousands of faithful in the streets of Santa Cruz cheered his arrival. At an open-air Mass, the pontiff spoke with pleasure of returning to the "steep hills, ravines and fertile valleys, in a land with Andean roots, where the Inca Empire flourished and which is the cradle of a profound Christian faith". But the communities are now under threat, he said, acknowledging the "suffering of those who are forced to leave their homeland in search of a better future" in the major coastal cities, such as Lima and Trujillo. Read more Pope Leo XIV returns to second homeland Peru and a nationwide welcome Over 40 percent of the population in the Cajamarca region, where Santa Cruz de Succhabamba is located, live in poverty – the highest such figure in the country, according to official data. The region has lost the most inhabitants to internal migration in Peru, with some 729,000 people who were born there now living elsewhere. But he praised those who, "with ingenuity and an entrepreneurial spirit, strive to provide people with dignified jobs", from farmers to shopkeepers and small-business owners. Leo did a tour in a popemobile, waving to pilgrims who have travelled across the region to see him, many camping out overnight or walking mountain paths from surrounding villages in the morning. "We are filled with joy and happiness that he is returning," 42-year-old Idaura Fernandez told AFP. Irma Villalobos, 61, who was born in Santa Cruz but lives in Chiclayo near the coast, said Leo's visit was "very profound, very significant", and she hoped his presence would "transform" the province. sources.title: EU forces board suspected Russian shadow fleet tanker in Mediterranean, Kallas says | Euronews
sources.text: Advertisement By&nbsp Nathan Rennolds Published on 15 November 2026 - 11:41 GMT+1 Share Comments Add Euronews on Google Share Facebook Twitter Flipboard Send Reddit Linkedin Messenger Telegram VK Bluesky Threads Whatsapp The shadow fleet helps Russia get around Western sanctions on its oil industry by utilising complex ownership structures, flags of convenience and other tactics designed to mask the origin of its cargo. European Union forces boarded a suspected Russian shadow fleet tanker in the Mediterranean earlier this week, according to Kaja Kallas, the EU's foreign policy chief. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Troops from the bloc's Operation Irini boarded the MV Midag tanker on Friday and confirmed that the vessel was sailing under a false flag, Kallas said in a post on social media on Sunday. "The EU will keep disrupting Russia’s shadow fleet at sea and through diplomatic means," she wrote, adding that EU foreign ministers were set to approve new sanctions against Russia on Monday, targeting "banks, buyers and companies supporting the shadow fleet." Kallas also shared images appearing to show the boarding. Russia uses its shadow fleet to evade Western sanctions on its oil industry. The shadow fleet gets around these restrictions by utilising complex ownership structures, flags of convenience and other tactics designed to mask the origin of its cargo. In August, Operation Irini forces carried out a flag verification boarding of the MV Sun oil tanker. A similar mission also took place earlier in the month targeting the MV Toa Payoh ship. Operation Irini was launched in March 2020 and was tasked with enforcing an UN arms embargo on Libya due to the Second Libyan Civil War. Its original mandate was to counter illegal arms trafficking, gather information on oil smuggling, help disrupt human smuggling and train Libyan institutions responsible for law enforcement and search and rescue operations. In October, Operation Irini's mandate was renewed through to 31 March 2029, with its objectives to include safeguarding the EU's interests in the Mediterranean and continuing to contribute to peace and stability in Libya. One of its new responsibilities is also to help "constrain" Russia's shadow fleet, which it says uses the Mediterranean as a "key transit and transfer area." sources.title: F.D.A. Rejects Closely Watched Lung Cancer Drug From China - The New York Times
sources.text:
Business | F.D.A. Rejects Closely Watched Lung Cancer Drug From China https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/business/fda-lung-cancer-drug-china.html Share full article
The Food and Drug Administration rejected a first-of-its-kind cancer drug that was invented in China, a setback for a medicine that had become a symbol of China’s ascendance as a powerhouse in drug development.
Summit Therapeutics, the Florida company that has been seeking to bring the drug to the American market, disclosed the agency’s decision in a news release on Sunday . Summit bought the U.S. rights to the drug from Akeso Biopharma, a Chinese drugmaker that invented the drug in its laboratories and sells it in China.
Summit had been seeking approval only for certain patients with advanced lung cancer. But the drug had raised high hopes because it is being tested in many more cancers, including tumors of the colon, bladder and breast.
Summit said on Sunday that the F.D.A. told the company it had rejected the drug because it had not shown a statistically significant benefit in prolonging patients’ lives in the global clinical trial that was the basis of Summit’s application.
Summit had been seeking F.D.A. approval based on the results of a study the company conducted in the United States, Canada, Europe and Asia that enrolled patients who had already tried a targeted treatment. The trial compared patients who received ivonescimab and chemotherapy with those whose only treatment was chemotherapy. In that study, the drug was successful in delaying the cancer’s progression.
Summit has argued that the failure to extend patients’ lives simply reflected slow enrollment in the study. Hoping to bolster its case, the company had sent the F.D.A. analyses that were not specified in the original research plan of patients’ longer-time outcomes, but those were not enough to persuade regulators.

sources.text: Advertisement By&nbsp Nathan Rennolds Published on 16 November 2026 - 16:53 GMT+1 Share Comments Add Euronews on Google Share Facebook Twitter Flipboard Send Reddit Linkedin Messenger Telegram VK Bluesky Threads Whatsapp Trump is planning to discuss nuclear disarmament when he meets with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China this week. US President Donald Trump said on Monday that he may meet with North Korean Supreme Leader Kim Jong-un in China this week. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Trump made the comments while speaking to reporters as he departed the White House to begin his trip to Asia, which will see him arrive in the Philippines early on Tuesday. The president is then set to travel on to China, where he is scheduled to take part in trilateral talks with his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping. "We may meet with Kim Jong-un also," Trump told the media. "So that would be good. We have the chance to accomplish a lot." Trump is planning to discuss nuclear disarmament when he meets with Putin and Xi in Shenzhen in southeastern China this week, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. "We're going to talk about denuclearisation. Tough subject because it's very hard for any of us say we'll get rid of our nukes," Trump said on Monday. "Especially since you do have other countries." He added that the wars in Iran and Ukraine would also come up, as well as "economics and trade." In August, Trump talked up his relationship with Kim and said the pair would meet at some point in the year, although he gave no further details. "The fact that I get along with him, that's a good thing not a bad thing. He has 57 very powerful nuclear weapons. Should have never allowed it to happen," the president said at the time, adding: "If I were president, I wouldn't have allowed it. But he's got them." The director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Rafael Grossi, said in September that the reported expansion of North Korea's production of weapons-grade nuclear material was a "cause for serious concern." Markdown Content:
US President Donald Trump said on Monday he might meet North Korean leader Kim Jong-un in China this week and planned to discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen.

“We may meet with Kim Jong-un,” Trump told reporters at the White House before leaving for Asia. He said any meeting would take place in China.

Trump and Kim met three times during his first term, and Washington has sought to draw Pyongyang back into talks over its nuclear programme.

Beijing said on Monday that Xi, Trump and Putin would hold their first trilateral meeting on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen.

The White House said on Friday that Trump planned to discuss reducing nuclear weapons. US media previously reported, citing sources familiar with the preparations, that the war in Ukraine had largely fallen off the agenda.

“We’ll talk about, my favourite subject, Ukraine,” Trump said. He did not specify what he would seek from Xi or Putin on the war.

02:29

Why Jensen Huang’s resignation may not be final

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said on Monday that the trilateral talks would be of “groundbreaking significance” and that Beijing wanted to discuss how the three countries could help safeguard peace and stability.

Trump also said he “would not mind” seeing Jensen Huang return as Nvidia’s chief executive and had suggested Apple’s Tim Cook for the job. The Financial Times reported on Sunday that Huang had discussed a possible comeback with confidants.

Huang resigned last week following reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer suspected of diverting advanced AI chips to China. Trump said his relationship with Jensen Huang had not put US national security at risk.

“I don’t know that she’s a Chinese spy,” Trump said of Alice Huang. “We’ll determine that.” Beijing has denied the allegation. Reuters reported that Trump said he might discuss the matter with Xi.

Trump defended sales of older chips to China while pointing to US restrictions on advanced chips such as Nvidia’s Blackwell.

“We’re heading to China, and I don’t think you want to insult China just before you get there,” he said.

Trump left the White House aboard Marine One at 9.50am and boarded Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews at 10.06am, according to the White House press pool.

Seoul deploys fighter jets after Russian aircraft enters air defence zone
The Joint Chiefs of Staff in Seoul said an unspecified number of Russian aircraft entered and later exited the Korea Air Defence Identification Zone over the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan, in the early hours of Tuesday.
File photo of a South Korean Air Force FA-50 fighter jet taking off at an air base in Wonju during an air drill on the sidelines of the annual Freedom Shield joint military exercise between South Korea and the United States on Mar 7, 2024. (Photo: AFP/South Korean Defence Ministry/Handout)
SEOUL: South Korea said it deployed fighter jets and conducted tactical manoeuvres after several Russian military aircraft entered its air defence zone on Tuesday (Nov 17).
The Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) in Seoul said an unspecified number of Russian aircraft entered and later exited the Korea Air Defence Identification Zone (KADIZ) over the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan, in the early hours of Tuesday.
"Our military detected the Russian aircraft before they entered the KADIZ and deployed Air Force fighter jets, taking tactical measures to prepare for any contingency," the JCS said in a brief statement.
An air defence identification zone is not sovereign airspace but a buffer area in which countries identify approaching aircraft for security purposes.

Seoul said the Russian aircraft did not violate South Korean airspace.
In June, more than 10 Chinese and Russian military aircraft entered South Korea's air defence zone, prompting Seoul to deploy fighter jets in response.
Those aircraft did not enter South Korean airspace.
Beijing said at the time that the joint manoeuvre with Russia was a "strategic air patrol" over the Sea of Japan, the East China Sea and the western Pacific Ocean, aimed at maintaining "regional peace and stability".
China did not specifically mention South Korea or its air defence zone.

sources.title: David Jones’ total debt is over $400m including millions owed to staff, administrators confirm | David Jones | The Guardian
sources.text:
Skip to main content Skip to navigation David Jones’ administrators revealed the retailer’s massive debt pile on Tuesday, at a meeting attended by about 500 creditors. Photograph: Con Chronis/AAP View image in fullscreen David Jones’ administrators revealed the retailer’s massive debt pile on Tuesday, at a meeting attended by about 500 creditors. Photograph: Con Chronis/AAP David Jones’ total debt is over $400m including millions owed to staff, administrators confirm Creditors meeting hears upmarket retailer owes $11m to employees and recorded a net loss of $228m last financial year Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
Upmarket retailer David Jones collapsed into administration earlier this month owing well over $400m, after accelerating financial losses and reputational damage threatened its ability to stock shelves for Christmas.
About 500 creditors attended its first meeting on Tuesday, where administrators McGrathNicol broke down the 188-year-old chain’s massive debt pile, including an estimated $180m owed to suppliers and $11m to employees.
There is also about $33m in unredeemed gift cards held by shoppers, which the retailer is still accepting, and significant sums owed to secured creditors including the retailer’s main financier, Hilco.
David Jones collapsed into voluntary administration in early November after years of steep losses left the heritage retailer falling behind on rent and supplier payments.
The retailer is set to shutter half of its 38 department stores by the end of the year, triggering mass job losses under a sweeping restructure.
Under a dual appointment, FTI Consulting has day-to-day control of operations, while administrators McGrathNicol seek a buyer or fresh injection of capital.
David Jones recorded a net loss of $228m last financial year, according to updated figures disclosed to creditors. It lost a further $69m in the first four months of the new financial year leading up to the administration.
Creditors were told that the funding pressures it was facing, coupled with reputational damage, was affecting its ability to get stock for the Christmas trading period.
Guardian Australia has reported that some suppliers are owed money from stock sent as early as April .

Promega Corporation: FDA erteilt Zulassung für OncoMate MSI Dx Analysis System von Promega als Begleitdiagnostikum für KEYTRUDA bei soliden MSI-High-Tumoren
Die US-amerikanische Food and Drug Administration (FDA) hat das OncoMate MSI Dx Analysis System von Promega zugelassen, das als Begleitdiagnostikum für KEYTRUDA , die Anti-PD-1-Therapie von Merck (außerhalb der USA und Kanadas als MSD bekannt), Patienten mit soliden Tumoren mit hoher Mikrosatelliteninstabilität (MSI-H) identifizieren soll.
Das OncoMate MSI Dx Analysis System ist ein PCR-basierter Assay zur Bestimmung des MSI-Status in soliden Tumorgeweben. Der MSI-Status kann als Grundlage für Therapieentscheidungen herangezogen werden und Strategien der Präzisionsonkologie unterstützen.
"Diese Zulassung unterstreicht unser Engagement, bedeutende diagnostische Lösungen zu entwickeln, die höchsten Qualitäts- und regulatorischen Anforderungen entsprechen", so Alok Sharma, Global Clinical Market Director bei Promega. "Mit unserem Test lassen sich Patienten der Therapie zuordnen, die ihnen am wahrscheinlichsten hilft. Dabei arbeiten wir eng mit unseren Pharma-Partnern und den behandelnden Ärzten zusammen, die die Ergebnisse des Assay nutzen."
Die Zulassung ist das Ergebnis einer Zusammenarbeit mit Merck, dem Vermarkter von KEYTRUDA . Gemeinsam arbeiten die Unternehmen daran, die personalisierte Medizin voranzutreiben und den Zugang zu Diagnostika zu erweitern, die fundierte Therapieentscheidungen ermöglichen.
Das OncoMate MSI Dx Analysis System war zuvor von der FDA als erster PCR-basierter molekularer Diagnosetest freigegeben worden, mit der sich Patienten mit Darmkrebs identifizieren lassen, die möglicherweise von weiteren Tests zur Diagnose des Lynch-Syndroms profitieren. Er ist außerdem als Begleitdiagnostikum zugelassen, um Patienten mit mikrosatellitenstabilem (MSS) Endometriumkarzinom zu identifizieren, die möglicherweise von einer Behandlung mit KEYTRUDA in Kombination mit LENVIMA (Lenvatinib) profitieren, dem oral verfügbaren Multi-Rezeptor-Tyrosinkinase-Inhibitor, der von Eisai entdeckt wurde. Diese Zulassungen gelten für die Vereinigten Staaten und ihre Territorien. Die MSI-Technologie von Promega trägt zudem die CE-Kennzeichnung gemäß IVDR in der Europäischen Union und wurde von der chinesischen National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) als Begleitdiagnostikum zugelassen, um Patienten mit soliden MSI-H-Tumoren zu identifizieren, die möglicherweise von einer Behandlung mit KEYTRUDA profitieren.
KEYTRUDA ist indiziert für erwachsene und pädiatrische Patienten mit inoperablem oder metastasiertem Krebs mit hoher Mikrosatelliteninstabilität (MSI-H) oder Mismatch-Reparatur-Defizienz, deren Erkrankung nach einer vorherigen Behandlung fortgeschritten ist und für die keine zufriedenstellenden alternativen Behandlungsoptionen zur Verfügung stehen. KEYTRUDA ist eine eingetragene Marke von Merck Sharp Dohme LLC, einer Tochtergesellschaft von Merck Co., Inc., Rahway, New Jersey, USA.

InnovAge Holding Corporation (InnovAge), headquartered in Denver, Colorado, has agreed to pay a total of $36 million to resolve allegations that it violated the federal False Claims Act and state laws by failing to provide required comprehensive medical services and timely referrals to medical specialists as expeditiously as its patients’ health conditions required.
“Failing to provide comprehensive medical services and timely specialist referrals threatens the health of our most vulnerable seniors,” said Acting Assistant Attorney General Jonathan D. Guynn of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. “This historic, first-of-its-kind settlement demonstrates the Civil Division’s commitment to combating healthcare fraud by PACE organizations.”
“Elderly patients suffer when PACE providers like InnovAge do not fulfill their obligations to schedule patient visits with medical specialists in a timely manner,” said U.S. Attorney Peter McNeilly for the District of Colorado. “The U.S. Attorney’s Office in Colorado is committed to holding PACE providers accountable to ensure they provide comprehensive and timely care.”
“PACE organizations that receive Medicare and Medicaid funding must meet their obligations to provide timely and comprehensive care to the vulnerable seniors they serve as delays can jeopardize the health of patients,” said Acting Deputy Inspector General for Investigations Miranda L. Bennett of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG). “This settlement demonstrates that organizations that fail to comply with those requirements will be held accountable. HHS-OIG remains committed to working with our law enforcement partners and leveraging the False Claims Act to help ensure providers comply with program requirements and deliver the care their patients need.”
InnovAge provides services to seniors under a dual Medicare-Medicaid program called the Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE). InnovAge has PACE centers in several states, including California, Colorado, New Mexico, and the Commonwealth of Virginia. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) pays PACE organizations a fixed monthly amount for each Medicare beneficiary enrolled in their programs. In return, PACE organizations must provide comprehensive health care services to their participants, and all services must be provided as expeditiously as the participant’s health condition requires.
This settlement resolves allegations that, from May 2016 to October 2022, InnovAge failed to provide comprehensive health care services as expeditiously as required by its patients. Specifically, InnovAge allegedly failed to maintain sufficient specialist provider networks and, in thousands of instances, InnovAge failed to timely schedule appointments or consultations for specialist medical care, such as for oncology, cardiology, surgery, and neurology, for its patients.
