Trump says he takes possible Iran bomb threat to Washington 'very seriously' - France 24 Skip to main content Advertising Trump says he takes possible Iran bomb threat to Washington 'very seriously' President Donald Trump said Tuesday that US authorities take any possible threats to Washington ‘very seriously’, following reports that Iran was planning to target senior Trump administration officials, possibly with a radioactive bomb. Tehran dismissed the reports as ‘fabricated’. Issued on: 17/11/2026 - 16:44 Modified: 17/11/2026 - 16:45 2 min Reading time Share By: FRANCE 24 US President Donald Trump speaks at the United States–Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila, Philippines, on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. © Aaron Favila, Pool AP via AP President Donald Trump said Tuesday that US authorities take "very seriously" any possible threat to Washington, following reports Iran was planning to target officials, possibly with a radioactive bomb. Asked about the potential threat during a visit to the Philippines , Trump said: "If there is (such a threat), they will pay a price the likes of which no other country has ever paid before." "I hope it's not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy." CNN, citing seven anonymous US officials, reported that US intelligence indicated that Iran was preparing to target senior Trump administration officials by detonating a so-called dirty bomb in Washington. The report said the sources characterised Iran's plans as "an effort to give itself options rather than an indicator of an imminent attack ". A dirty bomb is a conventional explosive laced with chemical or radioactive materials. Read more Trump says deal with Tehran 'could happen' amid 'intensive' talks Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei dismissed the report as "fabricated", suggesting Washington was "seeking to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs". "Step by step, they are attempting to manufacture a veneer of legitimacy for further aggression and atrocities," Baqaei wrote on X. Baqaei also criticised a recent New York Times article which said, citing analysts, that some dams, pipelines and water tunnels in Iran "may have been developed to support the country's military buildup". Iran's top negotiator in talks with the United States, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, posted a link to the same article on X, saying: "Prepping the next round on civilian infra(structure), their 'experts' tell NYT: 'dams near Iran's missile sites are dual-use'" – meaning they have both civilian and military application. "Cool. New rule: Any dam, port, or power plant near a US or Israeli base is dual-use. We'll apply your logic consistently and even-handedly," Ghalibaf added. Negotiations between the United States and Iran to end their war have stalled, and Iran recently targeted US infrastructure in the Middle East . Mediator Qatar called for restraint on Tuesday "to avoid any escalation that could undermine negotiation efforts". (FRANCE 24 with AFP) Advertising Keywords for this article Iran war

sources.text:
Russia to unveil monument honoring N. Korean troops' contribution in Kursk this year: KCNA | Yonhap News Agency Go to Contents Go to Navigation Facebook X More Pinterest Linked in Tumblr Reddit Facebook Messenger Copy URL URL is copied. OK SEOUL, Nov. 18 (Yonhap) -- Russian President Vladimir Putin has said Moscow plans to unveil a monument this year honoring North Korean troops participating in Russia's war with Ukraine, according to Pyongyang's state media Wednesday. Putin made the remarks Monday while meeting Jo Yong-won, a secretary of the Central Committee of the ruling Workers' Party of Korea and a close aide to leader Kim Jong-un, the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said, citing Russia's Tass news agency. "Russia is planning to unveil a monument to the common feats of the Russian army and the KPA in Kursk within this year," the KCNA quoted Putin as saying. KPA stands for the Korean People's Army, the North's armed forces. North Korean soldiers' role in "liberating Kursk Region added a new chapter to the history of militant friendship between the two countries," he said, adding Russia will never forget their "heroism" and "important contribution to restoring the peaceful life in Kursk." Putin also described the two countries' ties as a bond of long standing, now reinforced by a comprehensive partnership treaty he and Kim signed in June 2024. Under the treaty that includes a mutual defense clause, Pyongyang is believed to have sent an estimated 15,000 troops to Russia to help its war against Ukraine. Jo has been in Russia since Saturday, meeting a string of senior party and government officials. His visit appears aimed at reaffirming Pyongyang's commitment to deepening strategic ties and extending them beyond the military area through closer cooperation. It also came days before U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin are due to hold a three-way meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday on the sidelines of an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. sources.title: ‘Unacceptable’: Lawmakers react to revelations from ICIJ’s Cancer Calculus investigation - ICIJ
sources.text:
Skip to content Lawmakers and experts in several countries have called for pharmaceutical companies to be more transparent about drug pricing and tax dealings following revelations from ICIJ’s Cancer Calculus . The investigation, led by ICIJ and 47 media partners, explores how Merck & Co. — known as MSD outside the United States and Canada — keeps huge revenues flowing while pricing out many patients and governments from its blockbuster cancer drug Keytruda. ICIJ’s investigation revealed that Merck operates with a gross lack of transparency in pricing, even as the cost of Keytruda strains public health systems and counterfeiters reap massive windfalls from duping the expensive drug. The findings have so far elicited widespread reactions from politicians, government agencies, and health and financial accountability experts. Merck’s tax maneuvers highlighted in the U.S. The international collaboration found that Merck reduced its U.S. taxes by recording profits in lower-tax jurisdictions. In its 2025 annual report, Merck disclosed it paid around $1.6 billion in U.S. income taxes, compared to $4.5 billion in other countries. At a U.S. congressional hearing on corporate taxation on Tuesday, Zorka Milin, head of the Financial Accountability and Corporate Transparency Coalition, confirmed those findings. “Despite making more than half of its sales at outrageous prices to American customers, Merck paid more taxes to Switzerland than it did to the U.S.,” Milin said at the Democrat-led hearing. “For decades, major American pharma companies have been moving their profits and sometimes also their factories overseas. Their customers are mostly American, their intellectual property is developed here with support of American tax dollars, but somehow their profits are Irish, Swiss, Dutch.” Recommended reading
How Merck turned its wonder drug into a blockbuster — and priced out cancer patients worldwide
A ‘burgeoning black market’, inflated dosing and the over-judicialization of health care: reporters around the world tell stories about Keytruda
Report: Merck’s blockbuster cancer drug topped $200,000 a year under Trump
European lawmakers slam tax breaks, opaque pricing
In the Netherlands, ICIJ partners Trouw and Het Financieele Dagblad found that MSD received more than $1 billion in tax breaks in the Netherlands last year under a tax regime called the “innovation box,” which grants companies a reduced corporate tax rate for “innovative activities.” The program was meant to offset the cost of research and development to foster innovation, but the Dutch journalists revealed that more than 90% of its tax advantages benefit three big corporations — MSD, Booking.com and the Dutch company ASML — for older inventions.
Following the reporting, Luc Stultiens, a member of the largest Dutch opposition alliance, asked the state secretary for finance to clarify the “economic justification” of the innovation box for those companies.
Stultiens also raised questions about MSD receiving financial benefits despite ceasing many of its research operations in the country. For example, though Keytruda was originally produced in the Dutch province of North Brabant, it is now manufactured in Ireland.
“How do you explain to ordinary taxpayers and SME [small- or medium-sized enterprise] owners that they have to pay an extra billion in taxes annually for a tax rebate for a single company that has moved virtually all of its activities abroad?” he asked in an official inquiry.
In Belgium, opposition parties sought greater transparency on confidential agreements with pharmaceutical companies. Between January 2016 and June 2025, Belgium’s total gross expenditure on Keytruda — prior to substantial confidential discounts granted by MSD — was nearly $3 billion, straining the public health budget, ICIJ partners De Tijd , Le Soir and Knack reported. Six opposition members took issue with the opaque nature of the price negotiations.
No other medication is more expensive, yet the pharmaceutical company keeps the actual price secret
— Austria’s Green Party health spokesperson Eva Hammerer and parliamentary group leader Daniel Zadra
Citing Cancer Calculus reporting that shows the list price of Keytruda varies wildly across countries, Rajae Maouane, a member of the Chamber of Representatives, said during a parliamentary debate that “price is indeed a choice, a negotiation, and not an inevitability.”
Health minister Frank Vandenbroucke told members that they “must accept that confidential negotiations take place.” He also passed the buck to European lawmakers as he cited experts who told Belgian journalists that MSD doesn’t share enough data with governments on which patients are likely to respond to Keytruda.
“It is not Belgian legislation that falls short here, but European legislation,” he said.
The opposition called for hearings on price-setting for pharmaceuticals.
The issue of transparency was also raised in Austria. ICIJ partners profil , Paper Trail Media and Der Standard showed that Keytruda is the country’s single largest medication expense, costing a whopping 6,800 euros per standard 200 milligram dose (about $8,000) without discounts. That’s despite the AIM Institute calculating a fair price for the drug to be 80 euros (about $94) per dose, based on research by the Swiss nonprofit Public Eye.

In response, the Green Party demanded fair and transparent prices for lifesaving drugs in a parliamentary inquiry in the Austrian state of Vorarlberg.

sources.title: Hong Kong begins shift towards paperless share market in 5-year transition plan
sources.text:
URL Source: https://www.scmp.com/business/markets/article/3374744/hong-kong-begins-shift-towards-fully-digitalised-share-market-5-year-transition-plan

Published Time: 2026-11-18T07:00:06+08:00

Markdown Content:
Hong Kong began its shift to a paperless share market on Tuesday, with Beijing Sinotau International Pharmaceutical Technology set to become the first initial public offering (IPO) to not issue physical share certificates, while three listed companies – including the city’s bourse operator – will comprise the first batch of existing firms to transition to the new system.

Companies that went public on or after Tuesday and were constituted under the laws of mainland China, Hong Kong, Bermuda or the Cayman Islands would no longer issue physical share certificates, according to the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC).

The paperless regime was expected to provide better investor protection and greater trading convenience, the regulator said.

Sinotau launched its IPO on Monday and is scheduled to debut on November 24, making it Hong Kong’s first paperless new listing.

The company stated that it would not issue or mail any physical share certificates, adding that all warrants or rights issues associated with its shares would also be handled in paperless form, according to its prospectus.

Investors who wished to acquire IPO shares in their own names and had not yet opened an Uncertificated Securities Identifier (USI) account could still apply, said Richard Houng, CEO of Issuer Services Asia at Computershare.

However, if they were allotted shares, they would only be registered as “provisional system members”. While they could still receive dividends and attend shareholder meetings, they would need to complete the USI opening and identity verification process before they could transfer or sell their shares, Houng added.

![Image 1: Richard Houng (left), the CEO of Issuer Services Asia, at the Computershare offices. Photo: Handout](https://img.i-scmp.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=contain,width=1024,format=auto/sites/default/files/d8/images/canvas/2026/11/17/4c6452c9-1104-4165-a5ed-457f6a8573ff_f0efc083.jpg)

Richard Houng (left), the CEO of Issuer Services Asia, at the Computershare offices. Photo: Handout

As of Monday, more than 2,200 people had registered for a USI, which allows retail investors to hold legal title to Hong Kong-listed shares electronically in their own names.

Computershare is one of six securities registrars approved by the SFC for the paperless framework, formally known as the Uncertificated Securities Market regime (USM).

“This is a significant achievement for the Hong Kong market and continues to cement our place at the forefront of global capital markets,” Houng said.

The city’s roughly 2,700 listed companies were expected to transition to the paperless system in batches over the next five years, the SFC said. Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) would be among the first batch of existing issuers to join in early 2027.

Alongside HKEX, two listed companies using Computershare as their share registrar would go paperless by the end of March next year, according to Houng.

“Shareholders currently holding physical share certificates must keep them safe and wait until the respective listed companies join the USM, after which they can apply for digitisation,” he said.

Existing physical share certificates would remain valid, and the ownership and shareholder rights they represented would remain unchanged, the SFC said.

UK hands NATO-assigned US soldier accused of Russia spying to US military | Espionage News | Al Jazeera Listen (2 mins) Save Share UK hands NATO-assigned US soldier accused of Russia spying to US military on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google The unnamed US soldier has been accused of breaking UK laws related to obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service [File: Leonhard Simon/Getty Images] By Al Jazeera Staff Published On 17 Nov 2026 17 Nov 2026 A senior United States soldier assigned to NATO who was arrested in Britain last week on suspicion of spying for Russia has been transferred to US military custody, United Kingdom police have said. The Head of Counter Terrorism Police (CTP), Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, said on Tuesday that authorities in London have passed the investigation to US partners “in line with existing international protocols”. list 2 of 3 Thousands demand cancellation of Nathan Cofnas talk at Oxford University
list 3 of 3 Who is behind Habibi UK, an X account that targeted critics of Israel?
The 41-year-old man was arrested by British police on November 10 near Gloucester on suspicion of offences under Section 1 and Section 3 of the UK National Security Act 2023.
Section 1 relates to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while Section 3 relates to assisting a foreign intelligence service.
“These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place,” Taylor said.
He added, “We will continue to support our US colleagues as they take the matter forwards.”
US FBI Director Kash Patel said the army officer is in US custody as a “result of an espionage investigation” between the FBI’s Philadelphia field office and Legat London in addition to partners at “UK Counter Terrorism Policing, MI5, UK Defence Counter Intelligence, and the US Army Counterintelligence Command.”
Brigadier General Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command (ACIC), said the case illustrated the “remarkable partnership” between ACIC, US Army prosecutors, the FBI, the US Department of Justice, and the UK.
Stinchon added that this example sends a “stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath”.
The case is believed to be the first time a US soldier was found to be under suspicion of spying for a foreign government while in the UK.

sources.title: Landmark review recommends major shake-up to Australia's surrogacy laws - ABC News
sources.text:
Landmark review recommends major shake-up to Australia's surrogacy laws - ABC News Skip to main content Skip to news navigation, settings and search Explore the ABC news
Landmark review recommends major shake-up to Australia's surrogacy laws
The review says intended parents should be recognised as legal parents from birth under surrogacy arrangements. ( Flickr: Government of Alberta )
Surrogates should receive greater compensation and policies should be nationally consistent, under a proposed overhaul of the system.
Under the changes, intended parents would be legally recognised from birth, if a domestic arrangement was approved before conception.
The federal government says it will consider the recommendations alongside the states and territories.
Surrogates would be entitled to greater financial compensation for the impacts of pregnancy and childbirth under sweeping changes proposed by the country's law reform body.
The wide-ranging final report from the Australian Law Reform Commission (ALRC) found Australia's patchwork of state and territory laws made surrogacy unnecessarily difficult, were driving parents overseas, could leave surrogates financially worse off and did not adequately safeguard the rights of children.
As part of its 47 recommendations, it said there should be one nationally consistent surrogacy framework overseen by a regulator and proposed that intended parents be recognised as legal parents from birth.
"Good surrogacy laws should do two things: enable people to form families through surrogacy where it can be undertaken responsibly; and provide effective safeguards against exploitation and harm. Our current laws do not achieve either aim," ALRC Justice Mordy Bromberg said.
"Instead, they drive Australians to pursue overseas surrogacy arrangements, which can expose children, surrogates and intended parents to great risk of harm and exploitation."
The purpose of examining the laws is to protect the rights of children born of surrogacy. ( Public domain: Amanda Jordan )
The attorney-general asked the ALRC to examine the nation's surrogacy laws and practices in 2024, with a view to protecting the rights of children born of surrogacy and providing Australians with more clarity and certainty.
It was also asked to consider how surrogacy arrangements made overseas were recognised under Australian law and what information a child born from surrogacy should have a right to know.
The report recommended Australia maintain its ban on commercial surrogacy and only allow altruistic surrogacy, which is when the surrogate is not paid a fee or allowed to profit.
Currently, surrogates can be reimbursed for certain expenses, although what costs can be covered can vary between the states and territories.
However, the ALRC discussion paper said the current rules had left surrogates unable to fully recover their financial and non-financial costs and losses.
The report recommended a significant expansion of what can be paid to an altruistic surrogate, proposing intended parents would have to pay a broader range of costs, so a surrogate was not left worse off.
It also proposed a monthly payment for pregnancy capped at an amount set by the proposed national regulator, to address "non-economic" losses from pregnancy and childbirth, such as physical and psychological impacts.
However, the ALRC noted these changes would not count as a profit or reward, so the arrangement would be legally distinct from commercial surrogacy.
'Problematic laws' driving people overseas
Because commercial agreements are illegal, finding a surrogate can be a long and complicated process for many couples, leaving many reliant on family and friends.
For this reason, a growing number of Australians have entered commercial arrangements with a surrogate based overseas.
More than 300 Australian children are born through overseas surrogacy arrangements each year, accounting for an estimated four in five Australian surrogacy births

US President Donald Trump said he was eyeing one-on-one talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen.
US President Donald Trump speaks during an official dinner at the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila on Nov 17, 2026. (Photo: AFP/Pool/Aaron Favila)
MANILA: Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday (Nov 18) arrived in China ahead of a summit with his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump, who is on an Asian tour in search of diplomatic gains after a bruising election defeat back home.
Trump was in the Philippines on Tuesday for a meeting with the leaders of the so-called Quad countries and said he was eyeing one-on-one talks with Putin and North Korea's Kim Jong Un at his next stop, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China's Shenzhen.
"If it's available, I would do that," Trump told reporters as he stood for photos with fellow Quad leaders Narendra Modi of India, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Australia's Anthony Albanese.
He added that North Korea's Kim "would like" to meet in China, hours after Beijing said it had no information about an encounter between the two.

While the Quad - broadly aimed at counterbalancing China's regional influence - has quietly progressed in deepening coordination, the short time allotted for Tuesday's meeting meant it was unlikely to extend beyond pleasantries, according to analysts.
While Trump was greeted in Manila by a marching band and honour guard on the airport tarmac, elsewhere about 2,000 demonstrators faced off with police, carrying banners reading "Trump out now" and "Reject Pax Silica" - a reference to a US supply chain initiative that has divided opinion in the Philippines.
While ASEAN leaders have spent three days grappling with a raft of regional issues, the spectre of Trump's ongoing tariff blitz has loomed large.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Monday slammed what he called a "countercurrent of unilateralism and protectionism" while touting Beijing's own expanding trade with the bloc.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Canada's Mark Carney sang a similar tune on trade, with both explicitly citing a need to wean themselves off dependence on the US market.
On Tuesday, a combative Trump showed no let-up in his trade war with Beijing, saying the United States would catch China in rare earths production "within 10 months".
"We are making rare earths at a level that we've never made before. We're going to catch them within 10 months, they say," he said.

Oleg Kiper, the head of the Odesa region’s military administration, said three Russian strikes hit the city’s “historic centre”. Odesa city council said one of the strikes hit a UNESCO-protected area, causing a car to catch fire and blowing out hundreds of windows in at least seven buildings.
Ukrainian emergency services shared images showing wounded people on stretchers, buildings with shattered windows and firefighters extinguishing a blaze on a rooftop.
“There were double-tap strikes after first responders and police officers had already arrived at the scene,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.
He said the attack served as “further proof of what the Russians really want and how they truly regard diplomatic efforts”.
In the southeastern Zaporizhia region, a Russian drone strike killed a woman and injured a man in the town of Kushuhum, local military administration official Mykhailo Semykin said.
Attacks on the region also forced local authorities to order families with children to leave the village of Balabyne, he said.
“We are talking about 85 children from 80 families. In total, the evacuation affects 184 people,” he wrote on Telegram.
In northern Ukraine’s Rivne region, 80 settlements were left without electricity after a Russian attack, authorities said. No deaths or injuries were reported.
Ukraine’s Energy Ministry says Russia has launched more than 1,000 attacks on energy infrastructure since September. New power outages had been recorded in Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zhytomyr, Zaporizhia, Kharkiv, Sumy, Rivne, and Cherkasy regions in the last 24 hours, Interfax reported on Wednesday. Russia has increased attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in the lead-up to winter, in a strategy the United Nations said amounted to war crimes.
“The situation in the Dnipropetrovsk and Kharkiv regions remains extremely difficult. Energy workers are doing everything possible to restore power supply as soon as possible, but repeated attacks are significantly complicating repair work,” Ukraine’s energy ministry said.
The attacks came a day after Ukraine attacked Russia’s Kerch Bridge – a symbolic road-and-rail link from Russia to the annexed Crimean peninsula – killing two people.
As the warring sides continue to trade long-range attacks, the European Commission has proposed a new 45 billion euro ($49.5bn) loan to Ukraine to help fill a 70 billion euro ($76.8bn) funding gap for next year.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Ukraine would only need to repay the loan after Russia had paid reparations for damage caused since it launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

sources.title: Russian man accused of spying on US tech defence company that assists Ukraine - BBC News
sources.text:
Image source, US Department of Justice Image caption, The alleged foreign agent was discovered with two Russian passports By Max Matza Published 52 minutes ago
US investigators have arrested a Russian man who they say was recruited by Moscow to spy on employees of a technology and defence firm in California's Silicon Valley that has links to Ukraine.
Igor D'iu is accused of acting as an agent of a foreign government to conduct a spying operation in Palo Alto, near San Francisco.
He is also accused of stalking employees of the company and possessing falsified identity documents.
The company is not named in charging documents, but is described as a publicly traded technology and defence company that produces software used by Ukraine in its war with Russia. US prosecutors say the company was targeted by Russia due to its assistance to Kyiv.
"The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company's assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia," said US Attorney for the Northern District of California Craig Missakian.
"We will not tolerate any efforts - by foreign governments or otherwise - to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations."
Prosecutors say that D'iu entered the US unlawfully via the Mexico border, after travelling there from Istanbul in June.
He was allegedly recruited through the Telegram encrypted messaging app. His handlers referred to Russia as "'the Motherland' and directed D'iu to gather information about the company because it was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine".
On their instruction, he purchased computers, phones, wireless networking equipment and remote access software - tools he needed for his spy mission.
He then went to a coffee shop located near the company's offices in Palo Alto, where he photographed laptop screens of employees who were working there.
His handlers also allegedly "instructed him to position his laptop at designated locations near the company so they could remotely access it and attempt to collect information from company employees in the vicinity".
Image source, US Department of Justice Image caption, The suspect allegedly took photos of employees screens at a cafe near the office
According to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, the company in question is Palantir Technologies. Palantir did not reply to a BBC request for comment.
D'iu also allegedly conducted surveillance of employees and their residences.
On 3 September, he followed a vehicle driven by one senior executive for nearly 30 miles. He fled after she drove to a police station. Police later obtained evidence that he had followed other employees' cars on previous days.
During the investigation, officials discovered identity cards that had been falsified - including a US passport, California ID card, and a Social Security card with the fake name "Hugo Landry Johns".
A raid on his home in October in East Palo Alto turned up two Russian passports, and a handwritten notebook that contained numerous home addresses of employees "family members' names, educational and employment histories, and assessments of their strengths and weaknesses", prosecutors say.
He faces two charges related his alleged work as a foreign agent, one charge of interstate stalking, and one count of fraud related to his identity documents. He faces over 15 years in prison if found guilty.
Image source, US Department of Justice Image caption, The suspect was found with forged identification documents including a US passport

He has been held in jail since 2 November. It is unclear whether he has hired a lawyer who can speak on his behalf.

From Dependency to Sovereignty - What the International Conference On Public Health in Africa 2026 Must Deliver for Africa's Health Security - allAfrica.com From Dependency to Sovereignty - What the International Conference On Public Health in Africa 2026 Must Deliver for Africa's Health Security 17 November 2026 Content from a Premium Partner Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Addis Ababa) In late November 2026, Addis Ababa will host the 5th International Conference on Public Health in Africa (CPHIA 2026), co-convened by the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) and the Government of Ethiopia. Its theme, 'Africa's Health Security and Sovereignty: Transformation from health dependency and vulnerability to ownership and resilience', states its intent. It is also a response to a financing and epidemiological reality that no longer allows business as usual. The numbers are stark. External health aid to Africa was projected to fall by about 70% between 2021 and 2025, while African countries were expected to spend $81 billion United States dollars (USD) (on debt service in 2025 alone). Twenty-four years after the Abuja Declaration, only three countries, Botswana, Cabo Verde and Rwanda, have achieved the agreed target of 15% of national budgets allocated to health, and 30 African Union (AU) Member States allocate less than 10%. At the same time, public health emergencies on the continent rose by 41%, from 152 in 2022 to 213 in 2024. Africa faces more frequent threats with less external funding and constrained domestic budgets. The Conference on Public Health in Africa has become the continent's main platform for bringing scientific evidence and political leadership into the same room. Since its inception in 2021, it has grown into a gathering of thousands of scientists, policymakers, implementers, private-sector leaders and civil society. Conference on Public Health in Africa 2025 in Durban, convened under the theme 'Moving toward self-reliance to achieve universal health coverage and health security', closed with the Durban Promise. This outcome document set five catalytic priorities: an African manufacturing revolution, innovative health financing, primary healthcare (PHC) transformation, pandemic preparedness and response, and data ownership and governance. The Conference on Public Health in Africa 2026 should be judged by whether it turns those priorities into delivery. This year, the Addis Ababa conference is organised around six scientific tracks. Each corresponds to a decision that African governments, institutions and partners must make in the next few years. sources.text:

Published Time: 2026-11-19T08:30:06+08:00

Markdown Content:
Some second-hand luxury goods shops have claimed to have fallen victim to a suspected fraud involving two consignment stores that abruptly closed in Hong Kong, pushing the total number of police reports to 216 and total losses to HK$38 million (US$4.8 million), the South China Morning Post has learned.

More than 200 people have joined a victims’ concern group, including other second-hand shops that lent merchandise to Vootic in Causeway Bay and Obsessplanet in Admiralty, both of which shut down suddenly on Tuesday.

Police said on Wednesday that the force had received reports from 140 people claiming a shop on Russell Street had failed to settle payments totalling HK$26.5 million. Another 76 people filed reports relating to outstanding payments from a shop on Harcourt Road in Admiralty, totalling HK$11.5 million.

On Tuesday, police said they had received reports from at least 43 people about alleged outstanding payments totalling more than HK$16.6 million.

Vootic is registered under the name Exodia. Its director is Hideyasu Kunisato, who took over the role from Nobuhiro Enoki in 2018. According to sources familiar with the matter, Obsessplanet’s Admiralty outlet is operated by Kunisato’s wife.

A housewife in her late twenties, who asked to be identified only as Mrs Kan, said she first became suspicious on Monday night after being unable to contact the couple, whom she had known for more than a decade.

She said she had lent the couple more than HK$700,000 in late October through cash and credit card transactions, after they repeatedly appealed to her for financial help. Kan said the couple had only repaid her HK$150,000 so far.

In the early hours of Tuesday, after discovering her messages could no longer be delivered, Kan went to the couple’s Yau Tong residence around 4am. Finding their car gone, she filed a police report.

Kan believes the closures may have been premeditated, citing the unusually high prices the shops offered for consigned goods over the past one to two years.

She said the victims’ group chat had about 40 members when she joined on Tuesday, but membership had since grown to more than 240. In addition, the group included second-hand luxury goods shops that said they had lent merchandise to the two stores.

![Image 1: A business owner who lent items worth HK$844,000 to the two shops, including the handbags pictured, says only some of the merchandise has been returned. Photo: Handout](https://img.i-scmp.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=contain,width=1024,format=auto/sites/default/files/d8/images/canvas/2026/11/19/64f7367d-beb6-49e6-9116-f380afb353ce_8381516b.jpg)

A business owner who lent items worth HK$844,000 to the two shops, including the handbags pictured, says only some of the merchandise has been returned. Photo: Handout

One business owner told the SCMP that they had supplied the two shops with goods – mainly Hermes handbags – from early August for sale through live-streaming sessions, but the stores had not returned some of the handbags, which were worth a total of HK$844,000.

The owner said they had worked with the two shops for several years, during which the handbags they supplied were usually sold quickly and payments were made promptly.

This time, however, the shops repeatedly delayed payment, citing reasons including frozen bank accounts.

Kan said she knew of three other shops that had also been affected, each with alleged losses of about HK$4 million.

The cases involving the two shops have been classified as fraud and remain under investigation. They are being handled by the serious crime units of the Wan Chai and Central police districts respectively.

Former Liberal minister Sharman Stone dies after brain cancer battle
Sharman Stone has died at the age of 75. ( ABC News: Nick Haggarty )
Former Liberal MP Sharman Stone, a former minister under the Howard government, has died by voluntary assisted dying.
Dr Stone died after a long illness, surrounded by her three children in Shepparton on Wednesday. She had 12 grandchildren.
Her family said she "died on her own terms" after a long battle with an aggressive form of brain cancer, glioblastoma.
They said Dr Stone was a passionate fighter for regional Australia who never lost her drive.
"It's a great comfort we could spend final time with her at home and amongst the community she loved," they said in a statement.
John Howard and Sharman Stone pictured at a Liberal party event earlier this year. ( Supplied )
Born into a farming family, Dr Stone advocated for rural communities, Indigenous people, and the rights of prisoners through her work and writing.
She was regarded as a trailblazer, becoming one of the first women superintendents in the Office of Corrections and the first woman director in the Victorian Farmers' Federation. She also held a PhD in economics.
Sharman Stone with her daughter Nadia Stone, her granddaughter Olivia Yu and her grandson Alexander Yu. ( Supplied )
Elected to federal parliament in 1996, Dr Stone held what was then the seat of Murray, which covered Shepparton, Echuca, Cobram, Euroa and Yarrawonga.
She held the Victorian seat for 20 years before retiring and was then named Australia's Ambassador for Women and Girls.
Liberal Member for Northern Victoria, Wendy Lovell, said it was "a profound privilege to have enjoyed her friendship over the years, and to have seen up close her courage, determination, intelligence, and kindness".
"She was compassionate and cared deeply for those suffering hardship, and fought relentlessly on behalf of irrigators, farmers and workers in the region during the most difficult times," Ms Lovell said.
"Sharman was a constant advocate for gender equality, who lived by her words and actively supported other women who aspired to serve their community in politics or business.
"Sharman was deeply loved, and will be fondly remembered and sadly missed."
Dr Stone is being remembered as a strong local member for her community.
She was known for her passionate advocacy on women's rights, pushing for more generous paid parental leave and closing the gender pay gap.
She was a believer in the Liberal Party but never afraid to speak her mind, as she crossed the floor and challenged her own party on a number of issues.
Some of those included the Murray-Darling Basin Plan, her effort to overturn a ban on the abortion drug RU486, and a fight to protect the local fruit growing industry from the disease fire blight.
She also accused her own leader, then-Prime Minister Tony Abbott and Treasurer Joe Hockey, of lying about her impassioned push to get taxpayer-funded assistance for local fruit manufacturer SPC Ardmona .
Sharman Stone, pictured in 2014, fought for support for the SPC fruit company in her electorate. ( AAP: Alan Porritt )
Dr Stone held a number of roles during John Howard's government, including parliamentary secretary to the environment minister and parliamentary secretary to the minister of finance.
She briefly served as the workplace participation minister under Mr Howard in 2006 until the defeat of the Coalition in the 2007 election to Kevin Rudd.
In opposition, she took on the shadow portfolio of environment under Brendan Nelson's leadership and later was shadow immigration minister under Malcolm Turnbull.
Sharman Stone with her three children, Nadia, Kirk and Georgia, in 2024. ( Supplied )

The incident was detected on October 22 and there was ‌no evidence ​of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole, European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told reporters.
"This was an AI-generated ‌cybercampaign," he added.
Regnier did not elaborate on the attack or name a perpetrator. He said the Commission "has taken the necessary steps in response."
This is the first time the bloc reported an AI-assisted cyberattack.
Regnier's statement came after Politico reported earlier on Thursday that the Commission had been targeted. The report said the cyberattack disrupted several systems for 10 days and might have compromised large amounts of personal data. The European Commission has roughly 33,000 employees.
The ​Commission then convened its highest-level internal crisis management body for an urgent meeting about the cyber incidents, according to Politico.
"We temporarily took down several applications, and most of them have since then been restored," Regnier said. He also stated that they did not detect any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff.
Recent hybrid attacks on supermarkets , air traffic controllers , blood banks and broadcasters across Europe have raised worries among leaders that this may be part of a coordinated attempt at hybrid warfare.
France summoned the Iranian ambassador last week over cyberattacks that caused supermarket freezers to defrost, but Tehran has denied any involvement.

sources.title: EU must move beyond piecemeal trade deals with China, MEPs warn | Euronews
sources.text: Advertisement By&nbsp Peggy Corlin Published on 19 November 2026 - 16:30 GMT+1 Share Facebook Twitter Flipboard Send Reddit Linkedin Messenger Telegram VK Bluesky Threads Whatsapp MEPs are calling on the European Commission to “ease” the regulatory burden on EU companies and deploy “horizontal” trade defence tools to tackle Chinese competition. The EU needs a “systematic” approach to China that goes beyond its current sector-by-sector trade strategy, according to a cross-party coalition of MEPs. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič, the MEPs warn against pursuing more deals like the one the Commission struck with Beijing in October to curb imports of Chinese hybrid cars. “Carving out single-sector export limits cannot substitute for both, faster regulatory simplification and comprehensive defence of Europe’s industrial baseline against systematic market disruption,” reads the letter, initiated by Slovak MEP Miriam Lexmann (EPP). The EU faces a trade deficit with China of €1 billion a day, while a surge in low-cost Chinese imports is widely seen as a threat to thousands of jobs across European industries. EU countries gave the Commission a mandate in June to negotiate with Beijing to rebalance trade relations while developing new trade defence tools. In October, France and Germany called for a new instrument that would restrict market access for foreign competitors causing serious market disruption. In the letter sent to the Commission president, MEPs from the centre-right European People’s Party (EPP), the largest political group in Parliament, the liberal Renew group, the Socialists and Democrats (S&D), the Greens and the Eurosceptic European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR) call for “horizontal” quotas and tariffs to address Chinese overcapacities. The MEPs also highlight “weak” customs enforcement, which enables tax evasion and breaches of safety rules, and warn that lengthy EU investigations risk leaving European companies facing closure before protective measures are introduced. “The Commission must now implement a systematic approach,” the letter adds, including regulatory simplification to “ease regulatory burden” on EU companies and the deployment of “horizon-wide” trade defence instruments. The MEPs also call for “strict local supply chain content rules” and the “harmonisation” of EU customs controls. The letter comes as Šefčovič prepares for talks with his Chinese counterpart, Commerce Minister Wang Wentao, in January and March next year. The Commission is also expected to unveil the new trade defence instrument sought by Paris and Berlin before the end of the year. sources.title: Howard-era minister Sharman Stone dies via voluntary assisted dying, aged 75 | Liberal party | The Guardian
sources.text:
Skip to main content Skip to navigation Former Liberal MP Sharman Stone held roles during the Howard government including as parliamentary secretary to the environment and finance ministers . Photograph: Alan Porritt/AAP View image in fullscreen Former Liberal MP Sharman Stone held roles during the Howard government including as parliamentary secretary to the environment and finance ministers . Photograph: Alan Porritt/AAP Howard-era minister Sharman Stone dies via voluntary assisted dying, aged 75 The former Liberal MP had fought a long battle against glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast
Former Liberal MP Sharman Stone has died via voluntary assisted dying after spending much of her political career advocating that people should have autonomy over their bodies.
Stone died aged 75 on Wednesday surrounded by family after a long fight against glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer. She had a long political career, serving as the minister for workforce participation from 2006-07 and the ambassador for women and girls from 2016-20.
During her time in office, Stone championed contentious medical research and supported access to abortion, and readily – and publicly – disagreed with former leader Tony Abbott on both topics.
“Sharman and I disagreed on ‘life’ issues … but she was always upfront about what she thought and always handled disagreement well,” Abbott told the Sydney Morning Herald after her death.
“That actually made her a good colleague because being straight with people is just about the most important quality anyone can have.”
Stone was one of the first female superintendents in the Victorian Office of Corrections, the first female director of the Victorian Farmers Federation, and the recipient of an economics PhD.
She was elected to federal parliament in 1996, serving through the Howard years in what was then the seat of Murray in northern Victoria.
Nationals MP Sam Birrell, who now holds the same seat Stone once held, paid tribute to his predecessor in a post on Facebook .
“Sharman was an articulate and intelligent fighter for our region, and made significant contributions to parliament and Australian public life in areas such as women’s rights, regional manufacturing and indigenous affairs,” he wrote.
“Sharman was particularly strident in her advocacy for regional communities in relation to the Murray-Darling Basin plan, and she always warned of the dangers of water buybacks to the economies of the regions affected.
“She was never afraid to confront anyone on issues she believed in, even those in her own party.”
Stone was remembered as a strong voice for her local community, right up to her later days.
“She was born and bred in the heart of the electorate she served – a sixth-generation northern Victorian from a farming family,” the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said after her death.
“She understood the rugged and regenerative nature of the land and what makes regional Australia tick.”
Stone spent two decades in parliament and was characterised by her independence.
“Over all the years, on every day, I have striven to make a difference, to create more opportunities and more choices for the people I love, the people of Murray,” she said in her retirement speech from federal parliament in 2016.
“My Murray electorate is magnificent. Its people are heroic, innovative and resourceful.”
She held several roles during the Howard government, including as parliamentary secretary to the environment and finance ministers.
She also held the shadow environment portfolio after the Liberals’ defeat to Kevin Rudd.
Stone retired from politics in 2016, and served as the Australian ambassador for women and girls until 2020.
Her celebration of life is expected to be held after the 28 November Victorian election.

sources.title: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say - BBC News
sources.text:
Image source, Reuters By Jaroslav Lukiv , Laura Gozzi and Paul Kirby , Europe digital editor Published 19 November 2026
European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.
Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen , south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.
In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.
Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."
But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".
Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".
Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition.
Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions.
Zelensky and the three European leaders – Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron – were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."
The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".
"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.
He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen.

Brian Mast, a Florida Republican and chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, used his authority under the Export Control Reform Act to make public the details of Nvidia and AMD licence applications to sell AI chips to [China](https://www.scmp.com/topics/china?pgtype=search?module=inline&pgtype=article).

“[The Committee] determines that the withholding of the following information is contrary to the national interest,” the released document said.

The disclosure draws on a summary from the [US Commerce Department’s](https://www.scmp.com/topics/us-commerce-department?pgtype=search?module=inline&pgtype=article) Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) as dated May 11. Comanchero boss Allan Meehan and bikie associate Marco Coffen hit with US sanctions - ABC News Skip to main content Skip to news navigation, settings and search Explore the ABC news
Comanchero boss Allan Meehan and bikie associate Marco Coffen hit with US sanctions
Southern Highlands-based Allan Meehan has been hit with sanctions by the Trump administration. ( Supplied )
Two Australians have found themselves in Donald Trump's sights as part of sanctions on the Comanchero bikie gang.
Allan Meehan and Marco Coffen face restrictions prohibiting American companies processing transactions for the pair.
The move comes as part of the Trump administration's crackdown on people connected to Mexican drug cartels.
Two Australians connected to the Comanchero bikie gang have been targeted by the Trump administration as part of a wider crackdown on Mexican drug cartels.
The sanctions handed to Allan Meehan and Marco Coffen overnight prohibit American businesses or residents conducting financial transactions with the pair.
The restrictions approved by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent were part of sweeping prohibitions against the Comanchero and Italian gangsters the 'Ndrangheta, otherwise known as the Calabrian mafia.
"[Cartels] rely on other criminal organisations like the Comanchero and 'Ndrangheta to move drugs, launder illicit proceeds, and ultimately poison Americans with narcotics," Mr Bessent said.
Australia does not enforce US sanctions, but American businesses operating here may not process transactions for Meehan and Coffen, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) said.
Assistant Commissioner Stephen Nutt says the move will "constrain" the Comanchero. ( ABC News )
"The Comanchero provides logistical support to some of the world's most dangerous cartels, including organisations designated by the United States as foreign terrorist organisations," AFP Assistant Commissioner Stephen Nutt said.
"[The] sanctions will constrain the Comanchero's access to the international financial system and increase the risks for those who enable or do business with it.
"Our objective is to make it harder, riskier and more expensive for the Comanchero to operate."
The crackdown is the first time an Australian-based crime gang has been sanctioned, the AFP said.
Meehan is considered by the US government to be the Comanchero "world president", but keeps a low profile from his Southern Highlands, NSW home.
This is despite reports earlier this year that Meehan and a Comanchero sergeant-at-arms had been removed from the gang over an internal squabble.
Allan Meehan has been a target of law enforcement since rising through the Comanchero ranks. ( ABC News )
Meehan rose to power within the Comanchero as its national president four years ago after several high-ranking members found themselves imprisoned.
A former member of the Rebels bikie gang before patching over, Meehan has emerged as a key focus of law enforcement since.
Meehan found himself a target of rarely used police powers in 2022, with NSW Police placing restrictions on his associations, his money and his movements.
Seeking to escape those restrictions on the Gold Coast, Meehan was taken back to Sydney in handcuffs to face charges for breaching them.
The NSW Police served Meehan with a Serious Crime Prevention Order at a time when the Comanchero were at war with Sydney's Ahmad crime family.
The feud saw three people shot dead: Omar Zahed, Mahmoud "Brownie" Ahmad and Rami Iskander.
Meehan is not accused of having any involvement in those attacks and has never been charged with or accused of drug offences related to Mexican drug cartels.
Less is known about Coffen, who is described by the AFP and the US Treasury as an associate of the gang.
Coffen has been overseas since 2013 and is a person of interest in the murder of security guard Gary Allibon, suspected to have been perpetrated by the Comanchero.
His name has also emerged in the years since in connection with runnin

sources.title: Hong Kong joins global drug body ahead of schedule, boosting regulatory ambitions
sources.text:
URL Source: https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/health-environment/article/3375266/hong-kong-joins-global-drug-body-ahead-schedule-boosting-regulatory-ambitions

Published Time: 2026-11-20T20:03:00+08:00

Markdown Content:
Hong Kong has joined a global body for drug regulators ahead of schedule, a move health authorities say brings the city closer to establishing its own internationally recognised regulatory authority.

The city was admitted as the 20th regulatory member of the International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH) at an assembly meeting in Prague on Tuesday.

Hong Kong is poised to become a crucial “bridgehead” for mainland Chinese drugs to reach global markets amid current geopolitical tensions.

“After becoming an observer, it took us three years to become a regulatory member of the ICH, which is substantially faster than our original prediction of eight to 10 years,” Director of Health Ronald Lam Man-kin said on Friday.

“This shows that the [Hong Kong] government has long attained top standards in drug and medical device regulation, and our determination in safeguarding public health.”

The ICH is a non-profit organisation that brings together regulators and drug makers to harmonise technical requirements for the development and registration of safe, effective and high-quality medicines.

Since Hong Kong became an observer in 2023, health authorities have worked towards regulatory membership by attending meetings, appointing experts to ICH working groups and implementing its guidelines locally.

Lam attributed the rapid progress to the city’s strong regulatory foundations, as well as guidance and support from the National Medical Products Administration, the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office and the Chinese foreign ministry’s arm in the city.

He said health authorities had also set up a task force to engage industry representatives and understand their regulatory needs.

Other ICH regulatory members include authorities from mainland China, Singapore, Switzerland, the United Kingdom and the United States.

![Image 1: Ronald Lam credits strong regulatory foundations and national support for Hong Kong’s early admission to a global drug body. Photo: Edmond So](https://img.i-scmp.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=contain,width=1024,format=auto/sites/default/files/d8/images/canvas/2026/11/20/cf28d9c1-1ad0-4826-9707-7946593cf64f_1126e908.jpg)

Ronald Lam credits strong regulatory foundations and national support for Hong Kong’s early admission to a global drug body. Photo: Edmond So

“As a member of the ICH, we are now a player, a rule maker and potentially a forerunner in international standards,” Lam said.

“Why are we becoming an international health and medical innovation hub? Because many innovative drugs will be able to access the mainland market through the drug regulatory regime of Hong Kong.

“Similarly, innovative drugs from the mainland could go global thanks to our international recognition.”

Authorities previously announced plans to introduce primary evaluation in phases by 2030, allowing Hong Kong to assess and approve drugs and medical devices independently, without relying on overseas approvals.

To facilitate that process, the government launched the 1+ mechanism in November 2023, allowing drug makers to seek registration in Hong Kong for products supported by local clinical data and approval from one foreign regulatory authority rather than two.

Lam said the government would not rule out bringing the 2030 timetable forward once the city had built up sufficient talent, expertise and experience, particularly for major innovative drugs to treat serious or rare conditions.

Since the first phase began in March this year, authorities have received five applications from mainland and overseas drug makers covering changes to therapeutic indications, dosages and product presentations.

sources.title: How Beijing’s South China Sea stance benefits from rare joint warning to the ICC
sources.text:
URL Source: https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomacy/article/3375277/how-beijings-south-china-sea-stance-benefits-rare-joint-warning-icc

Published Time: 2026-11-20T22:00:05+08:00

Markdown Content:
A rare consensus reached by China, Russia and the US that challenges the authority of international judicial bodies matters for Beijing’s rejection of a 2016 arbitration ruling on the [South China Sea](https://www.scmp.com/topics/south-china-sea?module=inline&pgtype=article), according to analysts.

The joint declaration issued after the [unprecedented trilateral summit](https://www.scmp.com/topics/xi-trump-putin-trilateral-meetings?module=inline&pgtype=article) between Chinese President [Xi Jinping](https://www.scmp.com/topics/xi-jinping?module=inline&pgtype=article), Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump on Thursday said the three leaders “recognised that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of state officials are of paramount importance”.

It also urged the International Criminal Court (ICC) and “other similar bodies” not to “abuse their jurisdiction”.

For Moscow and Washington, the stakes are immediate: Putin faces an ICC arrest warrant, while the US has long resisted the court’s authority over American personnel and allies.

[Video 9](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y-Nm6cfGZ7U)

02:48

Xi, Trump and Putin meet for historic trilateral summit at Shenzhen Apec meeting

Yet for China, which is not a party to the 1998 Rome Statute that established the ICC, the careful wording could cover a range of international legal mechanisms.

Most notable among these is the arbitral tribunal established under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos), which in 2016 [issued a ruling](https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/article/3360410/how-philippines-reshaping-south-china-sea-defence-10-years-after-hague-ruling?module=inline&pgtype=article) on the South China Sea that went against Beijing’s position.

On Friday, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said Beijing supported international judicial institutions playing a constructive role, but he issued a warning.

“No international judicial institution should violate the principle of state consent or abuse its jurisdiction,” Guo said, adding that such institutions should “avoid politicisation and double standards”.

The reference to the ICC came amid escalating tensions between the Netherlands-based international court and both Russia and the US.

In 2023, the court issued arrest warrants for Putin and a Russian official over what it called the unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children. Additional warrants brought the total number of wanted Russian officials to six.

Last month, the Trump administration imposed sanctions against the ICC itself and earlier authorised asset freezes and visa bans on court officials investigating US personnel or allies, including Israel, whose outgoing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces an ICC arrest warrant over the [Israel-Gaza war](https://www.scmp.com/topics/israel-gaza-war?module=inline&pgtype=article).

In 2020, the US imposed sanctions on ICC officials in retaliation for the court’s investigation into alleged war crimes in Afghanistan.

From China’s perspective, the declaration’s phrase “other similar bodies” primarily refers to the South China Sea arbitral tribunal and “extends to any international institution claiming jurisdiction over sovereignty and territorial disputes”, according to Wang Jiangyu, a law professor at [City University of Hong Kong](https://www.scmp.com/topics/city-university-hong-kong?module=inline&pgtype=article).

While Washington has long supported the tribunal that issued the 2016 ruling, the Trump administration’s hostility towards the ICC has created an opportunity for tacit alignment, Wang said.

“In essence, the US has semi-explicitly accepted China’s position in opposing the jurisdiction of the South China Sea arbitral tribunal,” Wang added.

sources.text:
Skip to main content Welcome to Africanews Please select your experience Watch Live News
Ukraine: Rescue teams search wreckage after deadly Russian strike on Kyiv
Smoke billowed over Kyiv and flames tore through apartment blocks and offices after Russia unleashed more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles across Ukraine overnight, killing at least eight people, six of them in the capital, and injuring 15, according to Ukrainian authorities and emergency services. Alongside residential and commercial buildings, strikes hit hospitals, essential infrastructure and three bridges spanning the Dnipro River, leaving streets littered with shattered masonry, twisted metal and wrecked cars. Across the battered capital, firefighters battled blazes while rescue teams searched ruined structures for survivors, police combed the debris for forensic evidence and utility crews worked to restore vital services. Some fires had been brought under control, but responders continued working to extinguish remaining blazes, clear rubble and assess damage across the capital. The devastating barrage, coming just a day after an earlier wave of attacks damaged diplomatic premises in Kyiv, made good on Russian President Vladimir Putin’s warning of a "painful" retaliation for Ukraine’s strike on the Crimean Bridge earlier in the week.

sources.text:
Poland condemns Russian ‘provocation’ after airspace violations | Russia-Ukraine war News | Al Jazeera Listen (3 mins) Save Share Poland condemns Russian ‘provocation’ after airspace violations on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google Surveillance camera footage shows an explosion in eastern Poland amid reported Russian air space incursions [AFP] By Al Jazeera Staff , AP and Reuters Published On 20 Nov 2026 20 Nov 2026 Poland has said Russia violated its airspace three times overnight, in what Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said was a “provocation” by Moscow. Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told a news conference on Friday that investigations were under way at three locations – Nowy Lipowiec, roughly 60km (37 miles) from the Poland-Ukraine border, Molodycz, about 50km (31 miles) to the south, and Rudnik nad Sanem, about 50km to the west. Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Russia unleashes retaliatory barrage on Kyiv bridges
list 2 of 3 Kushner says Russia OK with ‘NATO-like’ security pact for Ukraine: Is it?
list 3 of 3 UK says new deal will ‘rebuild bridges’ with EU: What’s in it?
Kosiniak-Kamysz added that the three objects were probably two missiles and a drone.
The incursions were reported as Poland held military exercises involving the “ Coalition of the Willing “, a group of European countries coordinating help and support for Ukraine.
The potential crash site near Nowy Lipowiec is about 76km (47 miles) from where European troops were taking part in military exercises to prepare for a potential post-war mission in Ukraine, aimed at helping to stabilise the country and rebuild its military once the war ends.
“These exercises, combined with the presence of defence ministers from France, the United Kingdom, and the Baltic states – along with eight chiefs of staff, including those from our key allies – suggest that the convergence of these events is no accident,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said.
The defence minister said Poland would ask NATO for more support securing the alliance’s eastern flank.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said in a post on X that the incident was “clearly dangerous” and that NATO stood in solidarity with Poland.
Tusk said Rutte would visit Warsaw on Saturday. The Polish prime minister added that there was no doubt the objects that landed in Poland were Russian.
“It seems we are dealing with an intentional provocation,” he said. “Today, it is clearer than ever before that ⁠Poland must participate in decisions and discussions regarding the future of Ukraine and security in Europe.”
British ⁠Prime Minister Andy Burnham condemned Russia’s violation of Polish airspace, calling it “utterly ⁠unacceptable”.
“Europe will not be ⁠deterred from our support for Ukraine,” he said at an EU-UK summit news conference in ‌Brussels. “We will not allow [Russian President Vladimir] Putin to divide our continent, and ‌we recognise that the front line in Ukraine is the front line for freedom and democracy everywhere.”
Drones have repeatedly strayed into the airspace of countries on NATO’s eastern flank during Russia’s war in Ukraine, fuelling tension with the Western military alliance and stoking fears that the conflict ⁠could spread.
The incident in Poland came against the backdrop of Russian attacks in Ukraine that killed eight people, injured dozens more and damaged bridges and transport infrastructure.

sources.text:
URL Source: https://www.scmp.com/news/world/russia-central-asia/article/3375302/russian-missiles-land-poland-europe-holds-military-drills-nearby

Published Time: 2026-11-21T07:43:44+08:00

Markdown Content:
There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the missiles and suspected drone, or on Friday’s drills.

![Image 1: A French soldier flies a drone at the Nowa Deba military training ground in Poland on Friday. Photo: AFP](https://img.i-scmp.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=contain,width=1024,format=auto/sites/default/files/d8/images/canvas/2026/11/21/56cee487-56d9-467d-b6ef-5ea50a16509b_29f9159b.jpg)

A French soldier flies a drone at the Nowa Deba military training ground in Poland on Friday. Photo: AFP

One Russian missile is believed to have crashed around 35km (22 miles) from where the military exercises were taking place, officials said.

A Kh-101 cruise missile went down roughly 50km (30 miles) from the Ukraine border, and what officials believe was likely a jet-powered drone hit about 30km (20 miles) from the border with Ukraine.

There were no immediate reports of injuries or damage.

European troops were taking part on Friday in an unprecedented two-week military exercise that began November 9 in southeastern Poland. Forces are preparing for a possible post-war mission in Ukraine aimed at helping to stabilise the country and rebuild its military.

European countries have previously expressed alarm at what they deem to be Russia’s attempts to destabilise the continent.

US President Donald Trump discussed the war at a summit in China on Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, according to his envoy Steve Witkoff.

Another envoy, Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, told European leaders that the US believes Russia is “comfortable” with Nato-like security guarantees for post-war Ukraine, in what could be a step towards compromise.

![Image 2: Polish soldiers take part in combat vehicle servicing and technical support during an exercise at the Nowa Deba military training ground on Friday. Photo: AFP](https://img.i-scmp.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=contain,width=1024,format=auto/sites/default/files/d8/images/canvas/2026/11/21/e2ef23d3-1818-4ad1-a2cb-408fa72fba61_686e78c9.jpg)

Polish soldiers take part in combat vehicle servicing and technical support during an exercise at the Nowa Deba military training ground on Friday. Photo: AFP

But Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov said on Friday that even a quasi-membership in Nato for Ukraine would be unacceptable, Russia’s Interfax news agency reported.

“We discuss security guarantees primarily in terms of ensuring the security of our own country, and that’s what we’re talking about,” Ryabkov said.

Russia’s nighttime attack on Ukraine came hours after Putin vowed to retaliate for Ukrainian strikes this week on a bridge linking occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland. The bridge is vital to Moscow’s war effort.

Images from closed-circuit cameras and a mobile phone in the region collected by Poland’s PAP news agency showed a large, loud explosion and a bright flash, apparently in a wooded area, in one of the crashes.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte called the development in Poland a “grave violation” of that country’s airspace. “This incident is clearly dangerous – a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine,” Rutte said on social media.

Rutte is expected to go to Poland this weekend in response.

Under Nato’s collective security guarantee – Article 5 of its founding treaty – an attack on any ally should be considered an attack on all 32 members. It obliges members to provide support to that ally, most likely military backup, but does not limit them to that alone.

Article 5 is not triggered automatically. Ultimately, it is a political decision that all members must agree to. Poland also has the option to enact Article 4, which it did last year. This provides for emergency consultations only.

sources.title: With the new shift in the U.S. Congress, time is running out on bills targeting drug patents - ICIJ
sources.text:
Skip to content U.S. lawmakers are facing a time crunch to pass a group of bipartisan bills targeting drug patents – laws that risk losing critical ground if not passed by the end of the year. The bipartisan measures aim to stop drugmakers from using patents to delay cheaper competition, and legislators would be forced to start many from scratch if they fail to become law before the new Congress takes over in January. The bills address some of the industry tactics ICIJ exposed in Cancer Calculus , a year-long investigation that explored the price and impact of Merck & Co’s lifesaving anti-cancer drug Keytruda. Among the at least nine bills, the ETHIC Act would limit the number of related patents a company can use when it sues a rival over a cheaper version of its drug. The Drug Competition Enhancement Act would stop companies from steering patients to slightly altered versions of a drug just to extend its patent protection. Another bill would require companies to give the Food and Drug Administration and the U.S. patent office consistent information about a product. With several of the bills’ sponsors about to leave office, the future of the bills may hinge on what happens in the next two months. While supporters hope some will get added to a year-end health package that analysts are expecting, the rest would have to be reintroduced and repeat passing through committees and votes, all under a Democratic majority with a packed health agenda. Supporters of the measures say they would get cheaper drugs to patients sooner. Industry groups, including the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, are pushing back and argue that the bills would weaken patent rights and discourage innovation. Recommended reading
Lowering doses of cancer drugs could slash global health spending by $30B, new research shows
Merck takes Austria’s Keytruda price transparency battle to top court as journalists fight for information
How Merck turned its wonder drug into a blockbuster — and priced out cancer patients worldwide
The industry’s influence looms large, says Rep. Lloyd Doggett, a Texas Democrat who co-sponsors the ETHIC Act and is retiring when his term ends in January. “Big Pharma’s tentacles continue to have a stranglehold over Congress, buying the Republicans and obtaining a long-term lease on some Democrats,” he said in a statement to ICIJ. “This Congress is not going to adopt any significant legislation that Big Pharma opposes. Whether a Democratic Congress will be any better remains to be seen.”
Neither the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America, known as PhRMA and the industry’s leading lobbying group, nor the U.S. Chamber of Commerce responded to requests for comment. PhRMA’s lobbying reports list many of the bills among the issues it has lobbied on. The trade group reported spending about $38 million on lobbying last year and more than $19 million in the first half of this year, according to lobbying reports filed with Congress.
Reporters for Cancer Calculus found that Merck and other cancer research businesses built a fortress of patents around Keytruda — the world’s best-selling drug — that could extend its monopoly through at least 2042, 14 years after its main patent expired.
Meanwhile, the drug’s prices before any discounts ranged from more than $80,000 a year in Germany to as much as $208,000 in the U.S., and many patients around the world can’t afford it.
Earlier this year, Merck told ICIJ and its media partners that it is a “common myth” that companies use many patents to block competition. Merck also said that more patents do not determine when generics or biosimilars enter the market.
Those claims might soon be tested in the United States, where Merck holds dozens of active Keytruda patents. In October, the drugmakers behind the first publicly announced U.S. application for a Keytruda biosimilar said in a press release that the FDA had accepted it for review. ICIJ found at least 11 other companies, including some in China, India and Russia, that have registered trials of their own versions with the U.S. clinical trials registry since 2023.
Big Pharma’s tentacles continue to have a stranglehold over Congress.
—Rep. Lloyd Doggett, co-sponsor of the ETHIC Act
Outside the U.S., a few biosimilars are already on sale or approved in smaller markets. In Argentina, where until this year the law made it hard to win extra patents on later changes to a drug, a local company launched a biosimilar last year at a price 56% below Merck’s. Merck then cut Keytruda’s price there by about half.
Separately, last month a Dutch court barred Merck from selling its new injectable version of the drug in eight European countries after finding it infringed a patent held by Halozyme, a biotech company that says the shot uses its technology for delivering drugs under the skin. Halozyme has also sued Merck in the U.S., and that case is pending. The U.S. patent office is reviewing the patents at issue, and so far it has sided with Merck on several of them. Halozyme has appealed some of those rulings. Merck didn’t respond to ICIJ’s request for comment.
Among the legislation being considered in Congress, the ETHIC Act has drawn some of the sharpest opposition. Sponsored by Rep. Jodey Arrington, R-Texas, and Sens. Peter Welch, D-Vt.; Josh Hawley, R-Mo.; and Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., the bill takes on drugs protected by dozens of closely related patents. Once a drug’s patent protections have expired, other companies can try to sell cheaper copies of the drugs. But the maker of the original drug can still sue over its patents; supporters of the measure say that when manufacturers hold dozens of patents for the same drug, challenging them all can be slow and costly for the rival.
