sources.title: Bayer: US judge approves $7.25 billion Roundup settlement
sources.text:
Bayer: US judge approves $7.25 billion Roundup settlement Skip to content
Roundup contains glyphosate, a weedkiller ingredient at the center of thousands of cancer-related lawsuits against Bayer [FILE: February 23, 2019] Image: Haven Daley/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement A US judge on Friday approved German chemical giant Bayer's $7.25 billion (€6.60 billion) settlement of lawsuits claiming its Roundup weedkiller causes cancer.
Judge Timothy Boyer in the US state of Missouri ruled that the agreement was "fair, reasonable, and adequate."
The decision could help Bayer end years of costly legal battles over Roundup, which the company acquired when it bought US weedkiller producer Monsanto in 2018.
"The court's final approval is a decisive milestone in the company's strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation," Bayer CEO Bill Anderson said.
How much money will Roundup cancer patients receive?
The agreement covers tens of thousands of people who say they developed non-Hodgkin lymphoma, a type of blood cancer, after using Roundup.
It also covers people who may be diagnosed with the disease in the future after previous exposure to the weedkiller.
Bayer will pay up to $7.25 billion into a special fund over the next 21 years.
Individual payments are expected to average between $10,000 and $165,000. The amount will depend on factors including the patient's age, the severity of the illness and how long they were exposed to Roundup.
Some lawyers representing cancer patients have criticized the payments as too low.
But the judge rejected their objections, saying that further delays could leave seriously ill patients waiting years for compensation.
Christopher Seeger, a lawyer representing cancer patients, welcomed the decision.
"Today's final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice," he said.
Why has it become harder to sue Bayer over Roundup?
The settlement follows a major victory for Bayer at the US Supreme Court in June.
The court ruled that Bayer could not be sued under state laws for failing to put cancer warnings on Roundup packaging.
The judges argued that US federal rules did not require such warnings and that individual states could not impose additional labeling requirements.
The decision made it much harder for cancer patients to win lawsuits against Bayer.
In October, a Missouri jury also ruled in Bayer's favor in a separate Roundup cancer case.
However, some legal battles continue. Around 200 cases are still being fought in federal courts outside the new settlement, according to Bayer.
How much have the Roundup lawsuits cost Bayer?
Monsanto introduced Roundup in 1974. Its main ingredient, glyphosate, became one of the world's most widely used weedkillers.
Farmers use Roundup to kill weeds without damaging crops that have been genetically modified to survive the chemical. It has also been widely used in private gardens and on lawns.
Missouri decision could reshape Bayer's glyphosate fight
Bayer inherited the legal problems surrounding Roundup when it bought Monsanto for $63 billion in 2018.
Since then, around 200,000 claims have been made against Bayer by people who believe the weedkiller caused their cancer .
The company already agreed to a $10.9 billion settlement in 2020. However, it failed to secure approval for a separate agreement covering future cases.
Some lawsuits have resulted in huge payouts , including a $2.1 billion award to plaintiffs in Georgia.
Bayer has already set aside $16 billion for Roundup-related legal costs. Its shares have fallen by 46% since the Monsanto takeover.
The company has also removed glyphosate from newer versions of Roundup sold to private consumers in the United States.
Scientists and regulators disagree about whether glyphosate causes cancer.
In 2015, the World Health Organization 's cancer research agency classified the chemical as "probably carcinogenic" to humans.

sources.title: Kazakhstan's Mangystau: Exploring surreal landscapes, underground mosques and desert camping - CNA Lifestyle
sources.text:
Martian landscapes, underground mosques and wild desert camping in Kazakhstan's remote west
In Kazakhstan’s remote Mangystau region, a four-day journey across ancient seabeds, towering limestone formations and vast desert landscapes reveals a world shaped by millions of years of geological change.
Bands of colour run through the Kokala Jurassic Colored Valley in Kazakhstan, exposing geological layers that offer a glimpse into the region’s distant past. (Photo: Avantika Chaturvedi)
I am sitting in the back of a four-wheel drive (4WD), the camping equipment rattling in the boot as the car lurches over a track that barely seems to exist.
Over the next four days, I am set to cover roughly 970km on-road and another 230km off-road, and there is no graceful way to describe some of the latter.
About eight hours into the road trip, through the windscreen and the window beside me, I can see little beyond a thick cloud of dust and I begin to wonder about the driver's confidence in navigating through what is almost zero visibility, when we come to a staggering halt.
It takes a few seconds for the dust to settle before the view emerges. What I see is an 80m cliff dropping beneath us, with the vast white expanse of the Tuzbair salt flats stretching towards the horizon.
“We're here!" says Arailym, our 25-year-old Kazakh guide, as though we have simply pulled up outside a hotel.
In fact, it kind of is: This is the first campsite of our expedition through Mangystau with Red Maya Travel, in the far west of Kazakhstan.
I had met the Red Maya team in Aktau, the Caspian Sea port city that serves as the gateway to Mangystau. Travellers can connect to Aktau via international hubs such as Istanbul or Dubai, or fly into Almaty or Astana and take a domestic connection.
By sundown, the drivers have doubled up as chefs, preparing chicken pasta in a makeshift galley at the back of one of the three 4WDs in our convoy, while we lie on carpets watching the Milky Way spread across the sky.
Wedged between the Caspian Sea and the Ustyurt Plateau, a vast, arid tableland stretching across parts of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan, much of Mangystau lay beneath the now extinct Tethys Sea hundreds of millions of years ago­­.
As a scuba diver who has travelled far and wide to descend underwater, there is something absurdly pleasing about arriving in the world's largest landlocked country, only to find myself standing on a former seabed.
Marine life once thrived here and the region's rocks still contain fossils and traces of prehistoric sea creatures, including shells, ammonites and shark teeth.
The Tethys deposited layers of sediment that geological upheaval eventually exposed as chalk, limestone and clay formations now sculpted by wind and water over unfathomable stretches of time.
We are reminded of this at Torysh the next morning, where hundreds, if not thousands, of enormous stone spheres appear almost out of the blue, scattered across a stretch of desert only a few tens of kilometres wide.
Some are almost perfectly round, others cracked open, and some as large as a tractor.
“These are concretions,” explains Arailym. “They are geological formations that formed within ancient sediments and were later exposed as erosion stripped away the surrounding rock.”
The further we travel through Mangystau, the harder it becomes to separate the spectacular from the historical.
At Kokala, the earth changes palette completely and the desert is suddenly streaked with colour. Layers of Jurassic clay appear in shades of white, crimson, purple and greenish grey, weathered into ridges, columns, gullies and miniature canyons dating back around 200 million years, when dinosaurs walked this land.
But the story of Mangystau did not end with the retreat of the sea. Over the centuries, people learnt to navigate, inhabit and make meaning from this unforgiving landscape.

sources.title: Takaichi to meet ICC president on Tuesday - The Japan Times
sources.text:
Takaichi to meet ICC president on Tuesday
International Criminal Court President Tomoko Akane | jiji Jiji SHARE/SAVE X Facebook LinkedIn Reddit Bluesky Threads Email Print Bookmark story Copy link Nov 21, 2026 Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi will meet with Tomoko Akane, president of the International Criminal Court, at the prime minister’s office in Tokyo on Tuesday, the government said Friday.
Takaichi and Akane will meet for the first time since the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump added the ICC president to its sanctions list in August. The meeting aims to send a message to the international community that Japan continues to fully support the ICC.
The prime minister last met Akane in January.
In response to the sanctions, Japan plans to make an early payment of its assessed contribution to the ICC for 2027. Takaichi is expected to outline such support measures during the meeting with Akane.
On Tuesday, Akane is also due to give a lecture at an event hosted by the Nonpartisan Parliamentary Association for Reconsidering Human Rights Diplomacy.

Princess Catherine reflects on cancer journey in new documentary
Princess Catherine announced she was in remission in January 2025. ( Reuters: Chris Jackson )
Kensington Palace has announced a new documentary about Princess Catherine's personal journey with cancer will broadcast this month.
The Princess of Wales announced in March 2024 she was receiving treatment for an undisclosed type of cancer.
Heal will broadcast on the BBC on November 29 before airing in Australia on Channel 9 on December 1.
The Princess of Wales will share her experience with cancer and recovery in a new documentary to be broadcast internationally in the coming weeks, her office has said.
Described as a "deeply personal" documentary, Heal will broadcast on the BBC on November 29 before airing internationally. In Australia it will broadcast on Channel 9 on December 1.
"Cancer does change you," Princess Catherine says in the documentary.
Catherine, wife of heir-to-the-throne Prince William, announced in March 2024 that she was receiving treatment for cancer after tests following major abdominal surgery found the disease. She has not disclosed the type of cancer.
After undergoing chemotherapy she revealed she was in remission in January 2025.
The documentary "follows the princess on a personal journey through some of Britain's most spectacular landscapes" as she takes part in one of the UK's best-known endurance events, the Three Peaks Challenge, Kensington Palace said in a statement.
Participants in the challenge, which 44-year-old Catherine completed in June, climb the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours.
"Set against the backdrop of the challenge itself, the princess reflects on her own experience alongside individuals navigating their own health journeys," the statement read.
"Together they explore the profound impact serious illness can have on the whole person and the people, places and experiences that can help us heal."
Catherine's father-in-law, King Charles III, was also diagnosed with cancer , which was revealed by Buckingham Palace on February 5, 2024.
Charles, 78, has returned to public duties but is still being treated for an undisclosed cancer.
All funds generated by the documentary's distribution will go to Britain's Royal Marsden Cancer Charity.

Russian cargo ship Sparta II was damaged in the Baltic Sea. ( Reuters: Finnish Border Guard )
A Russian cargo ship subject to US sanctions has been hit by drones in the Baltic Sea.
Finnish authorities say the attack was likely carried out by Ukraine and the vessel later drifted to Finnish waters.
Authorities in Finland and Estonia worry this is another sign of the war spilling to neighbouring areas.
A Russian cargo ship with links to the military has been hit by drones and caught fire in the Baltic Sea in what Finland said was likely an attack by Ukraine, with the vessel later drifting to Finnish waters.
The 16-member crew of the Sparta II evacuated to lifeboats, then to a nearby Russian ship, and was on its way back to Russia, Finnish Border Guard Commander Ilja Iljin told public broadcaster Yle late on Saturday, local time.
Ukraine has sent waves of military drones towards Russia's north-west Leningrad region this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of the Baltic region, leading to fears that the war was affecting NATO territory.

Finland and Sweden are NATO's newest member states, joining the military alliance in 2023 and 2024, respectively, in response to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

sources.title: Ukraine: Dashcam captures massive explosion on Lviv street | Africanews
sources.text:
Skip to main content Welcome to Africanews Please select your experience Watch Live News
Ukraine: Dashcam captures massive explosion on Lviv street
The footage, recorded by a driver travelling through Lviv on Friday 20 November, shows the moment a projectile struck a building directly ahead of the vehicle. The impact sent debris across the road and forced the driver to reverse sharply before driving away. Two people were killed and at least 10 others injured in Lviv’s Zaliznychnyi district as a large-scale Russian missile and drone barrage tore across the western Ukrainian city and its surrounding region, igniting fires in residential blocks and garages. According to Ukrainian authorities, the bombardment left a trail of destruction spanning homes, vehicles, a dormitory, a warehouse and critical energy infrastructure, while also damaging a ticket terminal at Sknyliv railway station. The fallout extended beyond the city limits into the nearby Zolochiv district, where debris from a downed Russian drone damaged three houses and a vehicle, leaving one further person injured. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia had launched more than 400 attack drones and over 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles, in the wider assault. The strikes also affected Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine, underscoring the scale of the bombardment and the continuing threat to civilians and essential infrastructure.

sources.title: Russian strikes kill 6 in Kyiv region, Ukraine says
sources.text:
URL Source: https://www.scmp.com/news/world/europe/article/3375401/russian-strikes-kill-6-kyiv-region-ukraine-says

Published Time: 2026-11-23T02:32:59+08:00

Markdown Content:
Russian strikes across the Kyiv region, including on a block of flats that partially collapsed, killed at least six people, Ukraine said on Sunday, warning there could be more victims under the rubble.

Russia has been pummelling Ukraine with nightly aerial barrages as the war-torn country braces for another winter of the near-five-year invasion.

An overnight strike on Dymer, around 45km (30 miles) north of the capital, hit a five-storey building.

Agence France-Presse images showed rescuers combing through the mound of smouldering rubble.

“The bodies of three victims have been recovered from the rubble,” Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said on Telegram, adding that the dead included “a woman born in 1978 and a teenager born in 2008”.

On Sunday evening, rescuers managed to pull out a child alive, Kyiv region governor Tymur Tkachenko said on Telegram.

State Emergency Service earlier said they were searching for 11 people, including two children, who were “not responding or cannot be reached”.

![Image 1: Residents watch as firefighters work at the site of a Russian drone strike on a shopping centre in the town of Vyshneve, Kyiv Region, Ukraine on Sunday. Photo: Reuters](https://img.i-scmp.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=contain,width=1024,format=auto/sites/default/files/d8/images/canvas/2026/11/23/c6a2b4c4-1799-4c3d-97fa-9fa23c0af71a_8fbaf409.jpg)

Residents watch as firefighters work at the site of a Russian drone strike on a shopping centre in the town of Vyshneve, Kyiv Region, Ukraine on Sunday. Photo: Reuters

Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets called the attack part of “Russia’s genocidal war against Ukraine”.

“The world must stop looking away. Condemn this terror, hold Russia accountable, and act now to stop the killing of innocent Ukrainians,” he said on social media.

Two other people were killed and eight wounded in Vyshneve when a Russian strike hit a supermarket.

“People had simply gone to the store to buy groceries. An ordinary shopping trip turned into a tragedy due to a Russian attack,” Tkachenko said.

One more person was killed when a strike set a private home ablaze in Bila Tserkva, he added.

Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukraine’s Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said on social media.

Moscow has ramped up strikes on Ukraine – particularly on its energy network – as temperatures begin to drop to around freezing.

Earlier this week, Russian President Vladimir Putin vowed a “painful” response to Ukrainian strikes that damaged the Crimean bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule over the annexed region.

sources.title: Russia starts towing its ship hit by drones in Baltic, Finland says
sources.text:
URL Source: https://www.scmp.com/news/world/russia-central-asia/article/3375406/russia-starts-towing-its-ship-hit-drones-baltic-finland-says

Published Time: 2026-11-23T05:32:37+08:00

Markdown Content:
A Russian rescue vessel on Sunday began towing a Russian-owned cargo ship that was struck by drones in the Baltic Sea out of Finnish waters after two days of firefighting, Finland’s coastguard said.

The Finnish military has said the strike on the Sparta II on Saturday ‌was probably carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters.

The 16 crew members were evacuated onto a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly injured.

“Thermal cameras show that some containers are warm, but the vessel is stable enough for towing to begin,” Finland’s coastguard said in a statement. It said that responsibility for the rescue will transfer to Russia once the ship leaves Finnish waters.

Pictures and video released earlier by the Finnish coastguard showed several vessels spraying the Sparta ⁠II with water cannons during the night in a bid to put out the flames and cool down the containers stacked on its deck.

In a ‌rare instance of cross-border collaboration, out of the seven vessels helping to fight the fire, two were Russian, two were Estonian and the rest were Finnish.

Estonia and Finland are members of Nato and steadfast supporters of ‌Ukraine, and often at odds with Moscow on other issues. Finland shut all of its land border crossings with Russia in ⁠2023. Estonia will shut ⁠its own from December 1, for six months, on security grounds.

The ship, bound for the Russian exclave Kaliningrad, was damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland ‌island, Finland’s Defence Forces have said, corroborating an account by Russian officials.

“Smoke is still coming from the vessel and there is clearly still heat on board,” Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, sea safety officer and commander ‌of ‌the maritime sub-centre Helsinki for the Finnish Border Guard, told a press conference earlier on Sunday.

![Image 1: The Russian cargo ship Sparta II is sprayed with water as the fire continues in the Gulf of Finland on Sunday. Photo: Finnish Border Guard / Handout via Reuters](https://img.i-scmp.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=contain,width=1024,format=auto/sites/default/files/d8/images/canvas/2026/11/23/02000f57-6522-494d-af7d-b5f6d59f2570_7d5042dd.jpg)

The Russian cargo ship Sparta II is sprayed with water as the fire continues in the Gulf of Finland on Sunday. Photo: Finnish Border Guard / Handout via Reuters

Kyiv has sent waves ‌of military drones towards the Leningrad region on Russia’s northwest coast this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading ⁠to fears that the war was spilling onto Nato territory.

The risk of further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of ⁠the Baltic Sea, cannot be ruled out, Estonian Navy Commander Ivo Vark told public broadcaster ERR on Sunday.

Finland’s military said last week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.

The Sparta II ‌is a 121-metre (397-ft) Russian-flagged cargo vessel owned ‌by Russian shipping company Oboronlogistika that left St Petersburg on Friday, according to LSEG data.

Oboronlogistika provides logistics services for the Russian Defence Ministry, according to the company’s website.

The vessel is subject to US sanctions, according to the US Treasury Department.

Lumilahti said one concern was the weather, with rain, sleet, and stronger winds expected on Sunday night and Monday.

sources.title: Bone cancer survivor, 20, on life after two amputations - CNA Lifestyle
sources.text:
She survived bone cancer and two amputations – now this 20-year-old wants to be seen beyond her disability
From strangers pushing her wheelchair without asking to being overlooked in crowds and stared at on the MRT, Chloe Chew has faced struggles few realise. She is now finding confidence and a sense of identity through art and has taken up para-fencing.
Through art and para-fencing, Chloe Chew is finding confidence and a sense of identity while challenging how people see those with disabilities. An illustration student, she designed her wheelchair wheel cover to reflect her experiences getting around Singapore. (Photo: Annie Tan)
Annie Tan 23 Nov 2026 07:19AM Bookmark Bookmark Share WhatsApp Telegram Facebook Threads Email LinkedIn Set CNA as your preferred source on Google Add CNA as a trusted source to help Google better understand and surface our content in search results. Read a summary of this article on FAST. Get bite-sized news via a new cards interface. Give it a try. Click here to return to FAST Tap here to return to FAST FAST At 13, Chloe Chew had her right leg amputated below the knee to remove a cancerous tumour. At an age when other teens were discovering their newfound independence, Chew needed a wheelchair to get around.
Two years later, the cancer returned, and Chew underwent another amputation that removed the rest of her right leg and her right hip bone.
One of the first things Chew noticed was how tall everyone else now looked from her wheelchair. In crowded places, “sometimes, they don’t see me … they don’t look down”.
If people do notice her, they stare. “It feels like I’m under surveillance a lot of times,” she said.
Some even start pushing her wheelchair without asking her. Chew only realises this when she tries to stop her wheelchair, to find that it keeps going.
“They think they are helping, but it is really scary. I have to tell them, ‘Stop, stop, please!’ Then, they just walk off,” she told CNA Women.
Today, Chew is 20. She is a digital illustration and narrative student at Nanyang Academy of Fine Arts (NAFA) and recently took up para-fencing. “I hope people don’t see us as just a wheelchair,” she said.
Chew will be part of the annual Enabling Lives Festival on Nov 28 and 29, 2026, which promotes disability awareness and inclusion through sports, performances and workshops.
The weeks after the Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE) are supposed to be among the most carefree of a child’s life. But in 2017, shortly after completing her exams, Chew noticed a large, painful lump around her right knee.
She was diagnosed with osteosarcoma, an aggressive form of bone cancer.
“It was the first time I had ever seen my dad cry. I cried because I saw (my parents) crying,” she recalled.
At first, doctors told her they could remove the tumour without amputating her leg. However, one or two days before the surgery, doctors told her they had to amputate her leg below the knee.
The teenager did not cry about it. Instead, putting on a brave front, she smiled through it. “I listed the good things: I don’t have to do homework, I won’t need to cut my toenails,” she said.
However, when she woke up and saw what remained of her leg, Chew cried.
Chew was hospitalised for many months and spent the 13th year of her life undergoing chemotherapy.
Throughout this period, her wound did not fully heal and was raw and painful. She underwent at least seven surgeries to close the wound, she said.
Determined to look on the bright side, the young girl focused on the get-well presents she received – lots of sketchbooks, coloured pencils and colouring books. Passionate about drawing, Chew lost herself in art.
When feeling particularly low, she drew herself trapped in a dark room. Sometimes, she drew characters from the animated superhero series Teen Titans.
But most of the time, Chew drew pretty female characters from her imagination.

sources.title: Suspected Ukrainian sea drones struck a Russian warship in Libya, officials say
sources.text:
URL Source: https://www.scmp.com/news/world/africa/article/3375407/suspected-ukrainian-sea-drones-hit-russian-warship-libyan-naval-base-officials-say

Published Time: 2026-11-23T06:46:18+08:00

Markdown Content:
A suspected Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship on Sunday at a naval base in Libya, officials said, the latest attack in the North African nation linked to Russia’s war in Ukraine.

The strike at Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette, and ignited a fire at the facility, two Libyan military officials said.

They said several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya, according to an initial investigation into the attack. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, they said.

The officials, affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya, spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not allowed to talk to reporters.

Libya has been divided since a Nato-backed uprising toppled long-time dictator Muammar Gaddafi, who was later killed, in 2011. A UN-supported government is based in Tripoli and a rival administration is located in the east. The oil-rich nation remains a focal point for a long-running rivalry between Russia and the West.

The eastern Libya-based government said in a statement that the strike on Sunday caused an explosion and fire at the base, which was later extinguished.

The vessel had docked at the base for refuelling and supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said, without providing details on the vessel or its cargo.

A joint investigation was launched with Russia to “uncover the circumstances of the attack, its source, and the party behind it”, the statement said.

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack. There was no immediate comment from either Russia or Ukraine.

![Image 1: Fire burns after an explosion aboard a Russian ship docked at Benghazi port in Libya on Sunday. Photo: Social media via Reuters](https://img.i-scmp.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=contain,width=1024,format=auto/sites/default/files/d8/images/canvas/2026/11/23/37120c18-c31b-4bec-985d-3ae361eff981_d5db4872.jpg)

Fire burns after an explosion aboard a Russian ship docked at Benghazi port in Libya on Sunday. Photo: Social media via Reuters

On Sunday evening, local media said another sea drone hit a commercial vessel off the port of Benghazi in a separate attack. No further details were given. The Almasar satellite television channel said naval and air forces destroyed at least 12 other sea drones off the Mediterranean city.

The western Libya government expressed concerns about “dragging Libyan ports and civilian facilities into external conflicts”, in an apparent reference to the war in Ukraine.

“The government reaffirms its categorical rejection of turning Libya into an arena for international conflicts or a theatre for external powers to settle scores,” it said in a statement.

In March, Ukrainian forces operating in western Libya under a covert deal struck a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean in a suspected sea drone attack near Maltese waters, Libyan officials said at the time.

The Ukrainian forces, most of them drone experts, operated mainly at an airbase in the coastal city of Misrata but also at other military facilities in the capital, Tripoli, and the coastal town of Zawiya, the officials told Associated Press.

Facebook Twitter Print Email Security Council LIVE: Winter attacks on Ukraine's power grid and Black Sea shipping threaten lives and global food supplies 23 November 2026 Peace and Security As winter sets in, the Security Council is holding a high stakes meeting Monday to discuss how Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy grid are leaving civilians without heat, power and water. sources.text: Advertisement By&nbsp Doloresz Katanich Published on 23 November 2026 - 15:14 GMT+1 , Updated 17:59 Share Facebook Twitter Flipboard Send Reddit Linkedin Messenger Telegram VK Bluesky Threads Whatsapp Nvidia shares jumped more than 30% from their Friday close at the start of US trading on Monday after the board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as president, CEO and board member on Monday, effective immediately. The decision comes just eleven days after Huang's resignation. sources.title: Big fines and settlements barely dent cancer drugmakers’ revenues, fail to deter wrongdoing - ICIJ
sources.text: Skip to content T he two girls grew up five blocks apart in Mdantsane township, South Africa, and they were only distant friends until cancer pulled them together many years later. Babalwa Malgas, then 35, had just opened her law office when she learned she had breast cancer. Two years later, her neighbor Tobeka Daki received the same diagnosis. Both were single moms with two boys, and they bonded over their new, shared disease. Malgas said they talked about the “challenges of dating new people — how to explain, whether to disclose prior or not. The common interest of not wanting reconstruction. Fears of leaving our children.” In 2013, Daki’s oncologist told her she needed a mastectomy, chemotherapy and Herceptin, a cancer drug produced by the Swiss company Roche, to improve her chances of survival. But because of the cost, she couldn’t afford the medication. As Malgas explained, the two became “sisters” in a campaign against the high cost of cancer medicines. Their yearslong fight brought together various nonprofit advocacy groups that ramped up pressure on the government and Roche to reform patent laws. They picketed outside Roche’s Johannesburg office, demanding the company drop the price of Herceptin, which by 2016 cost around $36,000 for a year’s supply, about four times South Africa’s average household income. Daki’s cancer eventually spread to her spine, and the 49-year-old health club receptionist died at home in November 2016. Malgas left court early that day to see her friend. “But I was 30 minutes late,” she said. Daki’s death inspired Malgas and other activists to continue pushing for equitable medical treatment and healthcare justice. Their campaign triggered a government probe into alleged excessive pricing of Herceptin. “Our slogan was: My cancer, your profit,” said Malgas, whose own cancer returned in the midst of their campaign. “We learned of greed from Roche.” But she said their struggle went beyond Roche. Babalwa Malgas, left, and Tobeka Daki, right, became “sisters” in a campaign to fight for more affordable access to cancer drugs. Image: Supplied; Treatment Action Campaign For many decades, companies making cancer drugs have exploited ethically dubious practices that have generated great fortunes for shareholders but sometimes priced out patients who desperately need the medicines. Now a review of enforcement actions around the world by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists highlights yet another manifestation of a broken global healthcare system: Some cancer drugmakers face allegations of wrongdoing — again and again — and are not deterred when they have to pay fines or large settlement payments. Further adding to the industry’s generally wretched reputation, cancer drugmakers have sometimes crossed the line with such documented practices as exploiting the patent system to stifle competition, promoting higher dosages than necessary, taking advantage of industry regulatory shortcuts, and breaching criminal or civil statutes. That’s yet another fallout that can affect patients and raise the expenses of taxpayers and healthcare systems. This story is a follow-up to ICIJ’s Cancer Calculus investigation, which documented how Merck & Co. kept the price of its blockbuster cancer drug Keytruda high, straining healthcare systems around the world and delaying cheaper versions of the drug from reaching hundreds of thousands of cancer patients in the coming years. To examine enforcement actions in the cancer drug industry, ICIJ reviewed criminal and civil cases in 31 countries. ICIJ relied on public information and a variety of datasets collated by the nonprofit accountability groups Public Citizen and Good Jobs First, as well as a collection of global anti-competition cases compiled by Brazilian researcher Pedro Gomes Lacerda and Sao Paulo-based lawyer Luiz A. Azevedo de Almeida Hoffmann. Among the highlights of this review, in the past decade, authorities in seven countries have accused Roche of misleading doctors about a cancer medicine and colluding with another drugmaker. The company paid $14 million to settle charges in Romania that it thwarted competition to three cancer drugs, including Herceptin. An antitrust case in Belgium and the South Africa case of alleged excessive pricing are underway. For its part, the drug giant Novartis agreed to pay more than $51 million to the U.S. Justice Department in 2020 to resolve kickback allegations regarding the kidney cancer drug Afinitor and another medicine, and pledged to reform its business practices — the third time it had made that promise. What these companies are doing … they’re basically paying a fee for the license to break the law. — attorney Reuben Guttman And Celgene Corp., now controlled by Bristol Myers Squibb, paid $280 million to U.S. and state governments in 2017 to settle allegations that it had improperly promoted the medicines Revlimid and Thalomid to treat multiple myeloma, a blood cancer, and a range of other cancers beyond the uses then approved by the Food and Drug Administration. That was one of the largest settlements ever related to a cancer drug. It was the first for Celgene, but not for Bristol Myers, which acquired Celgene in 2019. And for Bristol Myers, it wouldn’t be the last. The New Jersey manufacturer paid $55 million in a multi-state settlement of anti-competition charges relating to a cancer drug in 2003; in 2024 it paid $2.7 million to settle anti-competition charges in Israel concerning yet another multiple myeloma drug. “What these companies are doing … they’re basically paying a fee for the license to break the law,” said Reuben Guttman, an attorney for the whistleblower whose disclosures led to the $280 million Revlimid settlement. Bristol Myers did not respond to requests for comment, but its Celgene unit previously denied wrongdoing. sources.title: EU targets Russian ex-soldiers, banks and sports in new sanctions push – POLITICO
sources.text:
BRUSSELS — The EU wants to target former Russian soldiers, banks, crypto platforms and sports teams in its 22nd sanctions package against Moscow since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced on Monday.
“We’re giving Ukraine the strength to secure a peace. And Russia, every reason to choose it,” von der Leyen said in a prerecorded video message launching the package.
The Commission’s proposals will now be negotiated by EU countries, with several diplomats telling POLITICO that they aim to reach an agreement by the end of the year.
One major measure would restrict visas for former Russian soldiers. The EU agreed on a legal framework for the restrictions in its previous sanctions package over the summer but has yet to put them into effect.
“Russian ex-combatants pose a security risk to Europe. They cannot be allowed to wander freely across our countries,” von der Leyen said, citing a recent escalation in covert Russian operations in Europe.
The Commission also wants to add 70 vessels to its sanctions list targeting Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, which Moscow uses to export oil and other commodities.
European companies would also be barred from repairing Russian refineries damaged by Ukrainian drone attacks. EU citizens would no longer be allowed to sit on the boards of Russian companies.
On sports, the Commission is proposing to bar Russian teams and athletes from competing in the bloc, a move that would prevent Russia from returning to next year’s ice hockey world championship in Germany.
“We propose to ban the display of official Russian symbols. We will also restrict financial flows from Russian sponsors to European based sports and cultural associations,” von der Leyen said.
An arbitration court had ruled that the International Ice Hockey Federation lacked sufficient grounds to exclude Russia from the tournament.
Closing sanctions loopholes and cracking down on shadow finance is another focus of the package. The Commission wants to disconnect 60 more banks from international payment systems and target cryptocurrency and payment networks used to circumvent sanctions.
“We will focus on Russia, but also include third countries that help Russia to evade our sanctions,” von der Leyen said.
The EU has previously been cautious about directly targeting third countries, but von der Leyen said the new measures would help “align with international partners.”
The latest proposals follow a difficult year for EU sanctions policy. A previous package was held up for weeks over restrictions on liquefied natural gas shipments, while France delayed the renewal of an existing sanctions framework over a national security dispute, demanding the removal of two Russian billionaires from the sanctions list.
Last week, the Commission announced the creation of a dedicated sanctions office to oversee the design, drafting and coordination of restrictive measures.

sources.title: Government approves US$50-billion Argentina LNG export project | Buenos Aires Times
sources.text:
President Javier Milei's government on Friday approved incentives for a massive liquefied natural gas (LNG) export project involving US$50.75 billion in investment through 2050.
The Argentina LNG project, to be developed by state-owned YPF, Italy's Eni and Emirati company XRG, is the largest investment initiative in the country's history.
It will exploit gas from the Vaca Muerta shale formation in Patagonia. The project is expected to reach a production plateau of 65 million cubic metres of gas per day, equivalent to more than 40 percent of Argentina's current output.
Argentina LNG will allow the country to export 12 million tonnes of LNG annually, alongside natural gas liquids, generating more than US$9 billion in export revenue a year, according to Economy Minister Luis Caputo.
Caputo said US$25 billion would be invested between 2027 and 2030, with total investment reaching US$50.75 billion by 2050.
The project will be incorporated into Milei's flagship RIGI investment incentive scheme for major donors, which was introduced in 2024 to attract large-scale domestic and foreign investment through tax, customs and exchange-rate benefits, alongside guarantees of regulatory stability for 30 years.
Argentina LNG will involve investments in gas production in Vaca Muerta, the construction of a 524-kilometre gas pipeline and a 524-kilometre liquids pipeline to the Atlantic coast of Río Negro Province, where two floating liquefaction units will operate.
Industrial facilities will also be built in Neuquén and Río Negro to process the gas and its liquids.
The project is expected to generate around 20,000 jobs during construction, with employment peaking at 40,000, and another 8,000 direct and indirect jobs once operations begin, Caputo claimed.
YPF chief executive Horacio Marín welcomed the approval, describing it as a major step for what he called the largest private investment in Argentina's history and in Latin America.
The partners are expected to formally sign the agreement on November 30, with the three companies present, Marín said.
"Argentina LNG would not have been possible without the RIGI," he said, praising the government for introducing the investment incentive scheme.
The announcement came amid a sharp sell-off in Argentine bonds, driven by domestic uncertainty and declines in international markets.
The country risk index, compiled by JPMorgan, surpassed 1,000 basis points, reaching its highest level since October 2025. The official dollar exchange rate for smaller-scale transactions also rose during the week to 1,600 pesos, according to Banco Nación.
Analysts cited by Ámbito Financiero said market concerns centred on Argentina's ability to finance debt maturities in 2027 and political uncertainty ahead of next year's presidential election, in which Milei is expected to seek re-election.
The concerns have been compounded by international market declines and the depreciation of the Brazilian real.

sources.text: Homes abandoned, harvests failing: Haiti’s farmers rebuild amid violence, hunger and El Niño | UN News Skip to main content / navigation UN News Global perspective Human stories English Search UN News Global perspective Human stories Search Homes abandoned, harvests failing: Haiti’s farmers rebuild amid violence, hunger and El Niño © UNICEF Farmers in Haiti continue to grow crops despite the challenges they face. Facebook Twitter Print Email Homes abandoned, harvests failing: Haiti’s farmers rebuild amid violence, hunger and El Niño By Daniel Dickinson 21 November 2026 Peace and Security Years of insecurity, violence perpetrated by murderous armed gangs and economic instability, combined with displacement, poor agricultural performance and climate shocks, have left millions of Haitians struggling to meet their food needs. It’s estimated that 6.35 million people, roughly half the population, will not get enough to eat between March and June 2027. Almost two million of them will be at emergency levels, where families have little or nothing to eat and may have to sell the things they depend on for a living just to get food. Combination of shocks A series of overlapping crises are currently shaping food insecurity. More than 1.5 million people have been forced to flee their homes due to the threat of gang violence, and many can no longer work or grow food. © WFP/Sylvain Barral Residents of Cité Soleil, a troubled neighbourhood in the Haitian capital, Port-au-Prince, gather at an aid distribution point. Insecurity is also disrupting farming communities and market supply chains. The El Niño weather phenomenon is now a third threat. It is bringing droughts and floods that are reducing harvests and affecting farmers' ability to prepare for the next planting season. The number of people affected by drought conditions is projected to reach four million by December 2026. What do the farmers say? “Rain isn’t falling,” said Dieula Célestin. “You work the soil, but there is no rain. You plant your crops, and you end up with nothing to harvest.” Délivrance Dovily lost her animals: “Because of the country’s crisis, we struggle just to eat. We used to raise livestock to help pay for school, the animals used to support us. But because of the crisis and diseases that came through, we lost them.” Less food is being grown in Haiti, and ongoing insecurity means it cannot easily be transported to the people who need it most. What is the UN doing? Short term: Keeping people alive. The World Food Programme ( WFP ) provides emergency food and cash to vulnerable families, including those displaced by violence. This year, working alongside the Haitian authorities, it has supported 2.6 million people. Its programmes also include school meals for more than 620,000 students and malnutrition prevention for young children and support to the government for the establishment of a social safety net system. © WFP/Irshad Khan An UNHAS helicopter touches down in the Haitian capital, Port-au-Prince. In the case of extreme weather, such as Hurricane Melissa which struck the south of the country one year ago, pre-positioned stocks can provide rice, beans and cooking oil to up to 300,000 people for one month. The UN Humanitarian Air Service (UNHAS) flies aid workers in and out of the capital Port-au-Prince, and to remote locations across the country, enabling humanitarians to reach the most vulnerable Haitians, wherever they are. The UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization ( FAO ) works alongside WFP during emergencies and has provided support including livestock, such as poultry but also goats in order to help farmers immediately generate cash and food to sustain their own family. “The animals are interesting because we can distribute them at any time. So, we do not have to wait for the planting season and farmers can immediately use them,” said FAO country chief, Pierre Vauthier. © FAO Community members receive livestock to rebuild their livelihoods and support their

sources.title: Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports - BBC News
sources.text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Nato chief Mark Rutte and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz respond to reports of Russian plans to launch nuclear weapons into space By Helen Davidson Published 24 November 2026, 02:15 GMT
Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after German reports that Russia is preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.
Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media. It was not clear which country had authored the reports.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said such reports were "not new, yet they remain no less shocking", and a government spokesman said the reports were being taken "very seriously".
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he had not seen the reports but dismissed stories citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously".
The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign".
Citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, public broadcasters NDR and WDR and newspaper Süddeutscher Zeitung, said the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including important communication and observation satellites.
Asked about the reports, the Nato secretary general told a press conference in Berlin alongside Merz: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element."
The Western defensive alliance had a variety of response options, said Rutte.
"When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary."
Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but said they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue".
German government spokesman Stefan Kornelius warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers".
Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, told the Handeslblatt newspaper that having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario".
Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit.
Bleddyn Bowen, co-director of the Space Research Centre at Durham University, said that exploding a nuclear weapon in space would have "massive infrastructural effects" as there were now more than 15,000 active satellites. But he told the BBC's Today programme that "the effect of these weapons would be extremely indiscriminate and also take out a lot of Russia's own space infrastructure".
Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or plan to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.
In 2024 the US accused Russia of developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead. Russia denied the accusation .
"Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin said at the time.
In September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".

sources.title: Why French pharma firm Sanofi is paying $41 billion for US company Insmed | Euronews
sources.text: Advertisement By&nbsp Quirino Mealha Published on 24 November 2026 - 16:28 GMT+1 , Updated 16:34 Share Facebook Twitter Flipboard Send Reddit Linkedin Messenger Telegram VK Bluesky Threads Whatsapp French drugmaker Sanofi has agreed a $41 billion (€37.4bn) all-cash takeover of Insmed, a US biopharma company. The deal, one of its biggest ever, is meant to refill its pipeline of new medicines before its best-selling drug loses patent protection. French pharmaceutical group Sanofi said on Tuesday it would buy Insmed, a US company specialising in treatments for lung diseases, for $41bn (€37.4bn) in cash. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT The acquisition is one of the largest in Sanofi's history as it aims to strengthen the group's line-up of new medicines before the main US patent on Dupixent, its best-selling drug, expires in 2031. Sanofi will pay $175 for each Insmed share, a premium of around 17% to the New Jersey-based company's share price at Monday's close on the Nasdaq. Sanofi expects the deal to start lifting its adjusted earnings per share by the end of 2028. The takeover is the first major deal for CEO Belén Garijo, whose appointment was announced in February and who took over in May. Her mandate is to bring new treatments to market faster after several setbacks in Sanofi's research. Two lung drugs and more in the works Insmed sells two main drugs. Brinsupri treats bronchiectasis, a long-term condition in which the airways widen and clog with mucus. Arikayce is used to treat adults with mycobacterium avium complex (MAC), which is a bacterial lung infection. Brinsupri brought in $1.1bn (€1bn) between its US launch in August 2025 and 30 September this year, according to a joint statement from the two companies, while Arikayce's sales grew 19% to $434 million (€396m) in 2025. "Together, these medicines represent a significant growth opportunity with combined peak sales potential expected to exceed $10bn [€9.1bn] and to last until the very end of the next decade," Garijo told reporters on a conference call. The US company is also developing TPIP, an inhaled drug being tested against pulmonary hypertension, a type of high blood pressure in the lungs, and fibrotic lung disease. Insmed CEO Will Lewis said the deal would push forward its products already on the market and those in late-stage trials, which together have "multibillion-dollar peak sales potential". Investors welcome the deal Sanofi plans to fund the purchase with cash on hand and borrowing, while keeping room to buy smaller, early-stage businesses. Garijo said the deal should also bring annual cost savings above $500m (€456m). Sanofi shares were 9% higher in Paris on Tuesday afternoon as investors welcomed the deal and bought up the stock throughout the day. The acquisition is possible "without jeopardising the dividend or the debt rating", analysts at the brokerage Jefferies said in a research note. The deal should also "provide greater stability through the Dupixent patent cliff" and give Sanofi time to rebuild its pipeline, according to the note. Dupixent is an anti-inflammatory treatment that generated more than €15bn in sales in 2025 for Sanofi. Oddo BHF, an asset management firm, said the deal showed that Sanofi's new management could take "important strategic decisions" to protect its range of treatments for years to come. The takeover is expected to be completed in the first half of 2027, subject to approval by Insmed shareholders and regulatory clearances in the US and abroad. sources.title: Argentina moves to restrict purchases and contracts involving Chinese tech | Buenos Aires Times
sources.text:
The internal battles within Javier Milei's La Libertad Avanza party, the President's outbursts and viral videos with an electoral slant tend to attract immediate attention. But away from the noise of the daily political agenda, decisions are also being taken that go largely unnoticed by the wider public, despite potentially having far-reaching consequences for the geopolitical landscape and causing major upheaval across entire sectors of the economy.
One such decision was the recently issued Directive 7/2026 by Argentina’s National Cybersecurity Centre (CNC). Behind what appears to be a technical requirement, the order places conditions on purchases made by the national government and threatens to shut Chinese technology suppliers out of the market.
The measure has opened a new front of conflict in recent days with Chinese companies such as Huawei and ZTE, while raising alarm bells across Argentina's telecommunications industry, which is demanding explanations from the largely silent National Communications Authority (ENACOM).
The move began on November 6, when the CNC introduced new security requirements for the supply chains of equipment intended for critical telecommunications infrastructure. The regulation adopts SCS 9001 certification as its benchmark, a standard developed by the Telecommunications Industry Association (TIA), a US private-sector organisation that assesses the security processes of manufacturers and suppliers.
In simple terms, any technology purchase or contract the national government wishes to undertake must involve companies certified under the standard. The TIA refuses to certify companies included on certain US restriction lists, such as the Federal Communications Commission's Covered List or the Commerce Department's Entity List.
Huawei and ZTE , which currently supply technology to Argentine government agencies, appear on the former. By imposing a standard that neither company can meet, the Milei administration has effectively ruled them out of the running.
But Directive 7/2026 goes well beyond government procurement. Article 9 instructs ENACOM to assess the incorporation of these requirements into the approval procedures for telecommunications equipment and the obligations imposed on providers of information and communications technology (ICT) services. Although the measure does not currently apply to the private sector, should the regulator move in that direction, certification could become a condition for operating, importing or incorporating equipment into telecommunications networks.
This is not simply a national security decision. Argentina adheres to ISO standards (International Organization for Standardization), which establish procedures to ensure quality, security and sound process management in companies and organisations.
Had the CNC directive taken these into account alongside SCS 9001, Chinese companies could have continued operating as they do now.
The directive's significance was underlined by the fact that US Ambassador Peter Lamelas welcomed the move in a post on his X account.
"It is encouraging to see Argentina take a firm, technical step to protect its critical telecommunications infrastructure. A free market must not be a blind market: supply chain security and the adoption of international standards provide the certainty that private capital needs to invest for the long term," he wrote.
Back in August, Lamelas pressured Neuquén-based cooperative CALF over its negotiations with Huawei to expand connectivity in Vaca Muerta. Far from observing diplomatic protocol and making little effort to conceal his intention to interfere, the US ambassador warned that if the cooperative went ahead with the Chinese company, the United States could restrict visas for its executives.

DOJ Menu U.S. Department of Justice About The Attorney General
Russian National Pleads Guilty to Evading Economic Sanctions on Russia
Alexander Suvorov, 52, a Russian national formerly residing in Sweden, pleaded guilty today to conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act (ECRA).
As part of his guilty plea, Suvorov admitted that between about March 2022 and April 2023, he led an illicit procurement network responsible for unlawfully exporting U.S. electronic components out of the United States to Russia. One of the procurement network’s main goals was to fraudulently obtain dual-use electronic components — that is, electronic components with both civilian and military applications — from U.S. companies for shipment to Russia. Suvorov’s primary role in the procurement network was to maintain front companies based in Hong Kong, including GS Group Limited, which the procurement network used to order electronic components from U.S. companies in an effort to conceal that the end users of the components were in Russia, and to then transship, via Hong Kong, the components from the U.S. companies to the end users in Russia. Suvorov and his companies also sent multiple wires, totaling more than $70,000 to various U.S. companies to pay for the electronic components. Some of the components unlawfully purchased and exported to Russia by Suvorov and his procurement network can be used in military communication and radar systems, as well as precision location systems.
Sentencing is scheduled for March 29, 2027.
Conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act (ECRA) carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison, a fine of up to $1 million, and three years of supervised release. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.
The FBI and Department of Commerce are investigating the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Rick Belliss for the Northern District of New York and Trial Attorney Garrett Coyle of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section are prosecuting the case.

sources.text: Kremlin declines comment on reports 700,000 Russian soldiers killed in Ukraine war - France 24 Skip to main content Advertising Kremlin declines comment on reports 700,000 Russian soldiers killed in Ukraine war Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Wednesday declined to comment on reports in Russian and international news outlets that around 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the Ukraine war so far. The reports were based on hacked data from Russia's official statistics agency. Peskov said only the defence ministry can disclose figures and told reporters "not to pay attention to any other data". Add France 24 to your favorites on Google to see France 24 content appear first in your search results. Issued on: 25/11/2026 - 16:14 2 min Reading time Share By: FRANCE 24 File photo taken November 4, 2026, of people walking past a St. Petersburg billboard featuring Russian soldiers from World War II and the current Ukraine war reading, "Each era has its own heroes". © Dmitri Lovetsky, AP The Kremlin on Wednesday declined to comment on reports that up to 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in its almost five-year-long offensive on Ukraine . After analysing a trove of hacked data from Russia's official statistics agency, several Russian and international media outlets say Moscow's own data shows that between 470,000 and 700,000 soldiers have been killed in the war. Russia has not given an official death toll among its army since September 2022, when it said almost 6,000 soldiers had been killed in the first six months of fighting – a figure widely seen as a large undercount even at the time. Read more ‘Three times the Soviet-Afghan war’: New data sheds light on scale of Russian deaths in Ukraine Asked about the new reports, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday: "The only entity that can officially disclose casualty figures is the defence ministry of the Russian Federation." "I suggest not to pay attention to any other data," he added. Earlier this month, hackers from two anti-Kremlin groups – the Belarusian Cyberpartisans and pro-Ukrainian outfit Silent Crow – published hundreds of thousands of records they said had been obtained by hacking the database of Russia's federal statistics agency, Rosstat. By analysing the unpublished data on causes of death among Russian citizens over the last five years, several international outlets said the data showed the number of soldiers confirmed killed was close to 500,000. A separate analysis by the banned independent Russian outlets Meduza and Mediazona said after including soldiers classified as "missing" – widely understood to have been killed but not yet registered – the toll could be as high as 700,000. sources.title: Why Russian bombers at South Korea’s doorstep raise stakes for US-led alliances
sources.text:
URL Source: https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/article/3375730/why-russian-bombers-south-koreas-doorstep-raise-stakes-us-led-alliances

Published Time: 2026-11-26T08:00:15+08:00

Markdown Content:
A spate of Russian military flights into airspace considered by [South Korea](https://www.scmp.com/topics/south-korea?module=inline&pgtype=article) to be within its defence zone appears to be aimed at testing the regional US-led security architecture and pressuring Seoul to improve strained ties with Moscow, observers say.

Several Russian warplanes, including a heavy strategic bomber, entered the Korean air defence identification zone (Kadiz) on Tuesday morning and approached close to South Korea’s sovereign airspace, prompting its military to scramble fighter jets.

“The Russian military aircraft approached right up to the edge of our territorial airspace” over Ulleung Island, off South Korea’s eastern coast, Joint Chiefs of Staff spokesman Jang Do-young told reporters.

The aircraft reportedly came within about 24km (15 miles) of Ulleung Island – or seconds away from potentially breaching South Korean airspace.

As South Korea’s F-15K fighter jets were deployed in response, the Russian aircraft veered towards Japan before leaving the zone and flying north. They spent around 20 minutes navigating through the Kadiz.

Jeh Sung-hoon, a professor of Russian studies at Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, said Moscow’s recent military activities in the region should be viewed against the backdrop of escalating tensions between [Russia](https://www.scmp.com/topics/russia?module=inline&pgtype=article) and the West.

Washington’s strategy had traditionally sought to link its Western alliances with its security partnerships in the Indo-Pacific, raising the possibility that confrontation between Russia and Nato could extend beyond Europe, he said.

![Image 1: A Tu-160 bomber taking off from an airfield in Russia in 2021. Several Tu-160s reportedly entered South Korea’s air defence identification zone on Tuesday. Photo: Russian Defence Ministry Press Service/AP](https://img.i-scmp.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=contain,width=1024,format=auto/sites/default/files/d8/images/canvas/2026/11/25/4a3f44d0-6085-4f49-8940-66d95864f2ae_2600545a.jpg)

A Tu-160 bomber taking off from an airfield in Russia in 2021. Several Tu-160s reportedly entered South Korea’s air defence identification zone on Tuesday. Photo: Russian Defence Ministry Press Service/AP

“Russia may now be preparing for the possibility of a confrontation with Nato. If that happens, the security situations in western and eastern Eurasia will inevitably become interconnected.”

Moscow’s increased military activities in East Asia could be testing the readiness of the South Korea-US and US-Japan alliances, Jeh said.

Doo Jin-ho, a military and security expert at Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies, said the Russian flights could be aimed at showing Moscow’s commitment to its military alliance with [North Korea](https://www.scmp.com/topics/north-korea?module=inline&pgtype=article) and pressuring Seoul to take steps towards mending their bilateral ties.

North Korea has reportedly sent thousands of its troops to fight alongside Russia in its war against Ukraine, while both countries have also signed a mutual defence pact.

The Pyongyang-Moscow alliance and South Korea’s support of Western-led sanctions against Russia following its invasion of Ukraine have fuelled tensions between Seoul and Moscow.

Russia could also be exploiting vulnerabilities in South Korea-Japan relations through grey-zone tactics, or coercive actions designed to test an adversary’s response without triggering an outright military confrontation, Doo said.

Previously, Russia deployed several Tu-95MS strategic bombers when entering the Kadiz. In contrast, Russian and South Korean defence reports said Tuesday’s formation included Tu-160 strategic bombers, which surpassed the Tu-95MS in speed, manoeuvrability

sources.title: California warns of flooding as king tides peak over Thanksgiving - BBC News
sources.text:
Figure caption, High king tides threaten California coastline, flood communities By Sareen Habeshian Reporting from Los Angeles Published 26 November 2026, 01:05 GMT
Coastal areas of California are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak in the state during the US Thanksgiving holiday.
Water levels across the US state's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Wednesday and Thursday, according to the National Weather Service (NWS) - breaking records set just last month.
The NWS has warned parts of California could face major coastal flooding, which is likely to be significant in low-lying areas. There have already been some reports of flooding.
Meanwhile, storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia, and eastern parts of the US.
Portions of a pier in northern California came crashing down into the ocean on Wednesday as high tides and strong waves battered the structure, video showed.
Beachgoers have been advised to stay away from the water's edge as large waves could suddenly form. Such waves could be damaging to piers and jetties, and could capsize small vessels, the NWS warned.
Flooding has already been reported in the San Francisco Bay Area.
In San Diego, a high tide of 8 ft 11in was recorded on Wednesday morning local time - potentially breaking the record for highest tide measured in the area, which was just set late last month at 7.98ft.
In Los Angeles, the tide on Wednesday was thought to be as high 8.19 - the record for the city that was set only weeks ago 27 October when parts of the California coast experienced flooding.
Recently set high tide records were also broken in Santa Barbara and La Jolla, according to preliminary data.
King tides are the highest predicted tide of the year and are above the highest water level reached at high tide on an average day.
While they typically occur once or twice a year in most coastal areas, they are happening more frequently in some as sea levels rise. These king tides are being strengthened by the strongest El Niño weather pattern on record.
Image source, Getty Images Storm systems are also expected to impact the US through the Thanksgiving holiday - one affecting the Pacific Northwest and another the eastern part of the country, the US National Weather Service said.
On the east coast, a developing Nor'easter storm is expected to bring heavy rain, strong winds, and coastal flooding.
Major impacts are expected to begin on Wednesday across the southeast, and move northward Wednesday night and on Thursday, the NWS said.
"Those along the eastern seaboard can expect gusty, possibly damaging winds, heavy rain, and major coastal and marine impacts," it added.
The developing storm system could bring about one to four inches rain along America's east coast and a peak of four to six inches in coastal North Carolina.
The US department store chain Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York, which was due to take place on Thursday, until Saturday because of severe weather - the first time this has happened.
The stormy weather on both coasts could disrupt travel for millions of people.
The American Automobile Association (AAA) has predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for Thanksgiving between Tuesday 24 November and Monday 30 November.
Officials have also issued a flood warning along Vancouver's coastline in Canada's most western province of British Columbia.
Residents were urged to take "immediate action to protect life and property", a weather warning from Environment and Climate Change Canada said.
King tides were expected to potentially increase already high water levels there too.

sources.text:
Europe’s top human rights court resumed proceedings against Poland on Wednesday, putting fresh pressure on Prime Minister Donald Tusk to deliver on his promise to restore the independence of the country’s courts.
The European Court of Human Rights said it has around 1,600 cases pending over judicial changes introduced by Poland’s former nationalist Law and Justice government. It suspended proceedings in 2023 to give Warsaw time to restore judicial independence.
Tusk’s promise to restore the rule of law helped unlock billions in frozen EU funding following his return to power in 2023. But his efforts have been hampered by two successive PiS-backed presidents, most recently Karol Nawrocki.
Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek has estimated that compensation payments could exceed €12 million. Speaking by phone Wednesday evening, he said the bill could grow considerably as judges appointed under the disputed system continued to hear cases, creating fresh grounds for compensation claims.
“So we’re facing armageddon,” Żurek said. He blamed PiS for undermining Poland’s judicial system and accused Nawrocki of obstructing efforts to repair it.
The decision comes amid a wider confrontation between Tusk and Nawrocki over Poland’s courts, including the Constitutional Tribunal .
At the heart of the ECHR cases is a 2017 overhaul that gave lawmakers greater control over judicial appointments. Nawrocki vetoed a bill in February aimed at reversing those changes, arguing it would usher in a “new phase of chaos.”
Nawrocki’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The ECHR has already sided with applicants ranging from a distributor of sex-enhancing supplements to former Polish President and Nobel Peace Prize winner Lech Wałęsa.
Wałęsa had won a defamation case against a former associate who accused him of collaborating with the communist secret police, only to see that victory overturned years later by a newly created chamber of Poland’s Supreme Court.
The ECHR awarded him €30,000 in damages in a landmark 2023 ruling that prompted the suspension of similar cases. It twice extended the suspension but let it expire Monday.
Another bill addressing the status of thousands of judges appointed under PiS-era rules has been on Nawrocki’s desk since Nov. 9. Żurek said it would address the ECHR’s main concerns but that he feared another politically motivated veto.

sources.title: US trading partners’ patience wears thin as Trump slaps on new tariffs
sources.text:
URL Source: https://www.scmp.com/news/us/economy-trade-business/article/3375819/us-trading-partners-patience-wears-thin-trump-slaps-new-tariffs

Published Time: 2026-11-26T07:30:23+08:00

Markdown Content:
Major US trading partners and companies on the economic front lines decried US President [Donald Trump’s](https://www.scmp.com/topics/donald-trump?pgtype=search?module=inline&pgtype=article) latest tariff salvo on Wednesday, even as they expressed resignation, as his playbook has become more predictable and better telegraphed with repeated use.

The new levies, subject to a public comment period, would lift total duties on targeted economies from 15 to 20 per cent. This comes as the transactional US president looks for alternatives after the [US Supreme Court](https://www.scmp.com/topics/us-supreme-court?pgtype=search?module=inline&pgtype=article) struck down his broad-based “emergency” tariffs in February.

“Partners have been waiting for this shoe to drop for some time,” said [Wendy Cutler](https://www.scmp.com/topics/wendy-cutler?pgtype=search?module=inline&pgtype=article), senior vice-president with the Asia Society Policy Institute. “Many have publicly and privately pushed back in recent months, stressing that they are being wrongly accused of producing too much in selected sectors.”

The latest tariff announcement tied to excess industrial capacity follows other levies outlined in July tied to forced labour.

[Video 13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ety4HXIu8jo)

01:16

US slaps new tariffs ranging from 10-12.5% on 60 economies

This steady drumbeat of trade barriers will only increase incentives among economies worldwide to shift their supply chains away from US shores. “Make no mistake. These tariffs will continue to accelerate diversification efforts,” added Cutler, a former senior US trade negotiator.

Trading partners from Beijing to Brussels expressed their displeasure on Wednesday even as they pushed back on the overproduction rationale.

“Tariff wars and trade wars serve no one’s interests,” said Chinese foreign ministry spokesman [Guo Jiakun](https://www.scmp.com/topics/guo-jiakun?pgtype=search?module=inline&pgtype=article). “The so-called issue of overcapacity is a false proposition, and China opposes using it as a pretext for political manipulation.”

“India does not have structural excess capacity in any sector,” the country’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry said, while Bernd Lange, head of the European Union Parliament’s trade committee, called such charges “absurd”.

“If Washington breaches its commitments, the EU must act swiftly,” Lange added. “It has the legal means to do so.”

[South Korea](https://www.scmp.com/topics/south-korea?pgtype=search?module=inline&pgtype=article), like many countries, said it was studying Wednesday’s [US Trade Representative](https://www.scmp.com/topics/us-trade-representative?pgtype=search?module=inline&pgtype=article) announcement, adding in a statement that an ultimate rate of 15 per cent would be a “good outcome”, while noting that Washington has left open the possibility of raising it to 25 per cent “depending on the outcome of future consultations”.

The tone from many countries after the announcement was relatively muted, however, analysts said. The Supreme Court slapdown of his use of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act has blunted his ability to apply punitive trade measures at will, they said.

sources.title: Jolie and Pitt settle French winery fight a decade after bitter split
sources.text:
URL Source: https://www.scmp.com/news/world/united-states-canada/article/3375827/jolie-and-pitt-settle-french-winery-fight-decade-after-bitter-split

Published Time: 2026-11-26T09:56:41+08:00

Markdown Content:
The long-running legal battles between Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt have come to an end a decade after the A-list celebrity couple split, with the actors settling a dispute over the ownership of a French winery.

The actors said in a joint statement Wednesday that they had reached a settlement of the lawsuit, which transcended business matters when a legal filing from Jolie surfaced abuse allegations against Pitt.

“We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further,” the statement provided by representatives for Pitt, 62, and Jolie, 51, said.

Jolie filed for divorce in 2016, citing the “health of the family”, after a private jet flight from Europe. The couple’s use of private judges – an increasingly common move among splitting celebrities in recent years – kept the details of the divorce largely under wraps, even after it was settled at the very end of 2024. But the winery lawsuit became a way for details of their dispute to become public.

Pitt sued Jolie in 2022, saying she had abandoned an agreement that he would buy her half of Chateau Miraval, a French winery they owned together. She instead sold her part to the Tenute del Mondo wine group. Pitt said it was a “vindictive” and “unlawful” move that should not have been made without his consent and ruined a private space that had been a second home.

The descriptions of the abuse alleged on the private flight were not public until Jolie filed a cross-complaint in the dispute. Jolie and her lawyers said Pitt had demanded she sign a wide-ranging nondisclosure agreement about him as part of the proposed deal that was an attempt to cover up his abuse of her and the children.

![Image 1: Brad Pitt at the premiere for ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ in Los Angeles. Photo: Reuters](https://img.i-scmp.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=contain,width=1024,format=auto/sites/default/files/d8/images/canvas/2026/11/26/ce7fe16e-c2ce-4d8c-8e33-cf87a6194a45_f1a6096d.jpg)

Brad Pitt at the premiere for ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ in Los Angeles. Photo: Reuters

The FBI and child services officials had investigated Pitt’s actions on the flight, centring on the treatment of their eldest son. The FBI released a statement in late 2016 saying it would not investigate further, and the US attorney did not bring charges.

Pitt has denied being abusive but did not defend his behaviour on the flight. Pitt said in a 2017 interview with GQ that he had a drinking problem at the time, but had since become sober and was going to therapy. In an interview with Esquire earlier this year, he said he was sober for seven years but had started drinking again “in a more restrained manner”.

A heavily redacted FBI report obtained by Associated Press in 2022 said an agent provided a probable cause statement to prosecutors on Pitt, but that after discussing the merits, “it was agreed by all parties that criminal charges would not be pursued”. The document said Jolie was “personally conflicted” about supporting charges, and in a later court filing she said she opted not to push for them for the sake of the family.

All six children are now adults; the youngest – twins Knox and Vivienne – turned 18 in July. Many of the Jolie-Pitt children have reportedly since dropped their father’s surname.

Publicly, both Pitt and Jolie have been extremely tight-lipped on everything surrounding their split, despite robust promotional tours for various projects – including the Pitt-starring _The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth_.
